title: A Cross-Cell-Type Atlas of Biomolecular Condensate Material States and Their Emergent Regulation of Gene Expression Noise
abstract: Biomolecular condensates exhibit emergent material properties, including viscosity and multiphase organization, which remain unpredictable from individual molecular components. This study investigates the hypothesis that the condensate material state functions as a mesoscale variable that systematically modulates transcriptional bursting and gene expression noise. The research integrates diverse datasets, including protein disorder features, imaging repositories, and single-cell transcriptomic measurements, to characterize condensate morphology and dynamics. A unified latent-variable model will map sequence grammars and imaging-derived features onto a low-dimensional material state manifold. Hierarchical Bayesian modeling will subsequently link this manifold to transcriptional outcomes, while causal discovery identifies regulators of phase behavior. Expected outcomes include the identification of conserved condensate classes, the determination of sequence motifs governing liquid-to-gel transitions, and the correlation of mesoscale states with gene expression variability. This interdisciplinary project establishes an open-access atlas, providing a reproducible framework for linking condensate material properties to emergent gene regulatory phenotypes.
background_and_significance: Biomolecular condensates organize cellular biochemistry through mesoscale assemblies, exhibiting emergent properties like viscoelasticity and percolation that arise from collective protein and RNA interactions. While public databases catalog condensate components and imaging repositories document their morphology, current research often treats these structures as categorical entities rather than dynamic material states. This project addresses the critical gap between descriptive condensate catalogs and quantitative models of their functional consequences, specifically regarding gene expression noise. By integrating disparate data—including protein disorder annotations, puncta morphology from imaging archives, and single-cell transcriptomic variability—this study will investigate how condensate material states influence transcriptional bursting. It is expected that transitions between liquid and gel-like states modulate reaction kinetics and promoter accessibility, thereby buffering or amplifying cellular noise. This synthesis will establish a cross-cell-type atlas, providing a framework to link mesoscale physical properties to phenotypic outcomes, ultimately transforming fragmented observations into a predictive theory of condensate-mediated gene regulation.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates whether condensate material state functions as a latent mesoscale variable, emerging from collective molecular interactions to influence downstream gene regulatory phenotypes. The study posits that transcriptional bursting and gene expression noise represent emergent cellular outcomes that integrate diverse molecular events. Four research questions will be addressed using existing public data to test hypotheses regarding condensate behavior. First, condensate states may form a low-dimensional manifold, capturing continuous variation from liquid-like to gel-like phases across cell types. Second, specific sequence grammars, including sticker-spacer architectures and charge patterning, are expected to predict these material transitions. Third, condensate states may systematically tune transcriptional bursting parameters, where liquid-like states potentially buffer noise while arrested states amplify variability. Finally, causal regulators, such as kinases and chaperones, will be identified as drivers that shift condensate states and modulate gene expression. These analyses will provide mechanistic insights into how mesoscale material properties propagate to influence cellular gene expression variability.
methods_and_approach:
This project aims to construct an integrated, cross-modal atlas linking condensate composition, mesoscale imaging dynamics, and single-cell transcriptional variability. By synthesizing heterogeneous data from public repositories, including PhaSepDB, the Human Protein Atlas, and the Human Cell Atlas, the study will infer a shared latent “material state manifold.” This framework will facilitate the investigation of putative causal relationships between condensate physical properties and gene expression noise.

Methodologically, the project will harmonize protein identifiers and cell-type ontologies to enable multi-view representation learning. Sequence-derived grammar features and imaging-based morphology metrics will be integrated into a low-dimensional embedding, which will be validated against known condensate markers and FRAP-derived dynamics. Hierarchical association models and causal discovery algorithms will then be applied to evaluate how manifold positions predict transcriptional bursting and perturbation signatures. All analyses rely exclusively on existing public datasets, ensuring a robust, reproducible computational approach to understanding the biophysical regulation of gene expression noise across diverse cellular contexts.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project will develop a comprehensive atlas of condensate material states, integrating protein-level features, imaging metrics, and gene expression data to assign probabilistic coordinates to condensate-associated proteins. A reusable computational toolkit will be released to standardize puncta segmentation and feature extraction across public datasets. Hierarchical statistical models will be employed to quantify the association between these mesoscale material states and transcriptional variability, including bursting parameters. By synthesizing LINCS and DepMap data, the study will generate ranked lists of regulatory nodes predicted to influence condensate states and gene expression programs. Furthermore, the project will establish community benchmarks and controlled vocabularies to facilitate future methodological development. This synthesis aims to transition condensate biology from qualitative descriptions to a quantitative, predictive framework. By linking mesoscale organization to emergent cellular phenotypes, the research provides a durable resource for investigating transcriptional heterogeneity in disease contexts, while fostering cross-domain training in reproducible bioimage analysis and multi-modal data integration.
budget_and_resources: This synthesis-only project prioritizes personnel, computational resources, and collaborative activities, excluding costs for experimental reagents or sample collection. Two postdoctoral researchers will develop robust pipelines for bioimage segmentation and statistical genomics, ensuring validated data integration across public archives. A dedicated research software engineer will implement production-grade workflow automation, containerization, and reproducible data releases to support community-scale synthesis. Graduate trainees will contribute to exploratory analyses, including manifold learning and causal discovery, while faculty provide essential cross-disciplinary supervision. Computational allocations are required for GPU-intensive image processing and memory-intensive Bayesian model fitting, alongside storage for derived feature matrices. Budgetary provisions for NCEMS-centered working groups and hybrid training workshops will facilitate multidisciplinary integration and workforce development. Finally, resources are allocated for open science infrastructure, including persistent identifiers and metadata curation, to ensure long-term data sustainability. This budget structure is expected to harmonize heterogeneous datasets, validate computational methods, and maintain reproducible infrastructure beyond the capacity of individual laboratories.

title: Predicting Organelle Contact Site Morphologies Through Integrated Cryo-ET, Proteomics, and Lipidomics Analysis of Membrane Curvature Codes
abstract: Membrane contact sites (MCS) represent mesoscale structures where collective organization of tethers, scaffolds, and lipids facilitates lipid exchange and signaling. This project integrates public datasets, including cryo-electron tomography, proximity labeling, organelle-resolved lipidomics, protein structures, and genetic perturbation phenotypes, to characterize these interfaces. A multiscale inference framework will be developed to predict mesoscale morphology from molecular components by extracting quantitative geometry from cryo-ET data and mapping compositional data to biophysical parameters. Graph neural networks will subsequently integrate tether interaction graphs and lipid features to identify generalized curvature codes across diverse organisms. Expected outcomes include a quantitative taxonomy of MCS morphotypes, predictive rules linking molecular composition to emergent geometry, and identification of minimal component sets sufficient for specific morphologies. This transdisciplinary effort will establish open-source pipelines and models to facilitate community-scale predictive cell biology, ultimately clarifying why certain contact sites maintain robustness while others undergo state transitions under perturbation.
background_and_significance: Membrane contact sites (MCS) function as mesoscale platforms coordinating lipid transfer, ion exchange, and organelle dynamics. While individual tethers and scaffolds are well-characterized, the relationship between molecular composition and emergent mesoscale morphology remains poorly understood. Current research is hindered by fragmented data across diverse imaging, proteomic, and lipidomic repositories, preventing the synthesis of predictive models. This project aims to integrate cryo-electron tomography, proximity labeling, and structural databases to establish a unified, quantitative taxonomy of MCS morphotypes. By standardizing geometric measurements and compositional datasets, the study will investigate how tether architecture and lipid species dictate membrane curvature and gap width. These parameters are expected to reveal the biophysical rules governing organelle organization and functional specificity. Ultimately, this collaborative framework will provide open-access pipelines to transform heterogeneous data into predictive models of MCS emergence. This approach may clarify how collective molecular interactions maintain cellular homeostasis and facilitate the rapid exchange of metabolites across organelle interfaces.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how molecular composition and interaction architecture generate emergent mesoscale morphology at membrane contact sites (MCS). The study posits that contact morphology is an emergent state determined by tether geometry, lipid mechanical properties, and mesoscale crowding. Using publicly available datasets, this research addresses five core questions. First, it seeks to define a minimal set of geometric descriptors to cluster MCS into reproducible morphotypes across cryo-ET studies. Second, it examines whether lipid mechanical signatures, such as sterol fraction and acyl-chain unsaturation, predict emergent curvature and gap width. Third, it evaluates how tether length, flexibility, and oligomerization constrain these geometric parameters. Fourth, it employs graph neural networks to integrate molecular and interaction data to predict morphotypes across diverse organisms. Finally, the study explores whether degenerate molecular compositions converge on universal physical codes that ensure morphological robustness. These analyses aim to elucidate how ensembles of tethers and lipids encode predictable, generalizable properties at membrane interfaces.
methods_and_approach:
This three-year project will integrate five public data modalities—cryo-ET geometry, proximity proteomics, organelle lipidomics, structural interactions, and genetic phenotypes—into a unified multiscale inference framework for predicting membrane contact site (MCS) morphology. The study aims to harmonize heterogeneous datasets into interoperable contact instances, mapping molecular composition to mesoscale geometry. Data sources include EMPIAR and EMDB for cryo-ET, PRIDE for proteomics, Metabolomics Workbench for lipidomics, and PDB/AlphaFold for structural data.

A contact-centric metadata schema will be developed to normalize identifiers and batch effects across species. Geometry extraction will utilize existing public segmentations to compute gap width, membrane curvature, and contact extent. Molecular data will be translated into physical proxies, such as spontaneous curvature and protein crowding. Integrative modeling will employ hierarchical Bayesian frameworks and multimodal graph neural networks to identify curvature-associated features. Validation will be conducted in silico through cross-study, cross-contact, and cross-species testing. The final output will provide a curated morphotype atlas, a feature database, and a validated model zoo.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project will establish a comprehensive framework for analyzing membrane contact site (MCS) morphotypes by synthesizing cryo-ET data, proteomics, lipidomics, and structural databases. A quantitative MCS Morphotype Atlas will provide standardized geometric descriptors, while an integrated multimodal database will harmonize molecular features to support community-wide analyses. Open-source pipelines and a benchmarking suite will facilitate geometry extraction and model evaluation, enabling the development of predictive "curvature code" models. These models are expected to map molecular compositions to mesoscale morphologies, offering insights into the physical principles governing contact site stability and degeneracy. By integrating perturbation phenotypes, the study aims to distinguish between essential and regulatable contact architectures. This research will advance the understanding of emergent mesoscale phenomena, providing a reusable blueprint for structural biology. Ultimately, the project will deliver durable, open-access infrastructure, including versioned datasets and containerized workflows, to accelerate hypothesis generation and foster cross-disciplinary training in computational cell biology and machine learning.
budget_and_resources: This two-year working group project focuses on community-scale data synthesis, integration, and training, requiring technical capacity beyond individual laboratory capabilities. The budget supports the reuse of public repositories, including EMPIAR, PRIDE, and PDB, to create reproducible resources. Personnel requirements include two computational postdoctoral researchers for cryo-ET morphometrics and multimodal machine learning, one graduate student for biophysical data integration, and a research software engineer to ensure workflow reproducibility through containerization. PI oversight will facilitate cross-disciplinary coordination. Computing resources, including cloud credits and secure storage, are essential for processing large, heterogeneous datasets and training machine learning models. Travel funds will support biannual in-person meetings to harmonize quality control standards and facilitate dissemination at scientific conferences. Furthermore, the budget covers two open workshops and infrastructure for persistent data archiving. This synthesis-only proposal prioritizes curation, benchmarking, and community engagement, with no funding allocated for wet-lab experiments, ensuring alignment with established institutional training and open science objectives.

title: Mesoscale Cytoskeletal Percolation: Synthesis of Actin and Microtubule Network Architecture and Emergent Intracellular Transport Efficiency
abstract: Intracellular transport is hypothesized to emerge from the collective mesoscale organization of actin and microtubule networks rather than individual molecular components. This study investigates percolation-like connectivity and anisotropy within composite cytoskeletal networks, which are expected to govern cargo routing and transport robustness. Public datasets, including super-resolution imaging, single-particle tracking, proteomics, and transcriptomics, will be integrated to reconstruct mesoscale network graphs. Computational pipelines will extract filament orientation, junction density, and graph-theoretic descriptors to correlate network architecture with transport metrics. A physics-informed machine learning emulator will be developed to predict transport efficiency across diverse datasets. The project tests whether cells occupy constrained regions of a universal phase diagram, where transitions between network states dictate emergent transport behavior. These findings may clarify how mesoscale architecture buffers perturbations and maintains long-range transport. This interdisciplinary effort aims to deliver open-source tools and a comprehensive atlas linking cytoskeletal states to transport phenotypes.
background_and_significance: Intracellular transport efficiency is determined by mesoscale cytoskeletal organization, including filament spacing, branching, and alignment, rather than single-molecule parameters alone. These structural features constrain cargo trajectories, potentially shifting dynamics between free diffusion and jammed states. Statistical physics, specifically percolation theory, suggests that cytoskeletal connectivity may undergo phase transitions that dictate long-range transport capacity. Although public repositories contain extensive super-resolution imaging, single-particle tracking, and omics data, these resources remain fragmented. Current research lacks a standardized framework to link molecular regulators to mesoscale architecture and emergent transport phenotypes. This project will integrate heterogeneous datasets to derive consistent network descriptors and map regulatory programs to structural states. By synthesizing these data, the study aims to construct a predictive phase diagram of intracellular logistics. Such a framework may clarify the mechanistic basis of trafficking defects in diseases like neurodegeneration, providing a comprehensive understanding of how cells maintain robust transport despite environmental perturbations and molecular noise.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates the mesoscale phenomena of percolation-like connectivity and anisotropy within composite actin–microtubule networks to determine their influence on intracellular transport efficiency. Utilizing publicly available datasets, the study addresses five core research questions. First, it examines whether cytoskeletal organization occupies constrained, low-dimensional manifolds across diverse cell types. Second, it explores whether percolation thresholds in network connectivity induce nonlinear transitions in transport regimes. Third, the project analyzes how the interplay between anisotropy and connectivity governs routing, congestion, and system robustness. Fourth, it evaluates whether molecular regulator modules predict specific trajectories within the mesoscale phase space. Finally, a physics-informed emulator will be developed to predict transport metrics from mesoscale descriptors across independent datasets. By synthesizing existing imaging and tracking data, this research aims to establish mechanistic links between emergent network organization and transport behavior. These findings are expected to provide generalizable insights into the fundamental principles governing intracellular dynamics and cytoskeletal architecture.
methods_and_approach:
This project will conduct a community-scale synthesis integrating five public data modalities—super-resolution imaging, live-cell tracking, proteomics, single-cell transcriptomics, and perturbation screens—into a unified mesoscale “network-to-transport” atlas. The study aims to develop a reproducible pipeline that converts heterogeneous cytoskeletal images into comparable network graphs, linking these descriptors to transport phenotypes via meta-analytic alignment and physics-informed machine learning. No new experimental data will be generated.

Data will be harvested from public repositories, including the BioImage Archive, IDR, PRIDE, and the Human Cell Atlas. Metadata will be normalized using controlled vocabularies, and images will be standardized to OME-NGFF formats. The reconstruction pipeline will extract mesoscale graph representations, quantifying filament connectivity, orientation, and anisotropy. Transport metrics, such as mean squared displacement and velocity distributions, will be derived from standardized trajectory data. Finally, a hierarchical Bayesian framework and physics-informed neural networks will be employed to model the relationship between cytoskeletal architecture and intracellular transport, providing a comprehensive, validated atlas of cellular organization.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project establishes a comprehensive framework for analyzing cytoskeletal organization and intracellular transport. A curated, citation-ready benchmark collection will aggregate public imaging and omics datasets, providing standardized metadata and quality-controlled train/test splits. Derived mesoscale descriptors, including filament connectivity and anisotropy metrics, will be released as modality-harmonized graph representations. These data will inform a phase-diagram atlas, mapping conserved network states and transitional boundaries across diverse cell types. A validated network-to-transport emulator will predict transport phenotypes from these descriptors, offering a tool for hypothesis generation. Furthermore, the integration of proteomics and transcriptomics will identify regulatory modules associated with specific network architectures and transport efficiencies. By bridging molecular composition with mesoscale logistics, this study aims to characterize emergent phenomena through a phase-transition lens. The resulting benchmarks, atlas, and predictive tools will be disseminated via open-access repositories and interactive portals, ensuring long-term sustainability and facilitating community-wide research into filamentous systems and cellular mechanics.
budget_and_resources: This project focuses on a synthesis-only, community-scale integration effort, prioritizing personnel, computing resources, and collaborative events over experimental data generation. Personnel funding supports two postdoctoral researchers for bioimage informatics and computational modeling, a full-time research software engineer for pipeline development, and a part-time graduate student for trajectory analytics. Faculty effort ensures scientific oversight and multidisciplinary coordination. Computing resources are allocated for large-scale image preprocessing, graph feature computation, and training network-to-transport emulators, alongside versioned storage for derived artifacts. Collaboration is facilitated through NCEMS-hosted working group meetings and annual hackathons, which provide training on OME-Zarr standards and community-driven benchmarks. Open science infrastructure costs cover persistent archiving, DOI-backed releases, and documentation to ensure long-term accessibility. This budget structure directly supports the integration of heterogeneous public datasets, the development of physics-informed machine learning strategies, and the creation of reproducible tools, thereby amplifying the project’s impact on the broader scientific community through sustained, dedicated technical effort.

title: Integration of Hi-C, Super-Resolution Imaging, and Epigenomics for Explaining Cell-Type-Specific Gene Regulation via Chromatin Nanodomain Topology
abstract: Chromatin forms mesoscale nanodomains (50–300 nm) that facilitate emergent regulatory behaviors, including enhancer–promoter communication and transcriptional bursting, which remain difficult to predict from individual nucleosome modifications. This project integrates 3D genome conformation and imaging data to investigate whether a limited set of mesoscale topological motifs explains cell-type-specific gene regulation across mammals. The study synthesizes public datasets, including Hi-C, Micro-C, super-resolution DNA FISH, epigenomic marks, and transcriptional outputs, alongside structural constraints from polymer models. A joint inference framework will be developed to map contact matrices to physical 3D geometries, utilizing multi-resolution community detection and unsupervised representation learning to identify recurrent folding patterns. The hypothesis suggests that chromatin nanodomain topology comprises a conserved motif dictionary, where developmental transitions involve motif switching and disease-associated variants disrupt these structures. Expected outcomes include a cross-cell-type atlas of nanodomain motifs and quantitative models linking motif composition to transcriptional variability, supported by collaborative, open-science practices.
background_and_significance: Chromatin organization at the mesoscale, ranging from 50 to 300 nm, emerges from complex molecular interactions that dictate gene regulation through probabilistic enhancer–promoter communication and transcriptional bursting. While chromosome conformation capture, super-resolution imaging, and epigenomic profiling have generated extensive public datasets, a unified quantitative mapping between contact-based representations and physical domain geometries remains elusive. Current research often focuses on isolated features, failing to capture how combinations of mesoscale structures, such as clustered loops or microcompartments, influence regulatory outcomes. This project aims to synthesize heterogeneous data from repositories like the 4DN Data Portal and ENCODE to identify a generalized vocabulary of topological motifs. By using imaging-derived distance distributions to constrain contact-based polymer models, the study will characterize how these motifs correlate with chromatin states and transcriptional phenotypes. This integrative approach is expected to elucidate how collective folding patterns drive cell-type-specific gene expression, providing a framework for understanding chromatin architecture across diverse mammalian developmental and disease contexts.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates whether mesoscale chromatin nanodomains organize into recurrent topological motifs that generate cell-type-specific regulatory behaviors. The study focuses on the 50–300 nm scale, where collective folding is expected to tune enhancer–promoter communication and transcriptional bursting. It is hypothesized that a minimal dictionary of conserved motifs, such as rosettes or microcompartments, recurs across mammalian tissues. These motifs will be identified through joint embeddings of contact-map and imaging data, with stability assessed via cross-study replication. Furthermore, the research examines whether motif composition predicts transcriptional variability more effectively than individual molecular marks. By integrating contact frequencies with imaging distance distributions, the study aims to resolve geometric degeneracies and produce constrained 3D conformational ensembles. Finally, the project evaluates whether developmental transitions and disease-associated variants are mediated by shifts between these mesoscale motifs. These hypotheses will be tested through rigorous synthesis of existing public datasets, providing mechanistic insights into how chromatin topology influences emergent regulatory outcomes.
methods_and_approach:
This project integrates orthogonal public data to infer mesoscale chromatin nanodomain motifs and link them to regulatory phenotypes. By synthesizing data from the 4D Nucleome, ENCODE, GEO, and BioImage Archive, the study will establish harmonized pipelines to extract nanodomain features from Hi-C and Micro-C maps, alongside geometric constraints from super-resolution DNA FISH. These data will be aligned with epigenomic annotations and transcriptional outputs to infer a comprehensive motif dictionary and motif–phenotype relationships.

The methodology involves standardizing genome builds and cell-type ontologies to facilitate cross-modality integration. Computational efforts will focus on multi-resolution community detection in contact graphs and Bayesian calibration of polymer models using imaging-derived spatial distributions. Unsupervised representation learning will identify discrete motif classes, which will subsequently be linked to gene expression and variant enrichment through hierarchical Bayesian modeling. Validation will rely on cross-dataset replication and held-out prediction tasks. This transdisciplinary synthesis aims to provide a standardized atlas of chromatin nanodomain motifs and their associated regulatory functions.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project establishes a comprehensive atlas of chromatin nanodomain motifs across mammalian cell types, providing a versioned resource of genome-wide occupancy tracks and uncertainty estimates. A modular open-source toolkit will be developed to facilitate joint inference of chromatin contacts and imaging-derived geometric constraints, enabling the calibration of polymer-based reconstructions. Statistical models will link these motif compositions to emergent regulatory phenotypes, including gene expression dispersion and lineage-associated stability. Furthermore, the study will quantify the enrichment of noncoding variants within specific motif classes to provide a mesoscale framework for interpreting genomic variation. By integrating imaging geometry with contact maps, this research aims to clarify the physical nature of nanodomains and their role in transcriptional regulation. These resources are expected to provide an interpretable state space for chromatin organization, offering a unifying language for multimodal genomic data. Ultimately, this framework will support mechanistic investigations into how mesoscale topology influences cellular identity and regulatory responsiveness.
budget_and_resources: This project facilitates a community-scale synthesis requiring extensive coordination, shared computational infrastructure, and dedicated personnel for data engineering, multimodal modeling, and open-science productization. Funding is requested to support a distributed working group across multiple disciplines, excluding experimental data generation. Personnel requirements include two postdoctoral researchers for 3D genomics and quantitative modeling, a research software engineer for workflow automation, and a graduate student for imaging-derived feature extraction. Supplemental trainee support ensures broad participation during working group sprints. Computational resources, including cloud credits and secure storage, are necessary for processing large matrices, executing polymer simulations, and training representation learning models. Annual in-person meetings and targeted conference travel will foster transdisciplinary integration and disseminate project outcomes. Furthermore, a capstone workshop and virtual tutorials are planned to train a data-savvy workforce. Finally, open-science infrastructure, including Zenodo releases and web-hosted documentation, will ensure that the resulting atlas and analytical tools remain discoverable, reproducible, and accessible to the broader scientific community.

title: Protein Crowding as an Emergent Mesoscale Regulator of Cytoplasmic Viscosity, Diffusion, and Reaction Rates
abstract: Cells exhibit emergent mesoscale physical properties, including effective viscosity and anomalous diffusion, which arise from collective protein and RNA concentrations at the 10–1000 nm scale. These properties influence signaling and metabolism but remain unpredictable from individual macromolecular characteristics. This study investigates whether crowding-related parameters can be predicted from proteome composition and subcellular organization across diverse organisms and conditions. The research integrates quantitative proteomics, spatial localization maps, and biophysical measurements of diffusion and viscosity derived from public repositories. By combining spatial proteomics with structural data, the project constructs mesoscale crowding fields to estimate excluded volume and interaction potentials. Bayesian calibration and machine learning models will then predict diffusion regimes based on local proteome composition. This work aims to identify conserved crowding setpoints and determine how specific protein classes regulate emergent viscosity. Ultimately, the study provides a cross-species map linking proteome composition to physical states, facilitating a mechanistic reinterpretation of cellular phenotypes.
background_and_significance: Mesoscale cell biology represents the regime where molecular composition transitions into collective material states, characterized by emergent properties such as viscoelasticity and anomalous diffusion. While these physical states influence reaction kinetics and signaling, predicting them from individual molecular properties remains a fundamental challenge. Current research indicates that intracellular diffusion frequently deviates from Brownian motion, yet quantitative links between proteome composition and transport dynamics remain largely system-specific. Although vast repositories of proteomics, structural, and imaging data exist, these resources are currently fragmented, hindering the development of predictive models. This project will synthesize these disparate datasets into a unified framework to characterize how mesoscale crowding emerges from proteome organization. By integrating structural annotations, spatial localization, and transport measurements, the study aims to establish predictive tools for inferring effective viscosity landscapes. This approach will clarify whether cells maintain conserved crowding setpoints, ultimately reframing intracellular transport as a regulated outcome of proteome architecture and collective physical state.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates whether emergent mesoscale transport properties, including effective viscosity and anomalous diffusion, can be predicted from compartment-specific proteome composition using existing public data. The study evaluates whether conserved crowding setpoints exist across diverse eukaryotes, hypothesizing that inferred crowding metrics remain within narrow ranges despite variations in total protein concentration. Research will utilize diffusion, FRAP, and FCS datasets alongside proteomic databases to test if transport parameters cluster by compartment rather than species. Furthermore, the project examines which proteome features, such as intrinsic disorder and assembly size, disproportionately influence mesoscale outcomes. Models incorporating these compositional proxies are expected to outperform those based solely on total protein concentration. Additionally, the study explores whether condition-dependent shifts in diffusion landscapes can be inferred from omics data, focusing on proteome mass reallocation and metabolite profiles. Finally, the research assesses whether spatial proteomics can predict heterogeneous crowding fields, establishing a predictive biophysical framework for cellular transport.
methods_and_approach:
This project establishes an integrated knowledge base linking compartment-specific proteome composition to measured transport and viscosity outcomes. By synthesizing existing public datasets, including ProteomeXchange, PaxDB, the Human Protein Atlas, and various imaging repositories, the study will map composition to emergent mesoscale parameters. No new experimental data will be generated; instead, existing literature and repositories will be curated, standardized, and analyzed.

The methodology involves harmonizing protein abundance, subcellular localization, and biophysical measurements through controlled vocabularies and standardized ontologies. Mechanistic models, such as obstruction and viscoelastic frameworks, will be combined with Bayesian calibration to relate macromolecular crowding to diffusion coefficients and anomalous exponents. Furthermore, machine learning approaches will be employed to predict transport properties from crowding state vectors, with feature attribution used to identify key compositional drivers. Validation will rely on cross-dataset testing and consistency checks against known biophysical trends. This synthesis is expected to provide a robust, scalable framework for understanding intracellular transport dynamics across diverse biological systems.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to advance the understanding of emergent mesoscale physical regulation in cells by developing open resources and mechanistic insights. The study will curate a structured database of intracellular transport measurements, including diffusion coefficients and viscosity estimates, alongside a multi-omics atlas that integrates proteomic and structural data to define cellular crowding states. A reproducible modeling toolkit will be provided to harmonize these datasets, compute crowding fields, and train machine learning predictors. These resources are expected to facilitate the investigation of conserved crowding setpoints, potentially identifying mesoscale homeostasis as a fundamental cellular objective. Furthermore, the project will characterize "crowding hubs" to link compositional features to viscoelastic properties and develop predictive models connecting omics profiles to transport landscapes. By integrating these data, the study will provide a framework for reinterpreting cellular phenotypes as material-state transitions, ultimately establishing protein crowding as a quantitatively predictable regulator of signaling, metabolism, and assembly dynamics within the cell.
budget_and_resources: This project facilitates a community-scale synthesis requiring sustained curation, multi-repository integration, and advanced computational modeling. The budget prioritizes personnel for data harmonization and research software engineering, alongside computational resources for large-scale reanalysis and model fitting. Two postdoctoral researchers will focus on biophysical transport modeling and proteome integration, while a dedicated software engineer will maintain ingestion pipelines and workflow automation. A graduate student will support literature curation and training notebook development, overseen by a multi-institutional team of principal investigators. Computational requirements include cloud-based processing of imaging datasets, structural feature computation, and Bayesian hierarchical model fitting, supported by secure storage for analysis-ready data. Funding for NCEMS-facilitated working groups and workshops will accelerate standard setting and trainee development. Furthermore, the project emphasizes open science through documentation hosting, automated testing, and the implementation of interoperable data exports. This synthesis effort aims to produce a reusable, harmonized database linked to multi-omics and structural annotations, exceeding the scope of typical single-lab initiatives.

title: Integration of Cryo-EM Intermediates, rRNA Processing Maps, and Proteomics for Explaining Emergent Ribosome Assembly Robustness
abstract: Ribosome biogenesis involves the coordinated folding and processing of mesoscale ribonucleoprotein intermediates through collective interactions among rRNA, ribosomal proteins, and assembly factors. This project integrates structural, functional, and genetic datasets to infer universal principles governing assembly robustness and failure modes. Data sources include cryo-EM structures, time-resolved rRNA processing maps, quantitative proteomics, genetic interaction networks, and subcellular localization imaging. A unified assembly state graph will be constructed, where nodes represent structural intermediates and edges denote transitions constrained by processing and factor exchange. Probabilistic graphical models and energy landscape concepts will be utilized to identify assembly bottlenecks and transition probabilities across species. The study hypothesizes that assembly robustness arises from redundant modules, that nucleolar subcompartments correspond to specific graph regions, and that ribosomopathy mutations target low-redundancy transitions. Expected outcomes include a cross-species atlas of assembly intermediates, identification of fragile transitions, and mechanistic insights into how specific perturbations influence global assembly stability.
background_and_significance: Ribosome biogenesis represents a complex self-assembly process, transforming precursor rRNAs and proteins into functional ribonucleoprotein machines. This study investigates the emergent properties of pre-ribosomal particles, including directionality, robustness, and quality control, which arise from collective molecular interactions rather than individual components. Although structural, sequencing, and proteomic data are available in public repositories like the PDB, GEO, and PRIDE, these datasets remain fragmented and inconsistently annotated. This project proposes the synthesis of these heterogeneous resources into a unified, cross-species assembly state graph. By integrating structural snapshots with processing kinetics, proteomic perturbations, and genetic interaction networks, the study aims to map the landscape of partially ordered assembly states. This framework may clarify how modularity and redundancy confer robustness to the assembly process. Ultimately, this research is expected to identify fragile transitions underlying ribosomopathies and provide a model for understanding mesoscale emergence in complex ribonucleoprotein systems, necessitating a multidisciplinary approach to translate disparate data into mechanistic insights.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how robust, directional ribosome assembly emerges from the collective behavior of mesoscale pre-ribosomal particles. By synthesizing publicly available structural, sequencing, and proteomic data, the study evaluates five core hypotheses regarding assembly dynamics. First, it examines whether cryo-EM intermediates represent combinations of conserved structural modules, potentially explaining observed diversity. Second, it explores whether rRNA processing events gate structural transitions to ensure assembly directionality. Third, the research assesses if network redundancy and partially ordered pathways provide robustness against factor fluctuations. Fourth, it investigates whether nucleolar subcompartments correspond to specific regions within the assembly state graph. Finally, the study tests whether ribosomopathy-associated mutations target low-redundancy bottlenecks, thereby causing tissue-specific vulnerabilities. Validation relies on cross-dataset consistency checks, held-out datasets, and benchmarking against established literature. Collectively, these analyses are expected to elucidate how large ribonucleoprotein complexes navigate energy-constrained landscapes, providing mechanistic insights into the modularity, gating, and fragility inherent in ribosome biogenesis.
methods_and_approach: This study integrates publicly available datasets to infer an emergent assembly landscape for ribosomes across bacteria, yeast, and humans. No new experimental data will be collected. The project focuses on harmonizing structural intermediates from the EMDB and PDB with rRNA processing data from GEO and SRA, alongside proteomics from PRIDE and genetic interaction networks. A unified identifier mapping layer will be established to standardize structural metadata and factor occupancy. Structural intermediates will be represented as feature vectors and clustered into reproducible state families. These states will be aligned with rRNA processing timelines using probabilistic models, while proteomics perturbations will be deconvolved to estimate state occupancies. An assembly state graph will be constructed to infer transition probabilities and energy landscapes. Finally, the study will evaluate network robustness, map disease-associated variants, and compare cross-species conservation. This integrative framework is expected to identify critical assembly bottlenecks and provide a comprehensive, reproducible atlas of ribosome biogenesis.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to synthesize heterogeneous public data into a comprehensive Cross-species Ribosome Assembly Atlas, providing a standardized catalog of cryo-EM intermediates, rRNA processing events, and proteomic perturbation summaries. By constructing directed assembly state graphs for bacteria, yeast, and humans, the study will identify metastable basins, transition probabilities, and gating constraints that govern assembly robustness. A dedicated software toolkit will facilitate network controllability analyses, utilizing a standardized assembly graph schema to ensure interoperability across diverse RNP systems. Mechanistic synthesis will link molecular events to nucleolar subcompartments, offering a quantitative explanation for directional assembly and identifying fragile transitions associated with ribosomopathies. These findings are expected to clarify how network structure dictates cellular vulnerability and emergent mesoscale phenomena. The resulting open-source framework will enhance the interpretability of existing omics datasets, provide a foundation for future experimental hypotheses, and establish a sustainable, community-governed resource for modeling complex biological assembly landscapes across multiple scales.
budget_and_resources: This community-scale synthesis project requires coordinated curation, integration, and modeling across multiple public repositories. Funding is requested to support personnel, computational resources, and collaborative working groups, with no allocation for new experimental data generation. Personnel costs include two postdoctoral researchers focused on structural graph modeling and multi-omics integration, two graduate research assistants for curation and reproducibility, and a research software engineer to maintain automated pipelines and the public portal. Principal investigators will provide scientific oversight to ensure cross-disciplinary integration. Computational requirements include cloud and high-performance computing allocations for large-scale feature extraction, Bayesian modeling, and secure data storage. Travel support facilitates biannual working group meetings and conference dissemination, prioritizing early-career researchers and under-resourced institutions. Annual workshops and trainee-led hackathons will provide training in workflow utilization and community annotation. These investments in infrastructure and personnel are essential for harmonizing heterogeneous datasets, establishing community-adopted standards, and fostering open science through versioned archiving and web-based dissemination.

title: Mesoscale Signaling Microclusters as Emergent Computation: A Synthesis of Immune Receptor Imaging, Phosphoproteomics, and Single-Cell Responses
abstract: Immune receptors organize into mesoscale microclusters that function as computational units, integrating ligand binding and mechanical forces to regulate signaling activation. This study synthesizes diverse datasets, including super-resolution imaging, phosphoproteomics, single-cell functional readouts, and structural kinetics, to investigate how receptor organization and kinase-phosphatase partitioning dictate signaling outcomes. A multiscale model will be developed using computer vision and dynamical systems identification to link microcluster architecture to downstream phosphorylation and transcriptional states. This research evaluates whether universal microcluster motifs, such as kinase-rich cores, correspond to distinct response modes. Hypotheses suggest that microcluster morphology encodes gain control, cytoskeletal coupling modulates system excitability, and disease-associated variants primarily alter protein partitioning. The project aims to establish predictive relationships between nanoscale organization and immune function, providing a standardized framework for microcluster analysis. Ultimately, this synthesis of immunology, quantitative imaging, and computational modeling is expected to clarify mechanistic discrepancies and provide an open-access toolkit for the scientific community.
background_and_significance: Immune receptor signaling is increasingly understood as a mesoscale process where receptor and adaptor proteins assemble into microclusters at the plasma membrane. These spatial arrangements, observed across T, B, and Fc receptors, are primary determinants of downstream signaling outcomes, including activation thresholds and noise filtering. Such collective organization generates computation-like behaviors—such as bistability and gain control—that remain unpredictable from single-molecule kinetics alone. While extensive imaging, phosphoproteomic, and single-cell datasets exist, they remain fragmented across disparate repositories. This project will synthesize these heterogeneous data to establish a standardized framework for analyzing microcluster motifs and their influence on cellular dynamics. By harmonizing metadata and linking spatial features to functional outcomes, the study aims to resolve how mesoscale architecture dictates immune activation. This approach will move the field toward predictive, cross-study models, ultimately clarifying why similar receptor affinities yield diverse responses and how spatial partitioning regulates signaling in both healthy and disease-associated contexts.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how mesoscale microclusters (50–300 nm) generate emergent signaling behaviors across immune receptor systems using existing, publicly available datasets. The study evaluates whether microcluster architectures form conserved motif families that predict downstream signaling regimes, such as digital or graded responses. It further examines whether microcluster morphology functions as a gain-control mechanism, modulating sensitivity beyond simple receptor–ligand affinity by altering local kinase–phosphatase balance. Additionally, the research explores whether cytoskeletal coupling shifts signaling dynamics between excitable and bistable regimes, potentially explaining observed single-cell heterogeneity. Finally, the project assesses whether disease-associated variants primarily influence signaling by altering protein partitioning into microclusters rather than modifying intrinsic enzymatic activity. By integrating imaging, phosphoproteomics, and single-cell data, this synthesis aims to formalize how microcluster geometry and composition determine network dynamics. These hypotheses provide falsifiable predictions, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of how mesoscale organization functions as a tunable reaction compartment to dictate immune cell fate.
methods_and_approach: This project establishes an end-to-end synthesis pipeline to integrate public datasets concerning immune receptor imaging, phosphoproteomics, and single-cell outcomes. By curating diverse repositories, including the Image Data Resource, PRIDE, and ImmPort, the study harmonizes heterogeneous metadata to link mesoscale microcluster features with time-resolved signaling and functional states. Standardized computer-vision pipelines will extract quantitative features from microscopy data, while sparse regression and hierarchical modeling will infer multiscale dynamical systems. These models are expected to map microcluster motifs to phosphoproteomic trajectories and subsequent single-cell activation states, providing a framework to explain outcome heterogeneity. No new experimental data will be generated; instead, the study relies on rigorous provenance tracking and cross-dataset validation to ensure robustness. This integrative approach aims to produce a comprehensive microcluster motif atlas, facilitating the discovery of organizational principles in immune signaling. The resulting software toolkit and documentation will be disseminated to support community-wide analysis of immune cell dynamics and regulatory mechanisms.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project establishes a standardized framework for quantifying immune receptor microclusters, comprising the Microcluster Feature Standard, a harmonized Motif Atlas, and open-source processing pipelines. These tools facilitate the transition from qualitative descriptions to quantitative, testable principles regarding mesoscale signaling hubs. The study investigates whether conserved architectural motifs implement gain control and thresholding, potentially explaining how spatial organization dictates signaling outcomes beyond ligand affinity. Furthermore, the research links cytoskeletal coupling to dynamical regimes, offering a mechanistic basis for excitable versus bistable activation. While focused on immune receptors, these methodologies—including point-pattern statistics and multiscale dynamical modeling—are expected to generalize to diverse membrane-associated signaling systems. By providing benchmark datasets and containerized workflows, this initiative lowers barriers for future research and enables large-scale meta-analyses. Dissemination will occur through open-access publications, a dedicated project website, and community workshops. Long-term sustainability is ensured through modular software design, semantic versioning, and the integration of all resources with stable, public data repositories.
budget_and_resources: This project budget prioritizes personnel and infrastructure to facilitate community-scale data synthesis, harmonization, and the development of reusable open-source tools. Funding is allocated to cross-disciplinary coordination, trainee development, and large-scale reprocessing of public imaging and omics datasets, with no resources requested for primary data generation. Personnel requirements include two computational postdoctoral researchers for imaging and multi-omics integration, a graduate trainee for single-cell modeling, and a research software engineer to maintain production-grade pipelines. Modest effort from the principal investigators supports scientific integration and mentorship. Computational resources are dedicated to cloud-based feature extraction and model fitting, alongside institutional high-performance computing for reproducible analysis. Travel support enables biannual working group meetings and conference dissemination to foster multidisciplinary collaboration. Furthermore, the budget covers hybrid workshops and virtual tutorials to promote community uptake of standards. These investments in curation, documentation, and infrastructure are expected to deliver curated benchmarks, robust pipelines, and validated multiscale models within a three-year timeframe.

title: Integration of Cryo-ET, Live Imaging, and Proteogenomics to Elucidate Emergent Mitochondrial Cristae Morphodynamics and Bioenergetic Plasticity
abstract: Mitochondrial cristae are mesoscale membrane folds whose collective organization dictates respiratory efficiency and cellular signaling. This study investigates how cristae architecture, including junction density and protein crowding, generates nonlinear bioenergetic outputs that remain unpredictable from individual OXPHOS complexes. Public datasets, including cryo-ET reconstructions, proteomics, and functional respiration readouts, will be synthesized to quantify mesoscale geometry through curvature analysis and topology measures. These data will be integrated using causal inference and multi-task learning, while physics-informed models of membrane elasticity are calibrated to predict morphotype transitions. The research aims to identify conserved architectural states across cell types and determine how MICOS components, ATP synthase dimerization, and OPA1 processing drive metabolic shifts. Expected outcomes include a comprehensive atlas of cristae states and mechanistic insights into mitochondrial diseases where morphology and function decouple. This interdisciplinary project will provide open-source tools for standardized geometric analysis, facilitating a deeper understanding of mitochondrial ultrastructure.
background_and_significance: Mitochondria adapt their energy-conversion capacity across diverse tissues, yet the mechanistic determinants of this plasticity remain incompletely defined. Cristae, the invaginated folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane, represent a mesoscale environment where geometry and molecular crowding dictate emergent bioenergetic properties. While cryo-electron tomography, quantitative imaging, and proteomic profiling have characterized individual components like ATP synthase and OPA1, a comprehensive synthesis is currently lacking. Specifically, the field requires a standardized morphometric language to connect structural reconstructions with functional outputs, such as respiratory efficiency. Furthermore, the molecular drivers of stable crista states and their tissue-specific variations remain unresolved. This project will integrate existing public datasets—including EMPIAR, the BioImage Archive, and PRIDE—to establish a predictive mapping between mitochondrial architecture and bioenergetics. By synthesizing these disparate resources, the study aims to define conserved architectural states and provide an open computational infrastructure. This approach will clarify how collective spatial organization governs mitochondrial resilience, offering insights into metabolic regulation in health and disease.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates emergent mesoscale phenomena where crista geometry and topology function as collective variables constraining bioenergetic activity. The study addresses four research questions using public datasets to test hypotheses regarding mitochondrial architecture. First, it examines whether cristae occupy a finite set of conserved architectural states, hypothesized to be discrete and partially conserved across species. Second, the research explores how MICOS composition, ATP synthase oligomerization, and OPA1 processing jointly determine transitions between these states through nonlinear interactions. Third, the study evaluates whether mesoscale geometry mediates the relationship between molecular composition and respiratory outcomes, potentially explaining tissue-specific functional variations. Finally, physics-informed generative models will be developed to determine if membrane elasticity and protein-induced curvature are sufficient to reproduce observed state distributions. Across all objectives, findings will be validated through cross-dataset replication and the integration of structural, omics, and functional data, aiming to establish a quantitative framework for bioenergetic plasticity as an emergent property of crista organization.
methods_and_approach:
This project will construct a comprehensive atlas of mitochondrial cristae architectural states by integrating publicly available datasets, including 3D ultrastructure, live-cell imaging, proteogenomics, and functional phenotypes. The study will synthesize existing data from repositories such as EMPIAR, BioImage Archive, PRIDE, and DepMap to model the relationship between crista morphology, molecular drivers, and respiratory capacity. Data ingestion will involve harmonizing metadata through standardized ontologies and mapping gene identifiers across diverse platforms. 

Geometric descriptors, including curvature analysis and topological measures, will be extracted from cryo-electron tomography reconstructions to quantify cristae mesoscale geometry. These structural data will be integrated with proteogenomic features and live-imaging dynamics using multi-task learning and causal inference frameworks. Furthermore, physics-informed generative models will be calibrated to simulate state transitions and predict bioenergetic outcomes. This transdisciplinary effort will utilize cross-dataset validation and robust statistical modeling to identify emergent architectural regimes, ultimately providing a mechanistic understanding of mitochondrial organization without requiring new experimental data generation.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project establishes a comprehensive framework for analyzing mitochondrial cristae architecture through an open-access atlas, computational toolkits, and predictive mechanistic models. The Cristae Architectural State Atlas will harmonize cryo-ET datasets with standardized metadata and quantitative geometric descriptors, facilitating the classification of architectural states. Accompanying open-source software, including CristaeDescriptor and CristaeGraph, will enable reproducible segmentation, topological analysis, and interactive visualization of these structures. By integrating proteogenomic data from public repositories, the study will develop multi-task models to map molecular drivers to specific architectural states and respiratory phenotypes. These efforts aim to quantify emergent nonlinearities, demonstrating how membrane geometry mediates the relationship between molecular composition and bioenergetic function. Ultimately, this synthesis provides a robust infrastructure for investigating mesoscale organization in cellular systems. The project will disseminate findings through peer-reviewed publications, community workshops, and sustainable data repositories, offering a scalable blueprint for understanding how collective membrane constraints influence higher-order physiological outcomes in health and disease.
budget_and_resources: This project supports a multi-lab working group focused on synthesizing integrated datasets, open software, and reproducible models over a three-year period. Funding is allocated exclusively for personnel, computational resources, and collaborative activities, excluding experimental data generation. A lead research software engineer will maintain the CristaeDescriptor pipeline and workflow automation, while a postdoctoral fellow in integrative modeling will oversee causal inference and cross-dataset validation. A membrane physics specialist will implement generative models to provide mechanistic interpretations of geometric patterns. Graduate trainees will contribute to dataset curation and benchmark analyses, supported by a part-time biocurator ensuring metadata harmonization. Computational requirements include cloud and HPC allocations for processing large cryo-ET volumes and hosting derived artifacts. The budget further facilitates biannual synthesis meetings, conference dissemination, and two specialized training workshops. These resources are essential for establishing shared standards and ensuring the long-term accessibility of community-developed tools, ultimately enabling cross-disciplinary integration that exceeds the capacity of individual laboratories.

title: Mesoscale Assembly of Viral Replication Compartments: A Cross-Virus Synthesis of Host Factor Recruitment and Emergent Replication Efficiency
abstract: Many viruses generate mesoscale replication compartments, ranging from 100 to 1000 nm, to concentrate viral and host factors for enhanced replication and immune evasion. This study investigates whether these compartments share universal design principles across diverse viral families. The research integrates viral imaging datasets, host–virus protein interaction networks, CRISPR/RNAi screens, transcriptomic responses, and structural data from public repositories. A comparative framework will be developed to analyze compartment morphology, including size distributions and subcompartmentalization, alongside network-based identification of recurrent host modules. It is hypothesized that replication compartments utilize convergent strategies, such as phase separation or membrane scaffolding, to optimize kinetics and shield nucleic acids. Furthermore, the study suggests that specific host modules act as mesoscale organizers, offering potential targets for broad-spectrum antiviral interventions. Expected outcomes include a cross-virus taxonomy of compartment architectures and predictive models linking host factor recruitment to replication efficiency, ultimately establishing standardized pipelines for integrative computational virology.
background_and_significance: Viruses remodel host cells into replication compartments (RCs), mesoscale structures that concentrate viral components while modulating antiviral responses. These assemblies range from membraneless condensates to membrane-bound organelles, representing a tractable model for emergent cellular organization. Current knowledge remains fragmented across virology subfields, as imaging, interaction, and functional genomics data are rarely synthesized into a unified framework. Although public repositories like the BioImage Archive, IntAct, and GEO provide extensive datasets, quantitative cross-virus comparisons of RC architecture and host dependency remain limited. This project will integrate imaging-derived morphotypes with network modules and functional screens to identify convergent design principles across diverse viral families. By harmonizing these heterogeneous data, the study aims to elucidate how mesoscale organization drives replication efficiency. The findings are expected to reveal conserved host organizer modules and establish generalizable principles of cellular remodeling. Ultimately, this synthesis will provide a mechanistic understanding of mesoscale emergence while offering reusable workflows for broader biological research.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This project investigates whether viral replication compartments (RCs) share universal mesoscale design principles across unrelated viruses. The study evaluates whether these principles manifest as measurable relationships between RC morphotypes, recruited host factor modules, and replication efficiency. Rather than focusing on single-protein enzymology, the research emphasizes emergent properties, including spatial organization, permeability, and dynamic assembly. 

The study aims to establish a quantitative taxonomy of RC architectures by mapping imaging datasets into a standardized feature space. It is expected that RCs will cluster into recurrent morphotypes, such as spherules or inclusion bodies, independent of viral phylogeny. Furthermore, the project will identify conserved host “mesoscale organizer” modules, such as RNA metabolism and membrane trafficking machinery, that are preferentially recruited to RCs. Finally, the research will test whether replication efficiency is an emergent outcome of these structural features and module recruitment. By integrating publicly available imaging, interaction, and transcriptomic data, this synthesis will develop predictive models linking mesoscale organization to viral replication.
methods_and_approach:
This project will conduct a community-scale synthesis integrating five public data modalities—imaging, host–virus interactions, functional genetic screens, transcriptomics, and structural models—across coronaviruses, flaviviruses, and herpesviruses. No new experiments or data generation will occur; all analyses will utilize existing, publicly accessible datasets. The study will harmonize diverse data types, including EMPIAR imaging, IntAct protein interactions, and NCBI GEO transcriptomic records, using standardized metadata schemas and entity normalization.

Imaging pipelines will extract mesoscale features to define a probabilistic RC morphotype taxonomy, while network analysis will identify recurrent host-virus interaction modules. Functional screen meta-analyses and transcriptomic signatures will be integrated to evaluate module activity. Multilevel regression and causal inference models will then link these morphotypes and modules to viral replication phenotypes. This transdisciplinary effort, involving virologists, imaging scientists, and network biologists, is expected to produce open-access resources and predictive models. The study will conclude with a comprehensive synthesis of mesoscale emergence, providing a reusable framework for the broader scientific community.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project will establish a standardized atlas of viral replication compartment (RC) morphotypes, providing quantitative feature datasets linked to public imaging repositories. A comprehensive catalog of conserved host “mesoscale organizer” modules will be generated by integrating protein interaction networks, CRISPR/RNAi screens, and transcriptomic data. These resources will support the development of interpretable predictive models that link RC organization to replication efficiency, utilizing causal graph analyses to investigate directional relationships. Furthermore, the study will synthesize structural and morphotype data to propose mechanistic hypotheses regarding convergent assembly strategies, such as phase separation and membrane-scaffolded organization. By characterizing system-level properties like kinetic enhancement and spatial segregation, this research aims to elucidate universal principles of mesoscale emergence. The resulting framework and standardized datasets will facilitate future investigations into cellular compartments, antiviral strategies, and AI-driven biological synthesis. All outputs will be disseminated through open-access publications, community workshops, and sustainable, extensible repositories to ensure long-term utility for the broader scientific community.
budget_and_resources: This project requires a 2.5 to 3-year budget to support a computationally intensive, multi-disciplinary synthesis of heterogeneous public datasets. Two postdoctoral researchers will lead the integration of imaging data from repositories like BioImage Archive and network biology modeling using IntAct and BioGRID. A graduate student will focus on transcriptomic integration and causal analysis, while a research software engineer will maintain reproducible pipelines and containerized workflows. Fractional effort from the principal investigators will ensure scientific coordination and adherence to open science standards. Computing resources, including cloud credits and high-performance storage, are necessary for large-scale image processing, graph embedding, and model validation. Furthermore, the budget covers annual working group meetings to standardize metadata, conference dissemination, and workshops to foster community training. These investments in personnel, infrastructure, and collaborative outreach are expected to facilitate the harmonization of community-scale data, ensuring that all project deliverables remain accessible, citable, and sustainable beyond the initial award period.

title: Emergent Nanomechanics of Fungal and Plant Cell Walls: Composition, Ultrastructure, and Growth Patterns
abstract: Cell walls function as mesoscale composite materials, where collective polysaccharide architecture generates nonlinear mechanical properties, including stiffness, anisotropy, and fracture behavior. This project integrates multi-omics and imaging data to identify universal principles of nanocomposite design across plant and fungal kingdoms. The study synthesizes diverse datasets, including glycomics, solid-state NMR, scattering profiles, AFM nanomechanics, and transcriptomic expression patterns. A mesoscale structure–property model will be developed to link polymer composition and enzymatic activity to ultrastructural descriptors and mechanical outputs. Bayesian meta-analysis and machine learning will harmonize heterogeneous data to infer ultrastructure from indirect measurements. This research investigates whether plant and fungal walls occupy shared regions of a design space that balances stiffness with extensibility. Expected outcomes include a cross-kingdom atlas of wall architectures, identification of convergent nanocomposite strategies, and mechanistic hypotheses regarding growth directionality. The project will provide open-access tools for quantifying wall ultrastructure, facilitating interdisciplinary collaboration in quantitative biomaterials analysis.
background_and_significance:
Cell walls function as complex mesoscale biological materials, where the self-organization of fibrils, matrix polysaccharides, and water-filled pores generates emergent mechanical properties. These properties, including viscoelasticity and anisotropy, are essential for morphogenesis and environmental stress resistance. Current research remains fragmented, as existing studies often isolate specific species or measurement modalities, preventing a comprehensive understanding of how biochemical composition dictates ultrastructural organization and mechanical response. 

The increasing availability of public multi-omics, imaging, and biophysical datasets now enables a synthesis of these disparate findings. By integrating carbohydrate-active enzyme annotations, glycomics, and transcriptomic compendia with structural data from electron microscopy and solid-state NMR, a unified analytical framework may be established. This project aims to bridge existing gaps by mapping the design space of cell walls across kingdoms. Through the application of machine learning and integrative modeling, this study will identify universal principles of nanomechanics, ultimately elucidating how molecular-level biosynthetic regulation scales to produce complex cellular phenotypes.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how mesoscale architecture (10–500 nm) generates emergent mechanical behavior in plant and fungal cell walls, evaluating whether universal design principles persist across kingdoms despite divergent chemistries. The study addresses whether these walls occupy shared regions of a mechanical design space defined by architecture-dependent tradeoffs between stiffness, extensibility, and toughness. It is hypothesized that walls cluster into limited architectural states, such as fibril-reinforced networks or crosslinked gels, which map to conserved mechanical signatures. Furthermore, the research examines how specific crosslinking motifs and network topologies facilitate anisotropic growth, testing whether these features can be inferred from integrated omics and structural proxies. The project will assess if mesoscale descriptors predict failure modes under stress more effectively than gene-centric models. Finally, latent-variable models will be developed to infer ultrastructural descriptors from indirect measurements. These efforts aim to identify architectural control knobs that integrate diverse molecular pathways into reproducible mechanical outcomes across biological kingdoms.
methods_and_approach: This project will conduct a community-scale synthesis to integrate public datasets concerning plant and fungal cell wall composition, enzyme repertoires, ultrastructure, and mechanics. By curating diverse data from repositories such as CAZy, GEO, EMPIAR, and BMRB, the study will harmonize metadata into a unified knowledge graph. Standardized mesoscale descriptors will be extracted from raw images and spectra using automated pipelines, including structure tensor analysis for fibril orientation and Bayesian meta-analysis for AFM nanomechanics. These features will inform integrative, uncertainty-aware models designed to link molecular inputs, such as CAZyme co-expression networks, to emergent mesoscale mechanical outputs and growth phenotypes. Machine learning approaches, including multimodal representation learning, will be employed to infer latent architectural states. The study will rely exclusively on existing public data, utilizing cross-dataset replication and known mutant controls for validation. This transdisciplinary effort aims to provide a comprehensive atlas of cell wall organization, facilitating a deeper understanding of structure-function relationships across kingdoms.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project will develop the WallMesoscale Atlas, an open, queryable resource mapping plant and fungal cell wall samples into a unified mesoscale design space. The atlas will integrate curated metadata, standardized composition features, CAZyme repertoires, ultrastructural descriptors from public imaging archives, and harmonized mechanical parameters. A modular, open-source toolkit will facilitate hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis of nanomechanics, reproducible ultrastructure quantification, and multimodal inference of architectural descriptors. These data will support interpretable models linking molecular programs to emergent mesoscale phenotypes, identifying latent architectural states and quantified mechanical tradeoffs. The study will evaluate whether these mesoscale descriptors predict growth and stress phenotypes more effectively than gene-centric signatures, establishing architectural biomarkers for biological failure. By synthesizing cross-kingdom data, this research aims to define universal laws of biological composites. The project will provide a generalizable framework for extracellular matrix analysis, accelerate discovery through data reuse, and inform rational engineering of resilient materials, supported by sustainable, versioned, and community-accessible digital infrastructure.
budget_and_resources: This project budget supports a 30-month synthesis initiative focused on data curation, harmonization, and integrative modeling without funding new experimental data generation. Personnel allocations include two postdoctoral researchers for cross-kingdom biological interpretation, a research software engineer for pipeline development, and a graduate student for benchmarking imaging descriptors. Statistical oversight is provided by senior personnel to ensure rigorous Bayesian meta-analysis and uncertainty quantification. Computational resources are dedicated to cloud-based image processing, high-performance computing for multimodal representation learning, and persistent storage for versioned datasets. Collaboration is facilitated through biannual in-person working group meetings and conference dissemination to promote tool adoption. Furthermore, the project includes open workshops and virtual tutorials to foster reproducible research practices and broaden participation. All expenditures are aligned with the NCEMS mission to integrate heterogeneous public datasets, produce reusable community resources, and maintain professional-grade open science infrastructure. This structured approach ensures the long-term discoverability and utility of the synthesized biomaterials data.

title: Integration of Spatial Proteomics, Imaging, and Ubiquitinome Data for Mesoscale Proteasome and Autophagy Hub Organization
abstract: Proteostasis is maintained through the mesoscale organization of degradation hubs, including proteasome-rich microdomains and aggresomes, which coordinate substrate sequestration and clearance. This project investigates how collective spatial organization confers system-level robustness to misfolded proteins, a phenomenon not fully explained by individual enzymatic activities. The study integrates spatial proteomics, ubiquitinomics, bioimaging, genetic perturbation screens, and disease-specific datasets to quantify hub features such as size and spatial distribution. Dynamical modeling will be employed to link hub formation kinetics to aggregation thresholds, while multi-omic factor analysis identifies latent proteostasis states.
