It is hypothesized that cells transition between distributed microdomains and centralized aggresome routing based on ubiquitin network topology. Furthermore, neurodegenerative signatures may reflect shifts in hub organization rather than simple expression changes. This research aims to establish a unified atlas of hub architectures and identify candidate biomarkers for early proteostasis collapse, necessitating interdisciplinary collaboration and standardized data harmonization pipelines.
background_and_significance: Proteostasis is increasingly recognized as an emergent property arising from mesoscale organization rather than the simple sum of individual molecular components. While chaperones and degradation systems are well-characterized, the spatial arrangement of these factors into microdomains and condensates likely regulates substrate routing and cellular robustness. Current research remains fragmented, as imaging studies, ubiquitinomics, and spatial proteomics are rarely integrated to link molecular chemistry with mesoscale architecture. This project aims to synthesize diverse, publicly available datasets—including the Human Protein Atlas, PRIDE, and various disease-focused repositories—to establish a quantitative framework for proteostasis hubs. By bridging imaging-derived spatial phenotypes with ubiquitin linkage topology and turnover flux, this study will investigate how mesoscale organization dictates emergent outcomes like aggregation thresholds. This integrative approach is expected to clarify whether proteostasis failure in neurodegenerative diseases reflects fundamental shifts in spatial routing. Ultimately, this synthesis will provide a robust model for understanding cellular organization and proteome maintenance.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how the mesoscale organization of proteasome- and autophagy-associated hubs generates emergent proteostasis behaviors. By integrating existing public datasets, the study aims to derive mechanistic insights inaccessible through single-modality analyses. The research first defines dominant hub architectures—such as microdomains and aggresomes—by quantifying spatial features like clustering and organelle proximity. It is hypothesized that cells occupy a limited number of recurrent proteostasis states, which may be identified through unsupervised embedding of image-derived metrics. Second, the study examines how ubiquitin linkage composition and substrate network topology bias routing toward specific hubs. It is expected that K63-linked chains favor autophagy-related structures, whereas K48-linked chains associate with proteasomal microdomains. Third, the project explores how hub organization modulates degradation flux and threshold-like aggregation behaviors. Finally, the study evaluates whether neurodegenerative disease signatures reflect shifts in these mesoscale states. These integrated analyses will clarify how spatial reconfiguration drives proteostasis robustness and, ultimately, system collapse.
methods_and_approach:
This study will integrate five public data streams into a unified framework to link mesoscale hub architecture, ubiquitin network structure, and functional phenotypes. By synthesizing data from the Human Protein Atlas, PRIDE, IDR, DepMap, and disease-specific repositories, this project aims to map the relationship between subcellular organization and proteostasis flux. No new experimental data will be generated; instead, all analyses will utilize existing datasets and metadata.

A standardized "Proteostasis Hub Synthesis Index" will be developed to harmonize heterogeneous metadata across cell lines, perturbations, and imaging modalities. Computational pipelines will extract mesoscale features from microscopy, while spatial proteomics and ubiquitinomics will be reprocessed to infer neighborhood associations and network dynamics. Multi-omics integration, utilizing methods such as MOFA+ and hierarchical Bayesian modeling, will identify latent proteostasis states. Finally, coarse-grained dynamical models will be employed to investigate thresholds of protein aggregation. This synthesis is expected to provide a comprehensive atlas of proteostasis regulation and identify vulnerabilities across diverse biological contexts.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project will establish a comprehensive Proteostasis Hub Atlas (PHA), providing a versioned, public repository of mesoscale proteostasis architectures across diverse cell types and disease contexts. By integrating quantitative hub features from existing imaging and omics datasets, the study will define a taxonomy of recurrent proteostasis states, including distributed microdomains and centralized aggresome-like structures. A secondary resource will link spatial proteomics, ubiquitin chemistry, and protein turnover data to genetic vulnerability signatures, facilitating the investigation of how molecular network properties influence cellular routing. Furthermore, an open-source software toolkit will be developed to support reproducible image segmentation, metadata harmonization, and multi-omic integration. These components will inform mechanistic models that relate mesoscale organization to emergent degradation flux and aggregation thresholds. Ultimately, this framework provides a computational layer for understanding how spatial organization dictates cellular robustness, offering a standardized language for cross-disciplinary research and generating falsifiable predictions regarding the principles of proteostasis collapse in biological systems.
budget_and_resources: This community-scale synthesis project prioritizes data harmonization, software engineering, and cross-disciplinary coordination over traditional laboratory experimentation. The budget allocates resources for personnel to ensure methodological rigor, including two postdoctoral researchers focused on bioimage analysis and multi-omics integration. A graduate student will support metadata curation, while a research software engineer will manage workflow automation and containerization to facilitate community adoption. Collective PI effort will provide project oversight and leadership within the NCEMS working group. Computing resources, including cloud and HPC allocations, are required for large-scale image processing and memory-intensive Bayesian modeling. Travel funds will support in-person working group meetings and conference dissemination to foster consensus and multidisciplinary collaboration. Furthermore, the budget covers training workshops and the development of open-access educational materials. Finally, funds are designated for persistent archiving and infrastructure maintenance to ensure the long-term accessibility of reproducible synthesis products, addressing the complex requirements of integrating heterogeneous proteomics and imaging datasets.

title: Design Rules for Bacterial Microcompartments: Integrating Genomes, Structures, and Metabolic Flux to Predict Organelle Function
abstract: Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) are proteinaceous organelles that facilitate metabolic pathways by sequestering enzymes and regulating substrate permeability. This study integrates genomic data from NCBI and IMG, structural information from PDB and AlphaFold, and metabolic flux measurements to characterize the relationship between shell architecture and emergent function. The research framework involves annotating shell protein families, modeling pore properties, and simulating metabolite gradients through reaction–diffusion models. By linking genetic composition to mesoscale assembly, the project aims to identify universal permeability motifs and determine how pore configurations influence metabolic throughput. Machine learning will be employed to map gene cluster features to performance metrics, such as toxicity mitigation and flux enhancement. These analyses are expected to establish design rules for mesoscale selectivity and provide a taxonomy of BMC architectures. Ultimately, this interdisciplinary effort will generate open-access tools for predicting organelle function and elucidate the fundamental principles governing protein-based metabolic compartmentalization.
background_and_significance: Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) are protein-based organelles that encapsulate enzymes within polyhedral shells to generate selective chemical microenvironments. These mesoscale structures facilitate emergent outcomes, including spatial confinement, selective permeability, and coupled transport-reaction dynamics, which enhance metabolic flux and mitigate toxicity. Although genomics and structural biology have identified numerous BMC components, significant gaps persist in linking molecular architecture to emergent mesoscale function. Current models often lack quantitative maps of pore properties and fail to integrate shell geometry with enzyme kinetics across diverse systems. This project proposes a synthesis of heterogeneous public datasets, including genomic, structural, and metabolomic repositories, to establish a unified predictive framework. By integrating these resources, the study aims to identify universal design rules governing how shell architecture and enzyme packing influence metabolic outcomes. This research will elucidate general principles of mesoscale organization, providing a rigorous, open-access model for predicting organelle function from genomic data and advancing the understanding of protein-based cellular compartmentalization.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how mesoscale organization in bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) generates emergent metabolic functions. The study posits that BMC performance arises from the coupling of shell pore physicochemistry, shell geometry, and pathway kinetics under confinement. Research will formalize this premise into testable hypotheses using public datasets. First, the project will determine if universal permeability motifs exist across BMC types by clustering pore properties derived from PDB and AlphaFold structures. Second, the study will examine how gene cluster composition constrains shell architecture, using stoichiometry priors and cryo-EM data to predict size and pore density. Third, reaction-diffusion modeling will be employed to assess whether specific pore configurations induce transitions between metabolite retention and throughput regimes. Finally, the project will evaluate whether environmental metadata and metabolic constraints predict BMC design, suggesting convergent evolution. By integrating these diverse data, the study aims to establish predictive models linking shell architecture to specific metabolic outcomes and ecological niches.
methods_and_approach: This project establishes a community-scale synthesis pipeline to integrate genomic data, structural pore features, mesoscale cryo-EM architectures, and functional metabolomics into a harmonized BMC Design Space Atlas. By leveraging publicly available datasets, the study will map bacterial microcompartment (BMC) loci to shell protein structures, inferred architectures, and reaction–diffusion performance metrics. An ID mapping layer will resolve entities across genomic, structural, and metabolic repositories, storing provenance in a relational schema. Candidate BMC loci will be identified via HMM profiles and classified by gene neighborhood signatures. Structural analytics will compute pore radius profiles and electrostatic potentials for shell proteins, while mesoscale models will infer shell stoichiometry by reconciling gene-paralog priors with cryo-EM constraints. These data will parameterize reaction–diffusion models to predict emergent metabolic flux and leakage rates. Finally, interpretable machine learning models will be trained to identify design rules linking genomic features to compartment performance. This synthesis is expected to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding BMC functional diversity.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to transform bacterial microcompartment (BMC) research into a quantitative science by integrating distributed public data into a predictive framework. The study will produce the BMC Design Space Atlas, a versioned, queryable resource linking genomic, structural, and kinetic data with explicit provenance. An open-source software toolkit will be developed to compute pore descriptors, annotate permeability motifs, and infer shell architectures from gene cluster compositions. Mechanistic models will evaluate emergent performance metrics, such as flux gain and leakage risk, while interpretable machine learning models will establish genotype-to-function design rules. These outputs are expected to quantify how collective pore properties and assembly constraints dictate mesoscale organelle function. The analytical framework may generalize to other confined systems, including viral capsids and biomolecular condensates. By providing reproducible pipelines and community-driven data synthesis, this project will facilitate future experimental research and advance the understanding of how molecular-scale changes drive nonlinear, system-level transitions in mesoscale biological compartments.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget prioritizes personnel and shared computational infrastructure to integrate, curate, and model large, heterogeneous public datasets, supporting NCEMS synthesis and open-science objectives. No funds are allocated for experimental data generation. Personnel costs include two postdoctoral researchers focused on structural mapping and systems modeling, two graduate assistants for genomics and machine learning, and a research software engineer to manage database pipelines and workflow automation. Undergraduate support facilitates data-centric training. Computational requirements include cloud credits for scalable structure processing, high-performance computing for simulation sweeps, and robust storage for versioned datasets. Travel funds support annual cross-disciplinary integration meetings and conference dissemination to enhance workforce development. Furthermore, resources are allocated for virtual workshops and the production of training materials to broaden participation. Finally, infrastructure funding ensures FAIR-compliant data archival and long-term maintenance of documentation. These investments are expected to facilitate consensus design rules and advance reproducible, data-intensive research within the mesoscale biology community.

title: Integration of Structural Proteomics and Imaging to Explain Cargo Selectivity in Mesoscale Vesicle Coat Self-Organization
abstract: Vesicle coats, including clathrin, COPI, and COPII, assemble into mesoscale lattices that facilitate membrane curvature and cargo selection. This study investigates how collective lattice geometry and adaptor clustering influence vesicle size and cargo sorting, properties that remain unpredictable from individual subunits alone. Data integration will involve cryo-EM structures, proteomics, high-content imaging, cargo annotations, and genetic perturbation phenotypes. Quantitative analysis will utilize graph-based models and physics-informed simulations to evaluate how adaptor competition and cooperative binding establish cargo sorting thresholds. The project tests the hypotheses that coats operate near geometric frustration points, that cargo selectivity arises from mesoscale adaptor subdomains, and that disease mutations often modulate lattice parameters rather than binding affinity. This research aims to develop a unified model of coat architecture and cargo selection. Ultimately, the study will provide open resources linking structural and imaging-derived features, requiring an interdisciplinary approach to harmonize disparate datasets and establish reproducible analysis pipelines.
background_and_significance: Vesicular trafficking relies on coat proteins that assemble into curved lattices to deform membranes and concentrate specific cargo. While individual subunit interactions are well-characterized, the emergent sorting function—whereby cargo selectivity and vesicle size are determined—remains poorly understood at the mesoscale. This project will integrate disparate public datasets, including structural cryo-EM maps, vesicle proteomics, interaction networks, and high-content imaging, to establish a unified quantitative framework. Current models often overlook the physical constraints of lattice assembly, such as curvature and binding-site density, which may amplify or suppress cargo recruitment. By synthesizing these multimodal data, this study aims to determine whether common mesoscale principles govern cargo selection across clathrin, COPI, and COPII systems. Furthermore, the research will investigate how disease-associated mutations may tune lattice flexibility or adaptor clustering rather than simply causing loss of function. These findings are expected to provide predictive insights into how molecular-level changes yield system-wide shifts in trafficking, with implications for understanding diverse human pathologies.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how mesoscale self-organization of vesicle coats generates emergent cargo selectivity and vesicle size distributions. By synthesizing publicly available structural, proteomic, imaging, and genetic datasets, the study addresses four primary research questions. First, it examines whether coat lattice geometry and adaptor density determine cargo enrichment profiles, testing if mesoscale recruitment capacity outperforms simple motif-affinity models. Second, the research evaluates whether adaptor subdomains and cooperative clustering induce switch-like cargo sorting thresholds, potentially detectable as multimodal distributions in imaging data. Third, the study explores whether coat assembly operates near geometric frustration points, where minor compositional shifts significantly alter vesicle size and cargo repertoire. Finally, the project assesses whether disease-associated variants primarily modulate mesoscale lattice parameters rather than disrupting canonical binding sites. These hypotheses will be validated through cross-study analysis of PDB, PRIDE, IDR, and DepMap resources. The findings are expected to establish a quantitative model linking lattice geometry and network competition to vesicle trafficking outcomes.
methods_and_approach: This project establishes an integrative, multi-modal atlas and modeling pipeline to characterize coat lattice dynamics and cargo sorting mechanisms. By synthesizing structural parameters, proteomics-derived compositions, mesoscale imaging phenotypes, interaction networks, and genetic perturbation data, the study aims to triangulate mechanistic claims through concordant evidence across independent datasets. Data will be harmonized into a "Coat Emergence Knowledge Graph," mapping proteins to standardized identifiers and experimental contexts to facilitate reproducible analytics. Feature extraction will quantify lattice geometry, binding-site density, cargo enrichment, and morphological signatures from public repositories such as PDB, PRIDE, and IDR. Integrative modeling will employ graph-based competition models and physics-informed simulations to evaluate how lattice architecture influences recruitment capacity and vesicle composition. Statistical validation, including nested cross-validation and null model testing, will ensure the robustness of findings. This transdisciplinary effort will provide a comprehensive framework for understanding trafficking systems, with all analyses relying exclusively on existing public data to ensure reproducibility and broad accessibility.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project establishes an integrated Coat Emergence Atlas, providing harmonized datasets that link structural parameters, adaptor–cargo networks, and mesoscale phenotypes. An open-source software toolkit will facilitate data ingestion from public repositories, enabling motif annotation and integrative modeling of vesicle formation. Mechanistic models will be developed to quantify how lattice geometry and adaptor clustering drive threshold-like cargo sorting and vesicle size regulation. Furthermore, the study will identify conserved subdomain motifs across clathrin, COPI, and COPII systems, while providing a structural-context resource for interpreting clinical variants. By integrating structural, proteomic, and imaging data, this research aims to transition from qualitative descriptions to predictive principles of mesoscale organization. The resulting framework is expected to be generalizable to other cellular assemblies, such as phase-separated condensates. All outputs will be disseminated through versioned, open-access repositories and containerized workflows to ensure long-term sustainability, community interoperability, and the advancement of quantitative models in cell biology.
budget_and_resources: This project facilitates a community-scale synthesis requiring coordinated expertise, substantial computational resources, and dedicated research software engineering to ensure reproducible outputs. The budget supports two postdoctoral researchers focused on integrative modeling and physics-informed simulations, alongside a graduate student tasked with imaging feature extraction. A research software engineer will maintain ingestion pipelines and workflow automation, while faculty effort ensures project coordination and supervision. Computational requirements include cloud-based HPC allocations for large-scale imaging quantification and likelihood-free inference, supported by versioned storage for data provenance. Travel funds will enable in-person working group meetings and conference dissemination to foster multidisciplinary collaboration. Furthermore, the budget covers virtual workshops and a hybrid hackathon to expand the user base of developed tools. Open science infrastructure costs include DOI archiving and documentation hosting. These resources are essential for integrating structural, proteomic, and imaging data, as the project scope exceeds the capacity of individual laboratories while strictly utilizing existing public datasets.

title: Emergent Nuclear Pore Selectivity at the Mesoscale through FG-Nup Disorder, Transport Kinetics, and NPC Ultrastructure
abstract: Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) function as selective permeability barriers, a property emerging from the collective behavior of FG-nucleoporin (FG-Nup) polymers. This study integrates structural data from cryo-electron microscopy, FG-Nup sequence annotations, quantitative transport kinetics, proteomics, and genetic perturbation phenotypes to investigate how mesoscale organization encodes transport selectivity. A multiscale model will be developed to link FG-Nup polymer physics to observed transport, using sequence-derived features to parameterize coarse-grained simulations constrained by NPC ultrastructure. Bayesian inference will fit model predictions to kinetic data, facilitating the estimation of emergent parameters such as mesh size and cohesive interaction strength. This research addresses whether diverse organisms utilize distinct sequence grammars to achieve similar selectivity and whether disease-associated mutations reflect shifts in barrier parameters. The project aims to produce a comparative atlas of FG-Nup grammars and provide open-source tools for modeling, ultimately elucidating the relationship between disordered protein architecture and cellular transport phenomena.
background_and_significance: Selective nucleocytoplasmic transport is a fundamental eukaryotic process that couples gene regulation and stress responses to spatial compartmentalization. The nuclear pore complex (NPC) facilitates this transport through a mesoscale barrier formed by intrinsically disordered FG-nucleoporins. While extensive public datasets exist regarding NPC architecture, sequence composition, transport kinetics, and functional genomics, these resources remain fragmented across disparate repositories. Current research often addresses these components in isolation, failing to capture how selectivity emerges from the collective behavior of these diverse elements. This project aims to synthesize heterogeneous data—including structural constraints, polymer descriptors, and kinetic readouts—into a coherent multiscale framework. By integrating these parameters, the study may elucidate the latent material properties governing NPC permeability. Such an approach is expected to reveal conserved design principles across species and provide a quantitative basis for understanding how mutations and post-translational modifications shift emergent barrier states, offering insights applicable to broader systems of confined, multicomponent biological materials.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how nuclear pore complex (NPC) selectivity emerges from the mesoscale organization of FG-nucleoporins under geometric confinement. The study aims to determine how this behavior varies across species, cell states, and perturbations by inferring latent mesoscale parameters from existing public data. Four primary research questions are addressed: the mapping between FG-sequence grammar and barrier states, the existence of discrete transport regimes, the role of pore ultrastructure in constraining selectivity, and the interpretation of pathogenic mutations as shifts in collective barrier parameters. Hypotheses suggest that distinct molecular implementations converge on conserved mesoscale states, that state space is low-dimensional, and that geometry acts as a critical control parameter. These inquiries will be validated by integrating sequence features, cryo-ET reconstructions, and kinetic datasets through polymer modeling and Bayesian inference. This approach seeks to elucidate how confined, heterogeneous polymers produce robust selectivity and how diverse molecular architectures converge on shared, functional mesoscale states.
methods_and_approach: This project establishes an integrated, multiscale inference pipeline to characterize nuclear pore complex (NPC) transport. The study links NPC geometry, FG-nucleoporin sequence descriptors, composition, and transport kinetics to infer latent mesoscale barrier parameters. These parameters are expected to explain diverse functional readouts and determine whether they form discrete regimes across divergent FG grammars. Data will be synthesized from public repositories, including EMDB, PDB, UniProt, PRIDE, and various kinetic databases. An NPC Synthesis Knowledge Graph will unify these heterogeneous sources through entity resolution and condition normalization. Mechanistic, coarse-grained models will map sequence features and structural constraints to emergent barrier properties, such as mesh size and cohesion. Bayesian inference will be employed to fit these models to kinetic datasets, accounting for modality-specific noise. Finally, the study will utilize cross-dataset validation and positive controls to ensure model robustness. This multidisciplinary effort requires expertise in polymer physics, structural biology, and computational modeling to achieve a comprehensive understanding of NPC transport mechanisms.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project establishes a comprehensive framework for analyzing nuclear pore complex (NPC) selectivity as an emergent mesoscale property. The study will synthesize a versioned knowledge graph integrating structural, proteomic, and kinetic datasets to facilitate cross-disciplinary analysis. An open-source inference toolkit will be developed to map FG-nucleoporin sequences and geometric constraints to emergent barrier parameters, such as mesh size and cohesion strength. Furthermore, a comparative barrier-state atlas will characterize how sequence grammar and post-translational modifications influence functional regimes across species. By quantifying the relationship between ultrastructure and transport outcomes, this research aims to resolve debates regarding barrier models and assess potential design degeneracy in molecular systems. The resulting framework provides a mechanistic vocabulary for interpreting disease-associated variants and genetic perturbations. Ultimately, these tools and datasets are expected to advance the study of disordered polymer systems, offering a scalable approach to understanding emergent phenomena in cellular biology while ensuring long-term accessibility through community-governed, open-access infrastructure.
budget_and_resources: This synthesis project requires sustained coordination, curation, and computational modeling to integrate diverse datasets into a community-accessible infrastructure. The budget prioritizes personnel, including two postdoctoral researchers for Bayesian modeling and data harmonization, a software engineer for workflow orchestration, and graduate trainees for focused analytical modules. Faculty effort will facilitate interdisciplinary mentoring and project integration. Computational requirements include high-performance computing for simulation-based inference and cloud resources to support reproducible, containerized environments for collaborators. Travel funding will support periodic in-person meetings and conference dissemination to ensure effective cross-disciplinary knowledge exchange. Furthermore, the project includes workshops and virtual curation sprints to promote community uptake and training. Open science infrastructure, such as DOI-backed releases and automated documentation, will ensure long-term accessibility. NCEMS support is essential to bridge the gap between specialized laboratory efforts and the comprehensive, durable synthesis of mesoscale geometry, transport kinetics, and mechanistic inference, ultimately providing a robust framework for future research.

title: Mesoscale Emergence in Bacterial Biofilm Matrix Nanostructure through Integrated Omics, Imaging, and Rheology for Predicting Community Robustness
abstract: Biofilms are stabilized by extracellular matrix (ECM) nanostructures, where emergent viscoelasticity and diffusional barriers facilitate antibiotic tolerance and metabolic stratification. This project synthesizes diverse datasets, including confocal and electron microscopy, metagenomic and transcriptomic profiles, proteomics, rheological measurements, and antibiotic susceptibility screens. Mesoscale structural descriptors, such as fiber thickness and network connectivity, will be extracted from imaging data and integrated with omics-derived compositional information. Predictive models will utilize reaction–diffusion frameworks to link matrix architecture to nutrient penetration and spatial gene expression. It is hypothesized that diverse biofilms converge on specific mesoscale ECM states, that community composition dictates architectural programs, and that transitions between these states explain shifts in tolerance. This synthesis aims to produce a cross-species atlas of ECM architectures and mechanistic insights into emergent tolerance. The study will establish standardized quantification tools, requiring interdisciplinary collaboration to curate heterogeneous data and advance integrative analysis of microbial communities under open science practices.
background_and_significance: Biofilms are complex microbial communities whose protective functions, including mechanical stability and antibiotic resistance, emerge from the mesoscale nanostructure of their extracellular matrix. While molecular components are well-documented, the relationship between matrix architecture and emergent material properties remains poorly understood. Current research is fragmented across microbiology, biophysics, and imaging, preventing a mechanistic synthesis of how molecular composition dictates community-level robustness. This project proposes to integrate existing, publicly available datasets—including imaging from the BioImage Archive, omics from the SRA, and rheological measurements—to establish a standardized framework for biofilm analysis. By developing a common vocabulary for mesoscale features, such as pore size and fiber connectivity, this study will investigate how matrix architecture mediates the transition between molecular inputs and functional outcomes. This synthesis is expected to reveal how nonlinear shifts in network topology influence biofilm resilience, providing a predictive model for understanding microbial persistence and informing the design of future therapeutic interventions.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how mesoscale extracellular matrix (ECM) nanostructure emerges from molecular composition to govern bacterial community robustness. By synthesizing existing public data through standardized pipelines, the study addresses whether diverse biofilms converge onto a limited set of recurring architecture states. It is hypothesized that ECM nanostructure occupies a low-dimensional manifold, where specific structural clusters correlate with distinct rheological and diffusion properties. Furthermore, the research examines whether these mesoscale states are determined by conserved, modular ECM programs rather than individual genetic components. The study will evaluate whether abrupt shifts in biofilm tolerance arise from transitions between these architecture states, which alter transport dynamics independently of resistance gene expression. Finally, a hybrid modeling framework will be developed to integrate omics, structural, and functional data. This approach is expected to reveal causal constraints and generalize across species, providing a robust, interpretable model of the composition–structure–function relationship within microbial biofilms.
methods_and_approach:
This study proposes a community-scale synthesis to integrate imaging, omics, proteomics, rheology, and phenotype data into a unified composition–structure–function framework for extracellular matrices (ECM). This non-experimental project will utilize publicly available datasets from repositories such as the BioImage Archive, SRA, and PRIDE to construct an “ECM mesoscale feature store.” Data ingestion will involve rigorous harmonization, mapping biological entities to standardized taxonomies and functional ontologies, and developing a minimal reporting schema. 

Image analysis will employ hybrid segmentation and network reconstruction to extract structural descriptors, including fiber statistics and pore topology. Concurrently, omics and proteomics data will be processed to quantify ECM-related functional modules. Integrative modeling will then be used to identify architecture states, map omics programs to structural features, and predict rheological and tolerance outcomes. The framework will be validated through cross-dataset testing and sensitivity analyses. This transdisciplinary effort aims to establish a predictive, interpretable model of biofilm architecture and function over a thirty-month period.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to establish a comprehensive framework for understanding biofilm extracellular matrix (ECM) architecture through five primary deliverables. First, a cross-species ECM mesoscale atlas will be developed, providing standardized, indexed metrics derived from public image repositories. Second, an open-source Python toolkit will facilitate reproducible image segmentation, network reconstruction, and quality control for high-performance computing environments. Third, a library of functional ECM modules will be mapped to multi-omic datasets to quantify molecular contributions. Fourth, predictive models will be constructed to link ECM composition, mesoscale structure, and functional outcomes, such as antibiotic tolerance. Finally, a reaction-diffusion framework will be parameterized by structural descriptors to analyze state transitions and transport properties. By shifting from qualitative descriptions to quantitative, predictive science, this study seeks to elucidate how emergent robustness arises from self-organized architectures. These standardized, interoperable outputs are expected to provide a generalizable template for investigating biological mesoscale networks, ultimately advancing research in infection control, environmental microbiology, and data science.
budget_and_resources: This synthesis-driven project focuses on integrative analysis, prioritizing personnel, computational resources, and collaborative training over wet-lab experimentation. Budget allocations support two postdoctoral researchers for quantitative imaging and multi-omic modeling, a software engineer for pipeline maintenance, and two graduate students for network reconstruction and mechanistic modeling. Faculty oversight ensures biological interpretability across diverse disciplines. Computational funds are designated for large-scale image processing, multi-omic reanalysis, and storage of derived data products, addressing requirements that exceed single-lab capacity. To foster cross-disciplinary consensus, the project includes travel support for biannual working group meetings and an annual synthesis summit. Furthermore, resources are dedicated to hybrid training workshops and trainee-led analysis sprints to promote reproducible methods. Finally, funding covers persistent infrastructure, including DOI-based dataset releases and documentation hosting, to ensure long-term usability. This multi-institutional effort leverages shared expertise and production-grade infrastructure to harmonize heterogeneous public data, ultimately providing the community-scale synthesis outputs necessary for advancing the field.

title: Integration of RNP Structural States, Proximity Proteomics, and Single-Cell Isoform Variability in Emergent Spliceosome Nano-Organization
abstract: Pre-mRNA splicing occurs through spliceosomes and nuclear speckle substructures at mesoscale dimensions, where collective factor organization influences cell-type-specific isoform distributions. This study integrates cryo-EM structures, proximity labeling proteomics, super-resolution imaging, long-read transcriptomics, and perturbation screens to characterize these assemblies. A multiscale model will be developed to connect structural intermediate occupancy and speckle organization to isoform outcomes, utilizing image-derived features and Markov models of assembly states. It is hypothesized that cells regulate splicing by modulating factor partitioning between speckles and the nucleoplasm, thereby altering assembly kinetics. Furthermore, specific speckle states may correspond to distinct isoform entropy levels, while disease-associated mutations are expected to increase noise by destabilizing intermediate transitions. This research aims to produce an atlas linking mesoscale states to isoform variability, identifying key factors that govern splicing entropy. The project requires interdisciplinary collaboration to harmonize disparate data modalities and establish reproducible workflows for integrating structural biology with single-cell genomics.
background_and_significance: Pre-mRNA splicing is a fundamental eukaryotic process where the spliceosome, a large ribonucleoprotein machine, generates mature mRNAs. Emerging evidence suggests that the mesoscale organization of splicing factors into nuclear speckles and dynamic subdomains significantly influences isoform distribution and stochastic variability. While cryo-electron microscopy and proximity proteomics have characterized spliceosome intermediates and local protein neighborhoods, a comprehensive synthesis connecting these structural states to mesoscale organization and cell-type-specific splicing outcomes remains absent. This project aims to integrate diverse public datasets, including structural models from the PDB, proteomics from PRIDE, and transcriptomic data from ENCODE and the Human Cell Atlas. By bridging these levels, the study will investigate how spatial organization regulates splicing kinetics and isoform noise. This framework is expected to elucidate the mechanisms underlying phenotypic heterogeneity and provide insights into how disease-associated variants disrupt splicing programs. Ultimately, this synthesis will establish a unified model for understanding how mesoscale RNP organization governs gene expression.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how the mesoscale organization of splicing factors, specifically within nuclear speckles, influences cell-type-specific isoform distributions. The study posits that splicing outcomes are governed by collective organization that modulates reaction kinetics and interaction networks. Three research questions will be addressed using existing public datasets. First, the partitioning of factors between speckles and the nucleoplasm may regulate spliceosome assembly kinetics and intermediate-state occupancy. Second, distinct speckle organizational states are expected to function as regulators of splicing determinism, where specific configurations either buffer or amplify isoform variability. Third, genetic and functional perturbations of splicing factors may increase isoform noise by destabilizing structural intermediate transitions, which can be mapped to altered speckle signatures. By integrating imaging, proteomics, and transcriptomic data, this research aims to determine whether mesoscale variables explain isoform outcomes beyond factor expression alone. The findings are expected to provide a quantitative framework linking structural intermediate landscapes and speckle organization to splicing variability.
methods_and_approach:
This project establishes a multiscale framework to synthesize five public data modalities, including spliceosome structural intermediates, proximity proteomics, quantitative imaging, isoform-resolved transcriptomics, and functional perturbation screens. By integrating these datasets, the study aims to characterize the relationship between nuclear speckle organization, splicing factor availability, and transcriptomic outcomes. All analyses will utilize existing repositories, such as the Protein Data Bank, PRIDE Archive, and the Human Cell Atlas, ensuring reproducibility through a standardized Spliceosome Mesoscale Synthesis Index.

The research will construct a kinetic state graph of spliceosome intermediates and map clinical variants to structural interfaces. Concurrently, unsupervised learning will identify recurring speckle organizational states from imaging data, while isoform-level entropy will be modeled across diverse cell types. A hierarchical Bayesian framework will link these structural, spatial, and transcriptomic features to infer regulatory mechanisms. This integrative approach is expected to provide a comprehensive atlas of splicing dynamics, validated through cross-dataset benchmarking and established biological controls.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project establishes the Speckle–Spliceosome–Isoform Atlas (SSIA), an integrated resource linking speckle organizational states, proximity proteomics, structural spliceosome intermediates, and isoform-resolved transcriptomics. The study will develop open-source computational pipelines for image segmentation, isoform entropy quantification, and structural feature extraction to facilitate multiscale data integration. Mechanistic models will be constructed to map mesoscale speckle states to spliceosome transition propensities, identifying control nodes that regulate deterministic versus stochastic isoform programs. Furthermore, a disease interpretation framework will map ClinVar variants and DepMap dependencies to vulnerable intermediate transitions. By connecting nanoscale RNP assemblies to transcriptome-scale outputs, this research investigates whether mesoscale organization explains isoform entropy beyond factor expression levels. The project aims to elucidate principles of kinetic gating and buffering, providing a framework for interpreting splicing regulation across diverse cellular contexts. Dissemination includes public data repositories, standardized software workflows, and community workshops, ensuring long-term sustainability through modular design and adherence to established biological data standards.
budget_and_resources: This project requests funding for a 30-month synthesis initiative focused on integrating heterogeneous public datasets, including structural, imaging, proteomic, and transcriptomic information. The budget prioritizes personnel and computational infrastructure, excluding new experimental data generation. A lead postdoctoral researcher will coordinate cross-modal integration, while a software engineer will develop reproducible pipelines and atlas packaging. Two graduate students will focus on quantitative imaging and isoform quantification, supported by a part-time statistician for hierarchical modeling and uncertainty quantification. Computational resources are allocated for large-scale processing, model training, and persistent storage within high-performance environments. Travel funds support multi-lab working group meetings and conference dissemination to facilitate team science. Additionally, the budget covers training workshops and professional data curation to ensure long-term accessibility and metadata quality. These resources are expected to enable rigorous, reproducible synthesis across multiple institutions, ultimately providing the community with reusable, high-quality datasets and models consistent with established scientific standards.

title: Mesoscale Organization of Metabolic Enzyme Filaments: A Cross-Species Synthesis of Cytoophidia and Emergent Metabolic Regulation
abstract: Many metabolic enzymes, including CTP synthase and IMPDH, assemble into mesoscale filaments that alter enzyme kinetics and pathway flux in ways not predictable from monomeric properties. This project integrates imaging, structural, and metabolomic data to elucidate universal principles of filament-based regulation. The study synthesizes fluorescence and electron microscopy, protein structures, and multi-omics datasets to quantify filament morphology and its relationship to metabolic states. Mechanistic modeling will evaluate whether polymerization functions as an inhibitory, activating, or buffering mechanism across diverse biological conditions. Phylogenetic comparative methods will further investigate the evolutionary convergence of these structures and the predictive capacity of specific sequence motifs. This research aims to determine if filaments act as metabolic capacitors that stabilize pathway flux during cellular stress or differentiation. The expected outcomes include a cross-species atlas of enzyme filament states and open-source analytical tools, providing a coherent framework for understanding mesoscale metabolic regulation through integrative, multi-disciplinary analysis.
background_and_significance: Metabolic enzymes are traditionally modeled as freely diffusing molecules, yet recent microscopy reveals that many enzymes reversibly self-assemble into mesoscale polymers. These filaments, including CTP synthase and IMPDH, suggest that polymerization represents a widespread regulatory mechanism. This project investigates how filamentation alters system-level metabolic behavior, such as catalytic activity, substrate channeling, and spatial sequestration. These emergent phenomena are inherently nonlinear, as minor changes in metabolite levels or post-translational modifications may trigger significant shifts in filament morphology and pathway flux. Current understanding remains fragmented across diverse organisms and experimental contexts, necessitating a comprehensive synthesis. By integrating public datasets from the BioImage Archive, EMPIAR, and the Metabolomics Workbench, this study will establish standardized metrics for filament morphology and link these states to metabolic variables. This integrative framework aims to determine whether filamentation functions as an inhibitory, activating, or buffering mechanism, ultimately providing a predictive model for how mesoscale organization governs cellular metabolic homeostasis and stress responses.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates mesoscale emergence in metabolic enzyme filamentation by addressing four testable questions using existing public datasets. The study first examines whether enzyme filaments occupy discrete, reproducible states across species and cell types. Unsupervised clustering of standardized morphometrics from the BioImage Archive and EMPIAR will be used to test if these states correlate with specific metabolic regimes, such as energetic stress or nucleotide imbalance. Second, the research evaluates the functional role of filamentation—specifically inhibition, activation, or buffering—by fitting mechanistic models to integrated morphology and omics data. Third, the project explores molecular determinants of polymerization, testing whether specific sequence motifs, structural interfaces, or post-translational modifications predict filament architecture and propensity across evolution. Finally, the study assesses whether filamentation stabilizes or destabilizes pathway flux, using dose-response datasets to identify signatures of homeostasis or bistability. These analyses aim to elucidate how nanometer-scale interfaces yield system-level consequences through synthesis across existing multi-modal data.
methods_and_approach:
This project establishes a cross-species, multimodal synthesis pipeline to link mesoscale filament phenotypes with metabolic states and evolutionary determinants. The study will construct an integrated “Filamentome” knowledge graph by aggregating publicly available datasets, including imaging, structural, metabolomic, transcriptomic, and perturbation-response information. No new experimental data generation will be conducted. Data ingestion involves metadata normalization, identifier harmonization, and batch correction to ensure cross-study compatibility. 

The analysis pipeline will quantify filament morphology using classical image processing and deep learning segmentation to derive feature vectors for state inference. Structural synthesis will map interface residues to evolutionary phylogenies and post-translational modification sites to assess their influence on filamentation. Hierarchical Bayesian models will be employed to relate filament states to metabolic and expression covariates, while mechanistic models will investigate enzyme-polymerization dynamics. The study will be validated through cross-dataset testing and established positive controls. This framework is expected to elucidate the functional roles of filamentation in cellular metabolism and evolutionary adaptation.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to establish a comprehensive cross-species "Filamentome Atlas," providing a curated catalog of mesoscale enzyme filament phenotypes for CTPS and IMPDH. An integrated multimodal knowledge graph will connect these imaging-derived states to structural, metabolic, and proteomic data, facilitating complex queries regarding regulatory mechanisms. Open-source computational pipelines will be developed to standardize filament detection and morphometric analysis across diverse biological systems. Furthermore, the study will evaluate mechanistic models to determine whether polymerization functions as an inhibitory, activating, or buffering process, generating testable predictions for future research. Evolutionary analyses will identify conserved interface motifs and post-translational modification hotspots associated with filamentation. By transforming qualitative observations into quantitative principles, this work will clarify how molecular-scale changes scale to cellular phenotypes. These resources are expected to enhance the interpretation of metabolic regulation in cancer and microbial stress, while providing a sustainable, community-driven framework for investigating mesoscale assemblies across the broader biological sciences.
budget_and_resources: This project facilitates a community-scale synthesis requiring the integration and analysis of heterogeneous public datasets. The budget prioritizes personnel for data engineering and cross-disciplinary analysis, alongside computing resources for large-scale image processing and collaborative workshops. No funding is requested for wet-lab experiments or primary data generation. Personnel requirements include two postdoctoral researchers to lead filament detection, metabolomics integration, and mechanistic modeling, supported by a research software engineer for workflow maintenance and knowledge graph infrastructure. Graduate assistants and trainees will contribute to evolutionary analyses and metadata curation. Computing allocations are designated for batch image segmentation, model training, and secure storage of derived products. Travel funds support intensive working-group meetings and conference dissemination to ensure cross-disciplinary synthesis. Furthermore, the budget covers two training workshops to foster a data-savvy workforce and maintain open-science infrastructure, including documentation and reproducibility tools. These investments are essential for harmonizing complex biological data into a unified, reusable framework for the scientific community.

title: Integration of Single-Molecule Imaging and Proteomics to Explain Nanoscale Heterogeneity in Endocytic Pit Uptake Variability
abstract: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis generates approximately 100 nm pits, where collective protein assembly and membrane mechanics produce heterogeneous trajectories and variable uptake outcomes. This study integrates diverse datasets, including single-molecule imaging, proteomics, cargo-specific uptake assays, lipid composition profiles, and perturbation screens, to characterize these dynamics. A probabilistic state machine model will be developed to capture transitions between assembly, maturation, scission, and abortive states using hierarchical Bayesian inference. Unsupervised clustering will identify recurrent mesoscale pit phenotypes linked to specific cargo classes. It is hypothesized that emergent variability is governed by a limited set of control parameters, such as adaptor cooperativity and membrane tension, which may allow cells to tune signaling noise. This research aims to provide a unified dynamical model of endocytic outcomes and an open atlas of pit phenotypes. The project requires interdisciplinary collaboration to establish standardized pipelines for trajectory harmonization and to advance integrative modeling of mesoscale membrane remodeling.
background_and_significance: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) facilitates the internalization of receptors and nutrients through the formation of clathrin-coated pits. Although the molecular components of this pathway are well-characterized, the mechanism underlying the emergent mesoscale heterogeneity of pit dynamics remains poorly understood. Individual pits exhibit significant variability in lifetimes, assembly rates, and maturation outcomes, which suggests that collective behaviors and feedback loops govern these processes. Current research relies on fragmented datasets from imaging, proteomics, and lipidomics, which complicates the development of a unified quantitative model. This project aims to integrate these diverse public data repositories to elucidate how molecular toolkits generate distinct dynamical regimes. By synthesizing imaging trajectories, post-translational modifications, and lipid profiles, the study will establish a probabilistic framework to predict endocytic outcomes. This integrative approach is expected to clarify how cells balance internalization robustness with functional flexibility, providing a generalized model for understanding complex membrane remodeling systems across various biological contexts.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how mesoscale endocytic assemblies generate heterogeneous outcomes, focusing on how cargo, molecular composition, and membrane context modulate these processes. The study aims to develop a mechanistic, predictive model that links pit state transitions to measurable biophysical correlates derived from public datasets. It is hypothesized that a limited number of conserved dynamical phenotypes explain observed lifetime variability across cell types. Unsupervised models will be applied to harmonized trajectory features to identify these phenotypes, which will be validated through cross-study replication using existing image archives. Furthermore, the research will evaluate whether pit maturation functions as a probabilistic state machine, where transition rates are governed by latent control parameters related to proteomic and lipidomic composition. Finally, the project will examine how cargo identity and signaling constraints influence the dynamical landscape of pits. By analyzing the variance-to-mean relationship of endocytic outcomes, the study will assess whether heterogeneity serves as an adaptive, tunable feature of cellular signaling.
methods_and_approach: This project will conduct a community-scale synthesis integrating five public data modalities—live-cell imaging, proteomics, cargo uptake, lipidomics, and perturbation screens—into a unified probabilistic framework of clathrin-coated pit (CCP) state transitions. The methodology involves harmonizing heterogeneous imaging trajectories into a common schema, constructing a pit state machine via semi-Markov models, and employing hierarchical Bayesian regression to link transition parameters to omics-derived covariates. Data will be aggregated from repositories including the Image Data Resource, PRIDE, GEO, and Metabolomics Workbench. Imaging harmonization will standardize metadata and reprocess trajectories to ensure consistent feature extraction. Proteomics and lipidomics data will be normalized to compute functional module scores and mechanical proxies. The integrative model will utilize unsupervised clustering to identify recurrent phenotypes and Bayesian inference to quantify the influence of molecular covariates on transition rates. Validation will rely on cross-dataset prediction and sensitivity analyses. This thirty-month effort will produce an open-source atlas of CCP dynamics and mesoscale control parameters.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project will establish an Endocytic Pit Phenotype Atlas (EPPA), a harmonized repository of clathrin-coated pit trajectories and standardized metadata across diverse cell types and perturbations. A validated probabilistic state-machine model will define mesoscale states, such as assembly and scission, while quantifying transition kinetics and dwell-time distributions. The study will identify latent control parameters, including adaptor cooperativity and membrane tension, to explain variability in pit outcomes through integration with proteomic and lipidomic data. Reproducible Python-based pipelines will facilitate trajectory harmonization, state inference, and Bayesian integration, supported by community-wide reporting standards. This framework aims to elucidate how nanoscale molecular assemblies generate heterogeneous mesoscale trajectories and fate decisions. By decomposing uptake variability into state structures and transition kinetics, the research provides a template for analyzing emergent cellular behaviors. These resources will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, workshops, and public repositories, ensuring long-term sustainability through modular software design and adherence to FAIR data principles.
budget_and_resources: This project budget supports community-scale data synthesis and integrative modeling over a three-year period, excluding new experimental data generation. Personnel costs prioritize a research software engineer for pipeline harmonization and two postdoctoral researchers tasked with computational microscopy, statistical modeling, and integrative omics analysis. A graduate trainee will assist with cargo-class annotations and reproducibility checks, ensuring sustained expert-level integration beyond typical single-lab capacity. Computing resources are allocated for cloud-based reprocessing of public imaging datasets and the execution of Bayesian hierarchical models. Furthermore, the budget facilitates biannual working group meetings and conference dissemination to foster cross-disciplinary collaboration among imaging, proteomics, and statistics experts. Annual workshops and hackathons will provide training in reproducible trajectory synthesis and open-science practices. Finally, funds support professional documentation and project portal hosting to ensure long-term accessibility of the synthesized data. These investments collectively enable the systematic integration of heterogeneous datasets and the advancement of mesoscale emergence science through coordinated, community-driven efforts.

title: Mesoscale Emergence of Synaptic Active Zone Nanoclusters via Proteomics, Super-Resolution Mapping, and Functional Plasticity
abstract: Synaptic active zones feature nanoscale protein clusters (20–200 nm) that regulate neurotransmitter release probability and plasticity through mesoscale spatial patterning. This project integrates super-resolution imaging, proteomics, electrophysiological data, genetic variants, and single-cell transcriptomics to characterize these organizational dynamics. Quantitative analysis of cluster geometry and spatial point-process modeling will link proteomic stoichiometry to nanoscale architectures, constrained by structural data from PDB and AlphaFold. The study investigates whether synapses occupy discrete organizational states that dictate functional plasticity modes. It is hypothesized that active zones utilize specific architectures to balance reliability and flexibility, with plasticity involving scaffold-mediated transitions. Furthermore, neurodevelopmental variants may shift synapses into maladaptive states. Expected outcomes include a cross-regional atlas of active zone architectures, mechanistic insights into release dynamics, and open-source analytical tools. This interdisciplinary effort requires the synthesis of disparate datasets to harmonize workflows and bridge the gap between nanoscale organization and systems-level synaptic function.
background_and_significance: Chemical synapses convert electrical signals into neurotransmitter release via the active zone (AZ), a mesoscale assembly of scaffold proteins and calcium channels. Current evidence suggests that the spatial organization of these proteins into nanoclusters dictates nonlinear release dynamics, including vesicle docking probability and short-term plasticity. Although super-resolution microscopy, proteomics, and functional electrophysiology have generated vast datasets, these resources remain fragmented across diverse biological contexts and experimental preparations. Consequently, the field lacks a unified framework to link genetic variants and proteomic stoichiometry to specific mesoscale architectures and physiological outcomes. This project proposes to integrate public imaging, proteomic, and functional data into a comprehensive mesoscale atlas. By applying spatial statistics and structural modeling, the study will investigate whether conserved organizational states exist across synapse types. This synthesis is expected to reveal how geometric features constrain synaptic function, ultimately providing a mechanistic understanding of how molecular perturbations influence emergent neurotransmission properties within the active zone.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how the nanoscale-to-mesoscale spatial organization of active zone proteins generates emergent presynaptic output and plasticity. By synthesizing existing datasets through integrative, cross-modal analysis, this study aims to identify latent organizational states and their mechanistic links to synaptic function. It is hypothesized that active zones cluster into discrete, reproducible mesoscale states defined by the joint geometry of scaffold and channel nanoclusters. These states may be validated by applying unsupervised models to standardized super-resolution imaging data. Furthermore, the research will examine whether specific geometric parameters, particularly the spatial alignment of calcium channels and priming machinery, predict presynaptic release probability and short-term plasticity. Proteomic stoichiometry is expected to constrain the feasible architecture of these nanomodules, potentially limiting the range of possible organizational states. Finally, this work will assess whether neurodevelopmental disorder-associated variants bias synapses toward maladaptive states. These analyses will establish a quantitative, generalizable theory of active zone organization and functional transitions.
methods_and_approach:
This project will synthesize publicly available datasets to establish a harmonized representation of active zone (AZ) organization. By integrating super-resolution imaging, proteomics, functional physiology, and genetic evidence, the study aims to link structural architecture to synaptic function. No new experimental data will be generated; instead, existing repositories, including the BioImage Archive, PRIDE, and DANDI, will be reprocessed using standardized, open-source workflows. 

Methodological efforts will focus on metadata harmonization and the application of consistent spatial statistics to quantify nanocluster distributions. Hierarchical Bayesian models will be developed to map these organizational features to functional outcomes, while stoichiometry-to-architecture constraints will be derived from structural priors and re-quantified proteomic data. Unsupervised learning may identify distinct organizational states and transitions, which will be further evaluated against genetic variants and phenotypic data. This integrative approach is expected to provide a comprehensive atlas of AZ architecture, offering insights into synaptic plasticity and the impact of disease-associated genetic variation on neuronal function.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to construct a comprehensive atlas of active zone (AZ) mesoscale organizational states by harmonizing publicly available super-resolution imaging and proteomics data. A reproducible software toolkit, AZ-Synth, will be developed to facilitate nanocluster quantification, spatial modeling, and state inference. These computational tools will support the creation of hierarchical Bayesian and machine learning models designed to link mesoscale structural parameters to emergent presynaptic functional outcomes. Furthermore, a stoichiometry-constrained framework will integrate proteomic data with structural priors to interpret the mechanistic basis of synaptic architecture. By synthesizing variant data from clinical and model organism databases, the study will generate testable hypotheses regarding how genetic perturbations influence organizational state occupancy. This synthesis is expected to establish general principles of mesoscale emergence, providing a transferable framework for other cellular assemblies. Ultimately, the project will provide the community with standardized datasets, open-source software, and prioritized predictions to guide future experimental investigations into synaptic function and synaptopathies.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget prioritizes personnel for cross-dataset harmonization and method development, alongside shared computing for large-scale reprocessing, while excluding experimental costs. Two postdoctoral researchers will lead super-resolution imaging analysis and proteomics integration, supported by a research software engineer tasked with maintaining reproducible pipelines and documentation. Two graduate students will focus on organizational state discovery and variant integration, while partial principal investigator support ensures effective coordination and synthesis. Computing resources will facilitate the reprocessing of large imaging and proteomics datasets, utilizing both institutional high-performance clusters and NCEMS-supported shared infrastructure. Travel funds are allocated for biannual working group meetings and trainee dissemination at major conferences. Furthermore, the budget supports hybrid community workshops and hackathons to expand the contributor base. These resources are essential for labor-intensive data harmonization and iterative cross-validation, ensuring the production of open, reproducible synthesis deliverables that exceed the capacity of individual laboratories and foster multidisciplinary collaboration across the scientific community.

title: Emergent Organelle Size Control through Mesoscale Substructure Integration of Imaging Atlases and Omics Scaling Laws
abstract: Organelle size regulation is governed by mesoscale substructures, including scaffolds and assembly intermediates, which establish scaling laws relative to cell size and growth state. This study investigates how collective assembly dynamics produce robust size distributions within stochastic molecular environments. The research integrates large-scale imaging atlases, single-cell omics, biogenesis pathways, perturbation datasets, and ultrastructural data to characterize organelle morphology. Analytical efforts will extract size distributions and texture features to evaluate competing mechanistic models, such as limiting pool, feedback control, and coarsening-limited growth. Key objectives include identifying universal control motifs, determining molecular regulators of size variance, and assessing whether disease states reflect a loss of homeostatic control. The project aims to establish a comparative organelle scaling atlas and provide open-source tools for substructure analysis. These findings are expected to elucidate generalized principles of organelle size control, linking mesoscale organization to emergent cellular phenotypes through quantitative imaging and stochastic modeling.
background_and_significance: Organelle size robustness emerges from mesoscale organization, where local molecular interactions dictate global scaling properties. While conceptual models—including limiting pools, feedback control, and active fragmentation—have been proposed, current understanding remains fragmented across specific organelles and cell types. Public repositories, such as the Human Protein Atlas and the Image Data Resource, now offer extensive morphological and omics data, yet systematic integration remains limited. Existing studies often lack standardized metrics, ignore internal sub-organelle texture, and fail to compare control mechanisms across diverse organelle classes. This project will synthesize heterogeneous imaging, omics, and ultrastructural data to identify universal scaling laws and mesoscale control motifs. By aligning morphological profiles with regulatory networks and cell-state contexts, the study aims to elucidate how sub-organelle architecture governs size homeostasis. Such integration is expected to provide a predictive framework for interpreting morphological phenotypes in disease, requiring multidisciplinary collaboration to harmonize large-scale datasets and develop robust, reproducible pipelines for mesoscale feature extraction.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how organelles maintain robust size distributions and scaling relationships despite inherent molecular noise. It is hypothesized that mesoscale substructures, including internal compartmentalization and scaffold organization, constrain stochastic growth processes. The study will evaluate whether shared control motifs explain scaling laws across diverse organelles. First, the research will determine if organelle size distributions follow universal parametric families that scale with cell size and cycle state. Second, mesoscale texture descriptors will be analyzed to classify organelles into mechanistic regimes, such as feedback-controlled or coarsening-limited growth. Third, the project will map molecular regulators to distinct network modules that govern either mean size or variance, utilizing existing imaging and perturbation datasets. Finally, the study will assess whether disease-associated states manifest as a loss of homeostatic control rather than simple size shifts. By integrating these analyses, this work aims to elucidate how mesoscale organization constrains stochastic assembly to produce emergent scaling laws across biological systems.
methods_and_approach:
This project will perform a community-scale synthesis integrating high-content fluorescence imaging, single-cell omics, curated interaction networks, perturbation resources, and ultrastructural electron microscopy datasets. By leveraging publicly available data from repositories such as the Human Protein Atlas, IDR, and EMPIAR, this study aims to characterize organelle morphology and mesoscale subcompartment architecture without generating new experimental data. 

The methodology involves harmonizing metadata and applying batch-correction techniques to unify diverse imaging and omics sources. Organelle features, including size metrics and texture-based mesoscale descriptors, will be extracted and analyzed using hierarchical Bayesian models to estimate scaling laws and distribution parameters. Stochastic assembly models, such as limiting pool and feedback control frameworks, will be tested against perturbational data to identify shared regulatory motifs. Finally, these morphological findings will be integrated with cell-state programs and network modules to elucidate mechanistic drivers of organelle organization. This comprehensive analysis is expected to provide a robust, validated atlas of organelle scaling and assembly principles.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project establishes a comprehensive framework for analyzing organelle scaling as an emergent mesoscale phenomenon. The study will produce an Organelle Scaling Atlas, providing a harmonized, cross-dataset resource of size distributions and texture descriptors for nucleoli, centrosomes, lysosomes, and peroxisomes. An open-source Python toolkit will facilitate reproducible phenotyping, enabling researchers to compute scaling laws and generate standardized reports from diverse imaging sources. Furthermore, the project will develop a mechanistic taxonomy of control motifs, such as limiting pool or feedback models, to classify organelle assembly processes. By integrating perturbation data with network knowledge, the study will identify gene modules regulating mean size versus homeostatic variance. These outputs are expected to advance the understanding of how cells maintain reproducible architecture despite molecular noise. Ultimately, this work provides a foundation for future research into disease-related loss of homeostasis, offering validated methods to translate morphological phenotypes into mechanistic insights across various cellular contexts.
budget_and_resources: This community-scale synthesis project requires coordinated personnel, high-performance computing for image feature extraction, and NCEMS-enabled convening for cross-disciplinary integration. Two postdoctoral researchers will lead the harmonization of imaging inputs and the application of hierarchical statistical modeling. A graduate student will integrate omics-derived state programs with morphological data, while a research software engineer will maintain reproducible pipelines and containerized workflows. Principal investigators will provide project coordination and mentorship. Computational resources, including cloud-based storage and GPU-accelerated instances, are necessary to process large-scale imaging corpora and perform Bayesian model fitting. Travel funds will support in-person working group sprints and conference dissemination to facilitate consensus on data standards. Furthermore, the budget covers virtual and in-person training events to foster a data-savvy workforce. Open science infrastructure costs, such as long-term data archiving and documentation, ensure the durability of project outputs. This budget exclusively supports synthesis, workflow development, and community resource generation, excluding all experimental wet-lab activities.

title: Mesoscale Emergence of DNA Damage Repair Foci Through Integrated Live Imaging, Proteomics, and 3D Genome Context
abstract: DNA damage repair foci function as mesoscale assemblies where protein and chromatin co-localization suggests phase-separation properties. This study investigates how collective recruitment and chromatin reorganization influence threshold responses, pathway choice, and repair timing. The research integrates live-cell imaging, proteomics, 3D genome maps, CRISPR screens, and cancer variant datasets to construct a unified model linking chromatin context to foci morphodynamics. Analysis will quantify nucleation, coalescence, and dissolution to extract kinetic parameters, while causal inference identifies regulators of pathway choice. It is hypothesized that repair foci exhibit discrete dynamical regimes corresponding to specific pathways, that chromatin topology constrains assembly growth, and that cancer-associated alterations shift these regimes rather than causing complete pathway loss. Expected outcomes include a cross-study atlas of foci dynamics, mechanistic insights into genome-assembly interactions, and open-source modeling pipelines. This project requires interdisciplinary collaboration to curate heterogeneous datasets, develop multi-modal workflows, and advance the integrative analysis of nuclear assemblies.
background_and_significance: DNA double-strand breaks trigger the formation of subnuclear DNA damage response (DDR) foci, which function as mesoscale assemblies regulating pathway choice and repair timing. These structures exhibit collective behaviors, such as phase separation, that remain poorly understood through isolated protein analysis. This project aims to synthesize existing public datasets to establish a quantitative framework connecting mesoscale morphodynamics, signaling network states, and 3D genomic contexts. By integrating time-lapse microscopy from the Image Data Resource, phosphoproteomics from PRIDE, and 3D genome maps from the 4D Nucleome portal, this study will model how collective organization drives robust repair outcomes. Furthermore, functional genetics and cancer genomics data will be incorporated to link genotype to emergent assembly phenotypes. This integrative approach is expected to reveal fundamental principles of nuclear decision-making and identify mesoscale biomarkers for therapeutic response. Ultimately, this work will provide a reproducible, open-access atlas to advance the understanding of DDR foci as emergent machines within the cellular environment.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how emergent mesoscale properties of DNA damage response (DDR) foci influence molecular signaling and chromatin architecture. The study posits that these foci function as dynamic nuclear states that regulate repair pathway choice, timing, and molecular noise. Four research questions will be addressed using existing public datasets to test hypotheses regarding regime discreteness, pathway mapping, topological constraints, and cancer-associated shifts. First, time-lapse trajectories of 53BP1, RAD51, and γH2AX are expected to cluster into reproducible dynamical regimes, such as stable scaffolds or transient bursts.
