Second, these regimes may correlate with specific repair pathway biases, where RAD51-dominant states align with homologous recombination and 53BP1-dominant states with non-homologous end joining. Third, chromatin topology and epigenomic states are hypothesized to constrain the spatial growth and coalescence of repair assemblies. Finally, cancer-associated DDR alterations may manifest as shifts in the probability landscape of these regimes. This synthesis of imaging, omics, and functional genomics aims to elucidate how mesoscale organization encodes decision-making in DDR.
methods_and_approach:
This project will execute a community-scale synthesis to convert heterogeneous public datasets into a unified representation of DNA damage response (DDR) mesoscale dynamics. By integrating foci morphodynamics with proteomic signaling, 3D genome architecture, functional genetic dependencies, and cancer variation, the study aims to establish a common mesoscale state space. This framework will facilitate cross-study learning and causal inference regarding DDR mechanisms.

The methodology involves harmonizing public data from the Image Data Resource, PRIDE, 4D Nucleome, ENCODE, DepMap, and TCGA. Standardized pipelines will quantify foci kinetics—including nucleation, fusion, and persistence—using probabilistic tracking and unsupervised regime discovery. These mesoscale regimes will be linked to signaling states and chromatin context through mixed-effect models and causal discovery algorithms. Validation will rely on cross-dataset testing, positive controls, and sensitivity analyses. This transdisciplinary effort will culminate in a comprehensive DDR Foci Regime Atlas, providing a robust, open-science resource for investigating the regulatory principles governing genome stability across diverse cellular contexts.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project establishes a comprehensive framework for analyzing DNA damage response (DDR) foci as emergent mesoscale states. A primary deliverable is a public atlas of harmonized dynamical regimes for canonical markers, including 53BP1, RAD51, and γH2AX, derived from existing time-lapse datasets. This resource will be supported by open-source computational pipelines for image processing, phosphoproteomics harmonization, and multi-omic integration. An integrative statistical model will link chromatin topology and signaling network states to regime probabilities, providing quantitative predictions for how regulatory modules influence mesoscale kinetics. Furthermore, the study will map cancer-associated DDR alterations to specific regime shifts, identifying potential mesoscale biomarkers. By characterizing these discrete transitions, the research aims to reconcile debates regarding the physical nature of nuclear assemblies. This synthesis of imaging, omics, and genome architecture is expected to provide a scalable blueprint for studying emergent phenomena, while fostering community-driven research through standardized, versioned resources and open-access training initiatives that ensure long-term scientific utility.
budget_and_resources: This project facilitates a community-scale synthesis effort requiring extensive coordination, computational infrastructure, and personnel to harmonize heterogeneous public datasets. The budget supports two postdoctoral researchers focused on quantitative imaging and multi-omics integration, alongside a graduate trainee and a research software engineer dedicated to workflow containerization and documentation. Partial support for principal investigators ensures domain expertise in DNA damage response and 3D genomics. Computational resources, including cloud credits and high-performance computing allocations, are required for large-scale image processing, machine learning optimization, and the storage of derived data products. Furthermore, funds are allocated for in-person working group meetings to accelerate consensus on metadata standards and analytical assumptions. A hybrid training workshop will disseminate reproducible pipelines to the broader scientific community. Finally, resources are designated for open science infrastructure, including long-term archiving and documentation hosting. This synthesis initiative focuses exclusively on data integration and workflow development, with no funding allocated for experimental laboratory work or new sample generation.

title: Emergent Mesoscale Patterning in Bacterial Division Machinery: Synthesis of FtsZ Ring Architecture, Dynamics, and Cell Shape Outcomes
abstract: Bacterial cytokinesis relies on the FtsZ-based divisome, which forms dynamic, treadmilling filament bundles that facilitate robust constriction and shape maintenance. This project integrates super-resolution microscopy, cryo-electron tomography, single-molecule dynamics, proteomics, comparative genomics, and morphological datasets to characterize divisome architecture. Quantitative analysis will relate ring parameters, such as bundle thickness and turnover rates, to emergent outcomes like septum symmetry and division timing. Statistical physics models and agent-based simulations will be employed to identify the mesoscale parameters governing division robustness. The study tests the hypotheses that divisomes operate within a self-correcting regime, that accessory proteins modulate force distribution, and that antibiotic susceptibility correlates with architectural shifts. This synthesis is expected to produce a cross-species atlas of divisome organization and establish general principles of cytokinetic machinery. By unifying structural and dynamical data, this research will provide open-access tools for analyzing cellular morphogenesis and advance understanding of bacterial division mechanisms.
background_and_significance: Bacterial cytokinesis serves as a model for mesoscale emergence, where molecular interactions generate robust cellular constriction. Although FtsZ polymerization is well characterized, the mechanisms by which dynamic filaments and accessory proteins ensure symmetric division remain unclear. Current research, utilizing super-resolution microscopy and cryo-electron tomography, has identified diverse divisome components and treadmilling dynamics across species. However, these data remain siloed, preventing a comprehensive understanding of how specific mesoscale parameters govern division robustness. This project aims to synthesize existing datasets from repositories such as the BioImage Archive, EMPIAR, and PRIDE to construct a multi-modal atlas of the divisome. By integrating proteomic, structural, and phenotypic data, this study will investigate how accessory proteins tune filament organization to buffer perturbations. This integrative framework is expected to reveal conserved principles of self-organization and morphogenesis. Ultimately, this work will clarify how collective filament dynamics produce reliable division outcomes, providing insights into both fundamental cell biology and potential antimicrobial strategies.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates mesoscale emergence within the FtsZ-based divisome by addressing testable questions through existing public datasets. The study evaluates whether divisomes occupy a constrained architectural manifold across diverse bacteria, suggesting that multi-species imaging data may cluster into distinct archetypes correlated with cell envelope types and accessory modules. It is hypothesized that robust division emerges from a self-correcting regime where treadmilling and crosslinking minimize spatial heterogeneity. Accessory proteins are expected to function as tuning knobs that modulate these coupling parameters rather than merely altering FtsZ abundance. Furthermore, the research explores whether antibiotic and genetic perturbations induce characteristic trajectories through this architectural state space, potentially predicting morphological failure modes more accurately than target identity alone. Finally, agent-based simulations will be employed to determine if a minimal set of effective parameters can reproduce observed mesoscale regimes. This synthesis of public data aims to establish quantitative, cross-species principles governing the emergence of cytokinetic machinery.
methods_and_approach:
This project establishes a community-scale synthesis initiative to integrate public datasets concerning bacterial cell division. Rather than generating experimental data, the study will curate and harmonize existing information from imaging, proteomics, interaction networks, comparative genomics, and phenotypic repositories. Coordinated data-to-model sprints will utilize standardized metadata templates and reproducible pipelines to analyze these diverse sources.

The research will define a divisome-specific metadata schema to facilitate the integration of imaging modalities, such as super-resolution microscopy and cryo-electron tomography, with genomic and proteomic data. Analytical modules will be developed to quantify mesoscale architecture, including filament density and ring continuity, alongside dynamics extracted from published tracking studies. These variables will be synthesized into a "Divisome Emergence Atlas," employing hierarchical statistical models and interpretable machine learning to relate molecular composition to cellular phenotypes. Finally, active polymer simulations will be constrained by these data to infer mechanistic parameters. This integrative approach is expected to identify architectural archetypes and compensatory relationships governing bacterial division across diverse species.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project will generate a comprehensive, versioned Divisome Emergence Atlas, integrating cross-species imaging, proteomics, and interaction networks with standardized metadata. An open-source Python toolkit will be developed to facilitate ring segmentation, dynamics extraction, and quality control for divisome imaging. Unsupervised clustering will define mesoscale architectural archetypes, establishing a quantitative framework for cross-taxa comparisons. Statistical models will relate these architectural variables to emergent phenotypes, such as division timing and septation symmetry, while mechanistic simulations will investigate how dynamic filaments and accessory proteins enable robust constriction. These outputs are expected to identify conserved state variables and demonstrate how diverse molecular networks achieve similar emergent outcomes. The project provides a generalizable template for studying mesoscale assemblies, such as actin rings or ESCRT systems, and offers insights into bacterial failure modes. Dissemination will occur through peer-reviewed publications, community workshops, and persistent data repositories, ensuring long-term sustainability through standardized versioning, interoperability, and community-driven maintenance of the developed software pipelines.
budget_and_resources: This project facilitates a multi-institutional synthesis working group focused on data curation and reproducible computational workflows. The budget prioritizes personnel for software integration, computing resources for large-scale reanalysis of public datasets, and travel to catalyze cross-disciplinary collaboration. No funding is requested for experimental reagents or new data generation. Personnel costs support two postdoctoral researchers for bioimage integration and biophysical modeling, a research software engineer for toolkit maintenance, and graduate trainees for comparative genomics. Faculty effort ensures domain expertise across imaging and statistics. Computational resources provide cloud and high-performance computing allocations for processing large imaging volumes and performing simulation-based inference. Travel funds support in-person synthesis sprints and conference dissemination to align standards and resolve integration bottlenecks. Annual hybrid workshops will be hosted to broaden the user base and improve output sustainability. Finally, resources are allocated for professional-grade documentation and release management to ensure that all developed tools and derived datasets remain accessible and reusable.

title: Mesoscale Emergence of Exosome Biogenesis Microdomains through Integrated Endosomal Proteomics, Lipidomics, and Imaging
abstract: Exosomes originate from intraluminal vesicles within multivesicular bodies, where mesoscale endosomal microdomains enriched in ESCRT components, tetraspanins, and specific lipids facilitate selective cargo sorting. This study integrates proteomics, lipidomics, imaging, RNA-seq, and perturbation datasets to investigate how collective microdomain organization influences vesicle size and composition. Quantitative analysis of electron and fluorescence microscopy will characterize microdomain states, while coarse-grained membrane modeling will link ESCRT polymerization to observed intraluminal vesicle distributions. It is hypothesized that discrete microdomain states dictate cargo classes, with lipid composition acting as a primary controller of domain stability and vesicle size. Furthermore, cell-type variations in extracellular vesicle cargo may reflect differential microdomain state occupancy rather than individual expression levels. This project aims to establish a unified mesoscale model of biogenesis, providing predictive compositional signatures for cargo selection. These efforts require interdisciplinary collaboration to harmonize public data and develop reproducible pipelines for integrative analysis of extracellular vesicle formation.
background_and_significance: Exosomes are extracellular vesicles generated as intraluminal vesicles within multivesicular bodies. Although these vesicles are critical for intercellular communication, the cellular logic governing selective cargo packaging and vesicle size remains poorly understood. Biogenesis is driven by mesoscale organization, where nanoscale protein and lipid interactions form microdomains that facilitate membrane deformation and budding. Current mechanistic models, derived from targeted assays, fail to explain the context-dependent nature of cargo, systematic variations in vesicle size, and the redundancy of sorting pathways. This study suggests that exosome biogenesis involves multiple microdomain states rather than a single linear pathway. By integrating fragmented public datasets—including proteomics, lipidomics, imaging, and genetic screens—this project aims to quantify microdomain organization and its relationship to emergent outcomes. This synthesis will provide a framework to link molecular composition with physical morphology, ultimately establishing a unifying theory of exosome biogenesis that accounts for the observed heterogeneity in vesicle populations across diverse biological contexts.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how mesoscale endosomal microdomains generate emergent properties of exosome biogenesis, specifically regarding cargo sorting and intraluminal vesicle (ILV) size distributions. The study evaluates whether a discrete set of latent microdomain states, defined by protein, lipid, and RNA composition, explains cross-study variability in extracellular vesicle profiles. It is hypothesized that these states, rather than individual gene expression, dictate cargo enrichment and morphological signatures. Furthermore, the research examines how lipid composition, particularly ceramide and cholesterol levels, influences microdomain stability and ILV geometry. Mechanistic models will be developed to determine if lipid-driven shifts in membrane properties predict observed changes in vesicle size distributions. Finally, the study assesses whether genetic perturbations in known secretion pathways induce predictable transitions between these microdomain states. By integrating public omics, imaging, and perturbation datasets, this work aims to establish a quantitative framework for understanding how cooperative endosomal organization governs the systemic properties of exosome secretion across diverse cellular contexts.
methods_and_approach:
This project aims to construct an integrated, open-access microdomain state atlas by harmonizing public extracellular vesicle and endosome multi-omics data with quantitative imaging and perturbation genetics. The study will map heterogeneous datasets into shared latent variables representing mesoscale microdomain states to determine if these states explain emergent outputs, such as cargo modules and intraluminal vesicle size distributions. Data sources include public repositories for proteomics, lipidomics, RNA cargo, and imaging, alongside genetic dependency databases. 

Harmonization will involve standardizing identifiers and metadata, applying modality-specific normalization, and using hierarchical models to account for study-level variance. Quantitative imaging analysis will utilize deep learning to extract morphological metrics from existing electron and fluorescence microscopy. Multi-omic integration will employ factor models and similarity network fusion to define reproducible states. Finally, the project will link these states to emergent outputs and evaluate mechanistic membrane remodeling models. All activities are synthesis-based, relying exclusively on the reanalysis of existing public datasets.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project establishes a comprehensive framework for exosome biogenesis by synthesizing public multi-omic and imaging data into a standardized Microdomain State Atlas. This resource integrates proteomics, lipidomics, RNA cargo, and morphological metrics to define reproducible microdomain states. Computational pipelines will be developed to harmonize these diverse datasets, providing end-to-end workflows for feature extraction and state integration. Mechanistic mesoscale models will subsequently quantify the relationship between lipid composition, ESCRT-related factors, and intraluminal vesicle geometry. Furthermore, predictive models will identify rules governing cargo selection, linking specific microdomain states to the recruitment of protein and RNA modules. By treating microdomains as mesoscale assemblies, this study aims to reconcile observed heterogeneity in exosome composition and size across cell types. These findings are expected to clarify the principles of emergent organization in EV biogenesis, providing a durable, open-access resource that facilitates future hypothesis generation and improves the interpretability of EV biomarkers in diverse biological contexts.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget supports community-scale synthesis by prioritizing personnel for data harmonization, computational resources for large-scale reprocessing, and collaborative activities. No funds are allocated to primary data generation or experimental sample collection. Two postdoctoral researchers will focus on multi-omics integration and quantitative imaging, while a scientific programmer will ensure the maintainability of reproducible workflows. Partial support for graduate students facilitates focused subprojects and workforce training, complemented by modest oversight from the principal investigators. Computational requirements include cloud and high-performance computing allocations for processing large-scale proteomics and imaging datasets, alongside necessary storage for versioned data releases. Travel funding supports biannual working group meetings and conference dissemination to foster cross-disciplinary collaboration. Annual training workshops will further broaden the project’s impact through instructional support and trainee scholarships. Finally, resources are dedicated to open-science infrastructure, ensuring that all software and datasets remain findable, accessible, and reusable in alignment with established standards for reproducible research.

title: Deciphering the Sequence Grammar of Mesoscale Viscoelasticity in Biomolecular Condensates
abstract: This project investigates the viscoelastic transitions occurring within biomolecular condensates formed through liquid-liquid phase separation. Although protein phase separation is well-documented, the underlying mechanisms governing mesoscale material properties, including viscosity and temporal hardening, remain insufficiently characterized. This study integrates data from the PhaSePro and DrLLPS databases with AlphaFold pLDDT scores and existing rheological literature. It is hypothesized that specific grammars within intrinsically disordered regions, characterized by charge patterning and aromatic content, deterministically encode the viscoelastic evolution of these condensates. Graph neural networks will be trained on these integrated datasets to map molecular features to mesoscale material states. Model validity will be assessed through cross-referencing with cryo-electron tomography data from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank. This research is expected to provide a predictive framework for the liquid-to-solid transitions observed in pathogenic aggregates. Such insights may clarify how these emergent properties contribute to neurodegenerative processes beyond the scope of single-molecule dynamics.
background_and_significance: Liquid-liquid phase separation is recognized as a fundamental mechanism for cellular compartmentalization, yet the mesoscale material properties of biomolecular condensates remain poorly understood. While these structures exhibit complex viscoelastic behaviors ranging from dynamic fluids to hardened glasses, the molecular determinants of these transitions are largely unknown. This project addresses the gap between atomic-resolution structural biology and cellular phenotypes by synthesizing fragmented rheological data with sequence-level disorder patterns. By integrating existing databases like PhaSePro with AlphaFold pLDDT scores, this study aims to decode the sequence grammar governing condensate material states. It is hypothesized that charge patterning, sticker-spacer architecture, and aromatic residue distribution dictate the transition from liquid droplets to solid aggregates. This research will employ machine learning to identify patterns in viscoelasticity, moving beyond individual protein case studies toward a generalizable biophysical theory. Ultimately, this framework may provide predictive insights into how mutations influence organelle states, potentially identifying new therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative diseases.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This research investigates how primary sequence features and local structural disorder encode the mesoscale viscoelastic properties and aging trajectories of biomolecular condensates. The study first examines how sticker-to-spacer ratios and specific residue chemistries dictate initial condensate viscosity, testing the hypothesis that aromatic sticker distribution promotes high-viscosity network percolation while charge-driven interactions favor lower viscosity. Regression models trained on PhaSePro-derived sequence data and rheological measurements will evaluate these relationships. Second, the project explores whether amyloidogenic motifs within intrinsically disordered regions trigger condensate maturation, with the rate of hardening expected to correlate with the ratio of low-complexity domains to amyloid-prone segments. Third, the study assesses whether variations in AlphaFold pLDDT scores correlate with condensate morphology, specifically testing if intermediate disorder promotes irregular viscoelastic networks. By synthesizing sequence data with imaging from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank, this work seeks to establish a predictive framework for condensate material states, bridging the gap between descriptive phenomenology and quantitative biophysics.
methods_and_approach: This project utilizes a Data-to-Knowledge pipeline to integrate heterogeneous biological and physical datasets over a 24-month period. The study synthesizes information from PhaSePro, DrLLPS, and CD-CODE to establish phase separation ground truths, while AlphaFold structural data provides pLDDT scores and PAE matrices for domain modeling. A specialized NLP pipeline, utilizing BioBERT, will extract rheological parameters from Europe PMC literature to construct the RheoPhase dataset, complemented by EMDB cryo-electron tomograms for morphological validation. Feature engineering involves physicochemical parameters and structural embeddings to construct a Condensate Knowledge Graph, facilitating the imputation of missing rheological values. A Graph Neural Network will map sequences to rheological states, employing attention mechanisms to identify critical residue contributions. Validation strategies include cross-dataset testing, in silico mutagenesis of disease-associated variants, and morphological cross-referencing with EMDB entries. This transdisciplinary effort, involving physicists, computational biologists, and machine learning engineers, is expected to provide a rigorous, physically grounded framework for predicting protein condensate material properties.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to provide standardized resources and conceptual frameworks for the molecular and cellular biosciences community. The initiative will develop RheoPhaseDB, an open-access database linking protein sequences to quantitative material properties, including viscosity and maturation rates, to address current data fragmentation. Furthermore, ViscoNet, a containerized graph neural network, will be deployed to predict mesoscale material states and aging trajectories from protein sequences. A synthesis manuscript will define the sequence-based grammar governing liquid-to-solid transitions, bridging the gap between angstrom-scale structural biology and micron-scale droplet mechanics. By examining viscoelasticity, the study will elucidate how linear sequences encode complex, time-dependent behaviors, addressing fundamental questions regarding emergent phenomena. These tools may facilitate the identification of mutations linked to protein aggregation diseases and support the design of synthetic organelles. Finally, the project will foster workforce development in data-driven biophysics and ensure long-term sustainability by integrating curated annotations into established databases and disseminating findings through interdisciplinary publications and community workshops.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget is allocated exclusively to personnel, computational resources, and collaborative activities required for high-level data synthesis, excluding wet-lab reagent expenditures. Personnel funding supports two postdoctoral fellows and one graduate research assistant to facilitate literature mining, database construction, and the development of physics-informed graph neural network models. Computational requirements include cloud-based infrastructure for training large-scale models, processing extensive text corpora, and hosting the RheoPhaseDB community tool. Collaborative efforts involve bi-annual in-person meetings at NCEMS headquarters to integrate theoretical physics with biological datasets, alongside conference presentations to disseminate findings and solicit community feedback. Furthermore, resources are designated for open-access publication fees and professional data stewardship to ensure the long-term utility of the generated databases. This investment prioritizes intellectual capital, enabling a transdisciplinary team to synthesize complex data into a dynamic, accessible resource. By focusing on these core areas, the project aims to establish a sustainable framework for future research within the scientific community.

title: Emergent Chromatin Rheology: Synthesis of 1D Sequence and 3D Topology for Predicting Nuclear Stiffness
abstract: This study investigates the emergent rheological properties of chromatin at the mesoscale, specifically examining how local genomic folding patterns dictate the physical stiffness and plasticity of the cell nucleus. The spatial organization of the genome is hypothesized to function as a mechanical scaffold that influences gene expression and nuclear stability. This project integrates high-resolution Hi-C and Micro-C data from the 4D Nucleome Project, atomic force microscopy measurements of isolated nuclei, and transcriptomic data from the Gene Expression Omnibus. It is proposed that specific topologically associating domains and chromatin loops act as mechanical springs, where collective stiffness emerges from the interplay of epigenetic marks and loop extrusion factors. By employing polymer physics simulations and machine learning regression models, this research correlates 3D chromatin architecture with nuclear stiffness. These findings may reveal how mesoscale folding changes, driven by differentiation or disease, result in mechanical alterations that impact nuclear migration and structural integrity.
background_and_significance: The cell nucleus functions as a dynamic, mechanically active organelle that balances structural integrity with the reorganization required for gene regulation. A critical knowledge gap persists at the mesoscale, where chromatin organization into Topologically Associating Domains may influence nuclear rheology. Although extensive genomic datasets from the 4D Nucleome Project and biophysical measurements from atomic force microscopy exist, these domains remain siloed. Genomicists typically focus on transcriptional regulation, while biophysicists often model the nucleus as a homogeneous continuum, neglecting sequence-dependent topology. This project aims to synthesize these disparate data sources to investigate how chromatin folding, driven by loop extrusion and phase separation, dictates nuclear stiffness. It is hypothesized that nuclear mechanical properties emerge from the collective behavior of dynamic chromatin loops. By integrating existing high-resolution maps with rheological data, this study will develop a predictive mechano-genomic framework. This approach may clarify how the genome maintains mechanical stability while remaining accessible for essential biological processes.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates the emergent mechanical properties of chromatin at the mesoscale through the synthesis of existing data and computational modeling. The first objective examines how Topologically Associating Domain density and arrangement dictate nuclear stiffness, testing the hypothesis that TADs function as mechanical subunits where insulation scores and loop frequency correlate with the Young’s modulus. This will be validated by training regression models on Hi-C data and publicly available atomic force microscopy measurements. The second objective evaluates how epigenetic marks and architectural proteins contribute to chromatin rheology independently of DNA sequence. By integrating ChIP-seq data into polymer physics simulations, the study will assess whether H3K9me3 and H3K27ac enrichment patterns predict solid-like or fluid-like viscoelastic behaviors. Finally, the project explores whether mesoscale topological degradation explains the mechanical softening observed in cancer and stem cells. Comparing contact maps from normal and oncogenic lines will determine if topological shifts alone reproduce the softening phenotypes observed in physical experiments.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates bioinformatics, machine learning, and computational polymer physics to synthesize existing data from the 4D Nucleome, ENCODE, and Gene Expression Omnibus. The study will harmonize high-resolution Hi-C, epigenomic, and transcriptomic data to the GRCh38 reference genome, alongside a curated meta-dataset of nuclear rheology measurements. A coarse-grained "Virtual Nucleus" will be constructed using OpenMM and LAMMPS, where polymer models are parameterized by loop constraints and phase-separation potentials derived from genomic data. These models will undergo simulated physical stress to calculate theoretical mechanical properties, including Young’s modulus. Subsequently, a Graph Neural Network will be developed to map chromatin topology to nuclear stiffness, utilizing Graph Convolutional Networks to aggregate local topological features. The model’s predictive accuracy will be assessed via leave-one-out cross-validation across diverse cell types. This two-year effort aims to bridge genomics and mechanobiology by extracting emergent physical insights from established datasets, ultimately providing a quantitative framework for understanding the relationship between chromatin architecture and nuclear mechanics.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to advance the understanding of mesoscale emergence by integrating genomic topology with nuclear mechanical properties. The primary deliverable is the NucleoMechanics database, a harmonized repository linking Hi-C metrics with physical properties across fifty cell types. Furthermore, the Virtual Nucleus toolkit, an open-source Python package, will enable users to derive rheological profiles from genomic data, while pre-trained graph neural networks will facilitate the prediction of nuclear stiffness. These efforts are expected to yield two peer-reviewed publications detailing the mechanical code of chromatin folding and methodological synthesis. The study posits that nuclear stiffness is an emergent property of chromatin architecture, suggesting a feedback loop where topology influences mechanics and vice versa. Beyond fundamental insights, this work may identify diagnostic biomarkers for cancer metastasis. By providing public access to these models and training researchers in interdisciplinary computational and biological methods, the project establishes a sustainable foundation for future investigations into nuclear mechanotransduction.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget allocates resources toward the human capital and computational infrastructure required to execute this synthesis project, which excludes wet-lab experimentation. Personnel costs, comprising 65% of the budget, support two postdoctoral fellows tasked with polymer simulations, mechanical data curation, and the integration of 4DN/ENCODE datasets with machine learning models. A graduate student will assist with data harmonization and database development, while the principal investigators will provide scientific oversight. Computational resources, accounting for 15% of the budget, will facilitate deep learning model training via cloud platforms and support high-performance computing for intensive Langevin dynamics simulations. Furthermore, 10% of the budget is designated for collaborative working group meetings and conference dissemination to ensure broad scientific engagement. The remaining 10% covers open-access publication fees and the organization of virtual training workshops. This targeted financial strategy ensures that resources are directed toward the intellectual labor and infrastructure necessary to model mesoscale emergence effectively.

title: Mapping Transient Metabolons through Integrated Interactomics to Elucidate the Emergence of Metabolic Channeling
abstract: This research investigates metabolic channeling, a phenomenon characterized by the formation of transient, mesoscale enzyme clusters known as metabolons. These dynamic structures are expected to enhance metabolic flux and stabilize intermediates by creating localized reaction environments. The study integrates protein-protein interaction data from STRING and BioGRID, kinetic parameters from BRENDA, and spatial proteomics from the Human Protein Atlas. It is hypothesized that low-affinity, transient interactions between enzymes establish substrate pathways that circumvent diffusion-limited kinetics. The analytical framework involves constructing spatially-constrained metabolic flux models that incorporate probability distributions of enzyme clustering derived from network data. Simulations will be conducted to identify specific conditions under which channeling functions as a primary regulatory mechanism. These findings may redefine current understanding of metabolic efficiency by demonstrating how mesoscale organization facilitates reaction rates exceeding those of well-mixed solutions. This project utilizes NCEMS resources to integrate static interaction maps with dynamic kinetic data across multiple scientific disciplines.

title: Lipid Raft Dynamics and the Emergence of Signal Fidelity During T-Cell Activation
abstract: This study investigates the role of lipid rafts, defined as mesoscale membrane nanodomains, in establishing high-fidelity signaling thresholds within immune cells. Because T-cell receptor triggering exhibits sensitivity and specificity exceeding simple ligand-receptor binding models, this project integrates lipidomics datasets, single-molecule tracking of receptor dynamics, and super-resolution microscopy data from the BioImage Archive. The research addresses how the dynamic clustering of cholesterol, sphingolipids, and proteins may function as a computational engine to filter noise and amplify antigenic signals. Agent-based modeling and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations will be employed to correlate lipid composition with protein mobility. It is expected that lipid rafts act as signal integration hubs, potentially undergoing phase transitions to stabilize activation states and facilitate immune decision-making. This interdisciplinary synthesis requires collaboration between immunologists, biophysicists, and computational modelers to elucidate the relationship between membrane composition and the spatiotemporal regulation of immune signaling outcomes.
background_and_significance: The molecular mechanisms enabling T-cells to discriminate between self and non-self antigens remain a fundamental challenge in immunology. Although atomic-scale interactions between T-cell receptors and peptide-MHC complexes are well-documented, they do not fully account for the high fidelity of immune responses. Current models, such as kinetic proofreading, often overlook the influence of the plasma membrane environment, specifically the role of dynamic lipid nanodomains in organizing signaling machinery. This project addresses the lack of a unified framework connecting membrane lipidomics with the spatiotemporal behavior of receptors. It is hypothesized that T-cell activation represents an emergent phase transition driven by the coalescence of lipid nanodomains, which may function as a noise filter. By synthesizing existing super-resolution microscopy data and quantitative lipidomics, this study will construct a virtual membrane model. This approach shifts the focus from static molecular binding to dynamic clustering, potentially clarifying how biological systems maintain signal fidelity through mesoscale organization.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This study investigates the hypothesis that lipid rafts function as mesoscale coincidence detectors, where T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling requires the temporal alignment of ligand binding and nanodomain residence. The research addresses three primary questions through data synthesis and computational modeling. First, the project examines how lipid composition influences nanodomain stability, testing whether specific cholesterol-to-sphingolipid ratios facilitate phase transitions near critical points. This will be validated by integrating existing lipidomics data with molecular dynamics simulations and super-resolution imaging. Second, the study evaluates whether nanodomains act as spatiotemporal noise filters by restricting TCR diffusion to amplify high-affinity interactions. This mechanism will be assessed using single-particle tracking data within an agent-based model to determine signaling thresholds. Finally, the research explores whether the immunological synapse represents a macroscopic percolation threshold. By applying spatial statistics to existing microscopy datasets, the study will determine if the transition to an activated state follows universal scaling laws characteristic of physical percolation systems.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates publicly available data to model T-cell membrane dynamics, adhering to the NCEMS mandate for multidisciplinary synthesis. The study harvests lipidomics profiles from LIPID MAPS and Metabolomics Workbench, spatiotemporal trajectories from the BioImage Archive and EMPIAR, and structural data from the Protein Data Bank. These heterogeneous datasets will be harmonized through a Mesoscale Membrane Ontology, converting lipid abundances into surface densities and standardizing microscopy trajectories into a unified HDF5 format. A two-tiered computational strategy will be employed, utilizing coarse-grained molecular dynamics with the Martini 3 force field to establish physical interaction rules. These parameters will inform agent-based models to simulate signaling thresholds at larger spatial and temporal scales. Validation will be conducted via hold-out testing, comparing model predictions against independent experimental datasets using statistical metrics. This three-year initiative aims to develop a comprehensive Virtual T-Cell platform, facilitating the systematic analysis of membrane organization and emergent signaling behaviors through rigorous computational synthesis.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to develop a comprehensive, physically grounded model of T-cell signal fidelity that explicitly incorporates mesoscale lipid organization. By transitioning from qualitative descriptions to a quantitative predictive framework, the study will provide a robust understanding of membrane-mediated signaling. Key deliverables include the Mesoscale Membrane Atlas, a curated database linking lipid composition to protein dynamics, and a containerized simulation suite designed to predict how metabolic shifts alter signaling thresholds. Furthermore, mechanistic models will be published to clarify the coincidence detection function of lipid rafts, potentially resolving existing controversies regarding their physical properties. This research addresses the emergence of cellular phenotypes from phase transitions, offering insights applicable to neuronal signaling and receptor tyrosine kinase pathways. By synthesizing public data to resolve the fidelity paradox, this work establishes a methodology for addressing complex biological questions. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed journals and community workshops, with all data and software archived to ensure long-term accessibility.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget prioritizes human capital and computational resources for high-level data synthesis, as the project entails no wet-lab expenditures. Personnel costs of $350,000 support two postdoctoral fellows tasked with data curation, biophysical modeling, and statistical pipeline development, alongside one graduate research assistant focused on data harvesting and synthesis training. Additionally, this allocation provides summer salary support for the principal investigators to ensure scientific oversight and integration. Computational requirements, estimated at $40,000, cover cloud-based high-throughput simulations and supercomputing time for coarse-grained molecular dynamics. Travel funding of $30,000 facilitates bi-annual working group meetings at the NCEMS center to foster interdisciplinary collaboration, while supporting conference dissemination of open science tools. Finally, $10,000 is designated for open-access publication fees, large-scale data storage, and project portal maintenance. This budgetary structure emphasizes the collaborative effort necessary to synthesize heterogeneous data and the computational power required to simulate emergent phenomena, thereby aligning directly with the established objectives of the NCEMS.

title: Emergent Mechanics of the Cytoskeleton from Molecular Motors to Cellular Tensegrity
abstract: This project investigates the emergence of cellular stiffness and shape stability from stochastic interactions between cytoskeletal filaments and molecular motors. The mechanical integrity of the cell is considered an emergent property of an active matter network comprising actin, microtubules, and intermediate filaments, which exhibit distinct behaviors compared to passive polymer systems. Data will be synthesized from the Cytoskeleton Registry, cryo-electron tomography, and traction force microscopy to evaluate the hypothesis that cells utilize a tensegrity architecture. In this model, mechanical robustness is expected to arise from the interplay between compression-bearing microtubules and tension-bearing actin filaments. Finite element analysis and active gel theory will be employed to model whole-cell mechanics based on these integrated structural datasets. This research aims to establish a unified quantitative law describing how local motor activity scales to global cell deformation and migration, necessitating a multidisciplinary synthesis of cell biology, continuum mechanics, and computational physics to standardize diverse experimental inputs.
background_and_significance: The mechanical behavior of eukaryotic cells represents a complex mesoscale phenomenon where individual cytoskeletal components self-assemble into dynamic, stress-bearing networks. Although atomic structures and macroscopic rheological properties are well-documented, the relationship between these scales remains poorly understood. Current models often oversimplify the cytoplasm as a homogeneous continuum, failing to account for the structural heterogeneity and active energy consumption inherent in vivo. This project aims to synthesize high-resolution cryo-electron tomography data with traction force microscopy measurements to bridge this disciplinary divide. By integrating these siloed datasets, the study will investigate how local filament topology, such as branching angles and cross-link density, dictates global stress propagation. It is hypothesized that cellular stiffness emerges as a topological phase transition regulated by the ratio of tension-bearing to compression-bearing elements. This research will utilize existing public repositories to identify universal scaling laws, potentially validating the tensegrity hypothesis and providing a predictive framework for cellular mechanical stability across diverse cell types.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This research investigates the emergent mechanics of the mesoscale cytoskeleton by synthesizing existing datasets to bridge structural topology and mechanical function. The first objective examines how network geometry determines cellular rigidity, hypothesizing that non-linear stiffness scaling arises from microtubule connectivity within the actin cortex. By training graph neural networks on cryo-electron tomography and atomic force microscopy data, this study aims to confirm that topology dictates local mechanical moduli. The second objective explores the sol-gel transition of the cytoplasm, positing that motor activity relative to cross-linker density governs phase transitions. Analysis of time-lapse fluorescence microscopy will identify critical thresholds where active stress induces cellular jamming. Finally, the project evaluates the existence of a universal scaling law for cellular mechanics across diverse eukaryotic cell types. By correlating transcriptomic proxies for metabolic energy with cytoskeletal stress, this research seeks to determine whether disparate cell lines collapse onto a single master curve, suggesting a fundamental principle of mesoscale emergence.
methods_and_approach: This project investigates mesoscale cytoskeletal mechanics by integrating structural biology, image analysis, and computational physics through a rigorous data synthesis pipeline. By harmonizing heterogeneous datasets from public repositories like EMPIAR, the BioImage Archive, and the Protein Data Bank, this study constructs in silico cells for finite element analysis. A mesoscale mapping pipeline will standardize imaging data into OME-Zarr formats, utilizing 3D U-Net architectures to extract vector-based network graphs from cryo-ET tomograms. These graphs will be imported into FEniCS to model actin filaments as semi-flexible cables and microtubules as stiff rods, incorporating active dipole force distributions to represent motor activity. The analytical strategy employs a simulate-then-compare approach, validating predicted stress fields against held-out traction force microscopy datasets. This cross-dataset validation aims to assess the universality of the model across different cell types. The project will proceed through data ingestion, computational synthesis, and final validation, supported by a transdisciplinary team of structural biologists, computational physicists, and data engineers.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to develop a comprehensive, data-driven Virtual Cytoskeleton model that quantitatively links mesoscale architecture to macroscopic cell mechanics. The study will produce the Cyto-Mesh database, an open-access repository of harmonized cytoskeletal network graphs derived from cryo-electron tomography data. An integrated predictive model, constructed using FEniCS, will enable researchers to simulate mechanical stress maps based on specific cytoskeletal topologies. Furthermore, the research will establish quantitative scaling laws to describe how cellular stiffness relates to filament density and motor activity. This work is expected to shift the understanding of cellular mechanics from a molecular inventory toward a topological logic based on tensegrity architecture. By providing accessible modeling tools, the project may facilitate the generation of mechanical hypotheses within experimental biology laboratories. These resources will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and community workshops, with all data and software archived in stable repositories to ensure long-term utility for the broader scientific community.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget reflects the computational and human resource requirements of this synthesis research, excluding wet-lab reagents or equipment. Personnel costs of $450,000 support two postdoctoral fellows specializing in computational biophysics and computer vision, alongside a data engineer dedicated to cloud infrastructure and database sustainability. An allocation of $80,000 for cloud computing credits and storage is necessary to facilitate deep learning model training and parallelized finite element analysis, enabling the processing of large-scale datasets beyond local workstation capacity. Furthermore, $40,000 is designated for biannual synthesis hackathons at the NCEMS center and conference dissemination to bridge disciplinary gaps between biologists and physicists. Finally, $30,000 supports open science initiatives, including virtual training workshops and open-access publication fees. This investment is justified by the intellectual and computational labor required to synthesize terabytes of cryo-ET data, ensuring that all project outputs remain freely accessible and that the research infrastructure remains scalable for future scientific inquiry.

title: Emergent Geometric Diversity in Viral Capsids Derived from Identical Protein Subunits
abstract: This research investigates capsid polymorphism, a phenomenon wherein identical viral coat proteins self-assemble into diverse mesoscale geometries, or T-numbers, contingent upon environmental conditions. This structural plasticity is hypothesized to be an emergent property of the subunit interaction energy landscape. The study will synthesize structural data from the Protein Data Bank and the Electron Microscopy Data Bank alongside existing thermodynamic stability literature. The primary objective is to identify hidden assembly codes within protein interface sequences that dictate the transition between geometric flexibility and rigidity. Geometric deep learning and symmetry-aware molecular docking simulations will be employed to map the energy landscapes of capsid assembly. It is expected that this analysis will reveal conserved interfacial motifs acting as hinges, which facilitate curvature variations and support viral evolution and immune evasion. This interdisciplinary project integrates structural virology, geometric topology, and artificial intelligence to characterize the extensive structural space of viral assemblies.
background_and_significance: Viral capsid self-assembly exemplifies emergent biological phenomena, where individual protein subunits spontaneously organize into symmetric, closed shells. Although Caspar and Klug established the geometric principles of quasi-equivalence, the molecular mechanisms enabling subunits to adopt distinct conformations remain poorly understood. This capsid polymorphism significantly influences viral lifecycle progression, genome packaging, and evolutionary fitness. Current structural biology often focuses on static, high-resolution snapshots, failing to elucidate the assembly codes—specific interfacial motifs and flexible loops—that dictate geometric selection. This project will synthesize extensive data from the Protein Data Bank, the Electron Microscopy Data Bank, and VIPERdb to bridge the gap between atomic-level protein interactions and mesoscale assembly outcomes. By applying geometric deep learning and topological data analysis, this study aims to uncover universal principles governing these emergent structures. These findings are expected to clarify the relationship between genotype and assembly phenotype, providing essential insights for fundamental virology and the engineering of programmable, bio-inspired nanomaterials.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates the hypothesis that viral capsid polymorphism emerges from conserved interfacial motifs that regulate the assembly energy landscape. It is proposed that proteins capable of forming multiple geometries contain bistable switch regions, whereas rigid assemblers lack these features. The study first examines structural determinants of plasticity by analyzing interface flexibility scores across fifty viral families, comparing interfacial angle variance between T>1 and T=1 assemblies. Second, the research explores energy landscape topology using coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to map potential energy wells. This analysis aims to determine how environmental factors, such as pH, influence barrier heights and mesoscale state transitions. Finally, the project evaluates whether monomeric graph topology can predict allowable T-number assemblies. A Graph Neural Network will be trained on existing structural data to classify monomers and predict assembly outcomes. This model will be validated against recently deposited structures to assess the predictive capacity of the proposed emergent assembly code theory.
methods_and_approach: This project investigates mesoscale emergence through a transdisciplinary framework integrating structural bioinformatics, computational biophysics, and geometric deep learning. The study relies exclusively on existing data synthesis, bypassing wet-lab experimentation. A unified Viral Assembly Database will be constructed by harmonizing atomic coordinates from the Protein Data Bank, geometric parameters from VIPERdb, and sequence metadata from UniProt. Thermodynamic data will be extracted via literature mining, and all structures will be re-oriented to a standard icosahedral frame. Analytical methods include topological data analysis to quantify subunit polymorphism and symmetry-aware molecular docking to calculate strain energy across different lattice configurations. Furthermore, SE(3)-equivariant graph neural networks will be trained to identify non-linear assembly codes by mapping local interface topologies to global mesh structures. The project will validate these findings through cross-family generalization tests and negative control assessments. This three-year initiative aims to link atomic-scale hinge residues with mesoscale outcomes, ultimately mapping the energy landscapes that drive viral assembly.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project investigates the mechanisms of mesoscale emergence within molecular and cellular biosciences. The study will produce the Viral Assembly Database, a curated, machine-learning-ready resource linking atomic coordinates, interface energetics, and geometric parameters for over 5,000 viral structures. Additionally, the CapsidCode Python library will be developed to predict the polymorphic potential of viral protein sequences, providing probability distributions for assembly geometries. A theoretical framework will further describe how interfacial flexibility facilitates mesoscale complexity. By defining these assembly codes, the research aims to clarify how limited genetic information generates adaptable biological containers, thereby addressing the emergence of system properties from chemical interactions. These findings may inform the design of protein nanocages for drug delivery, elucidate viral evolutionary strategies, and provide methodologies applicable to other self-assembling systems. Results will be disseminated through open-access publications and community workshops, while the database will be preserved on Zenodo to ensure long-term accessibility for the scientific community.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget allocates resources exclusively toward human capital and computational infrastructure, as the project requires no wet-lab equipment. Personnel funding supports two postdoctoral fellows, one specializing in computational biophysics for molecular docking and energy landscape mapping, and another focused on geometric deep learning and the development of the CapsidCode tool. A graduate student researcher will assist with thermodynamic data mining while receiving training in synthesis research methods. Computational expenditures cover cloud-based GPU access for training deep learning models and high-performance storage for the multi-terabyte VAD database. Furthermore, funding is designated for bi-annual synthesis meetings to facilitate cross-disciplinary integration and for conference travel to disseminate findings. Finally, the budget provides for open-access publication fees and the organization of community workshops on artificial intelligence in viral assembly. This investment reflects the intellectual labor necessary to integrate topology, biology, and computer science, ensuring the development of a workforce capable of navigating complex molecular data.

title: Emergence of Synaptic Memory through Nanocolumn Organization and Postsynaptic Density Stability
abstract: This project investigates the postsynaptic density as a mesoscale storage device, where long-term synaptic plasticity may emerge from the trans-synaptic alignment of receptor and scaffold protein nanocolumns. Memory is hypothesized to reside in the stability of these supramolecular assemblies rather than individual molecules. The study will synthesize super-resolution microscopy data, electrophysiological datasets from the Allen Brain Institute, and proteomic turnover rates. It is expected that the alignment of presynaptic release sites with postsynaptic receptor nanodomains creates a quantal efficiency that remains robust against molecular turnover. Reaction-diffusion simulations and stochastic modeling will be employed to integrate spatial maps with functional transmission data. These insights may clarify how the brain maintains stable information storage despite the rapid turnover of individual synaptic proteins. This interdisciplinary synthesis aims to bridge the gap between static nanostructure and dynamic neural function by integrating expertise from neurobiology, biophysics, and stochastic modeling.
background_and_significance: The biological basis of memory presents a paradox, as synaptic proteins undergo rapid turnover despite the long-term persistence of mnemonic traces. This suggests that information storage emerges from the mesoscale organization of the post-synaptic density (PSD) rather than individual molecules. Recent super-resolution microscopy reveals that the PSD is organized into trans-synaptic nanocolumns, where presynaptic release sites align with postsynaptic receptor clusters to optimize synaptic efficiency. However, current research remains fragmented across structural, electrophysiological, and proteomic disciplines, preventing a holistic understanding of how molecular turnover maintains structural stability. This project addresses this gap by synthesizing publicly available datasets, including those from the Allen Brain Institute and the BioImage Archive, to develop a unified model of synaptic architecture. By integrating protein dynamics with geometric alignment, this study investigates how system-level memory stability emerges from component interactions. Such insights are essential, as disruptions in PSD organization are frequently implicated in the pathogenesis of various neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This study investigates how trans-synaptic nanocolumn alignment generates emergent stability in synaptic transmission despite stochastic protein turnover. The research evaluates whether geometric alignment quantitatively predicts synaptic efficacy across diverse neuronal types, testing the hypothesis that quantal efficiency depends on the precise nanometer-scale alignment of release sites and receptor clusters rather than total receptor abundance. Furthermore, the project examines the Dynamic Slot Hypothesis, which suggests that mesoscale scaffolding lattices of PSD-95 and Homer proteins create energetic slots that maintain nanocolumn structure during rapid receptor exchange. The study also explores whether the degradation of nanocolumn alignment precedes total synaptic protein loss in cognitive disease datasets. By synthesizing super-resolution structural data with MCell reaction-diffusion models, the project will simulate synaptic transmission to compare output currents against empirical electrophysiological data. If these models reproduce the variance and kinetics of physiological observations, it will suggest that synaptic stability is an emergent mesoscale phenomenon rather than a product of molecular quantity.
methods_and_approach: This project utilizes publicly available data to bridge the gap between synaptic structure and function through computational modeling. The methodology involves three phases: data harmonization, stochastic simulation, and analytical synthesis. Structural data from the BioImage Archive and EMPIAR will be integrated with functional recordings from the Allen Brain Institute and CRCNS, alongside kinetic parameters from SynaptomeDB. A mesoscale mapping pipeline will convert super-resolution point-cloud data into geometric meshes, utilizing spatial statistics to quantify nanocolumn alignment. These meshes will inform the construction of digital twin synapses within MCell and BlenderNEURON environments. By simulating glutamate release and receptor activation, the study will generate synthetic miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents. Bayesian parameter estimation will then compare these synthetic outputs against empirical physiological data to identify structural configurations that best explain observed variance. This three-year initiative, supported by a transdisciplinary team, aims to infer dynamic synaptic properties from static imaging, ultimately culminating in a validated model of synaptic stability.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to generate both tangible deliverables and conceptual advancements within the molecular and cellular biosciences. The research will produce a Virtual Synapse Repository, providing spatially accurate, three-dimensional mesh models derived from public super-resolution data for use in MCell or STEPS simulations. Furthermore, a mathematical framework will be developed to link mesoscale structural alignment to synaptic reliability, offering predictive equations for synaptic strength based on nanostructure. An integrated database will also be established to link structural identifiers from the BioImage Archive with functional parameters, thereby annotating static images with dynamic metadata. This study is expected to resolve the turnover paradox by demonstrating how biological systems maintain permanence through dynamic equilibrium. These findings may provide a template for understanding how other supramolecular complexes maintain function. Finally, the project will lower barriers to mesoscale modeling by providing open-access pipelines, ensuring long-term sustainability through public repositories and workshops designed to train early-career researchers in data synthesis methodologies.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget prioritizes personnel and computational infrastructure, as the project requires no wet-lab expenditures. Annual personnel costs of $350,000 support two postdoctoral fellows specializing in computational biophysics and neuroinformatics, one graduate research assistant for data curation, and a part-time data engineer to maintain the codebase and web portal. Computational resources totaling $50,000 per year are allocated for high-throughput cloud simulations and the long-term storage of generated datasets on public repositories. Furthermore, $40,000 is designated for biannual working group meetings to facilitate transdisciplinary collaboration and for conference dissemination by project fellows. An additional $20,000 supports the annual Synapse Synthesis hackathon and training workshops, covering virtual hosting and speaker honoraria. This financial structure aligns with the NCEMS mandate by emphasizing human capital and computational capacity over physical equipment. Consequently, the allocation is expected to support the synthesis of new knowledge from existing data through robust infrastructure and sustained interdisciplinary engagement.

title: Data-Driven Modeling of Emergent Selectivity in Nuclear Pore Complex Transport
abstract: This project investigates the Nuclear Pore Complex (NPC) and the mechanism of selective transport emerging from the disordered meshwork of FG-nucleoporins. The NPC functions as a selective gate, a property that appears to operate without direct energy consumption at the pore site. This study synthesizes structural models from PDB-Dev, single-molecule transport kinetics, and biophysical characterizations of FG-nup phase behavior. The research addresses how the collective behavior of tethered, disordered proteins creates a filter that facilitates the rapid passage of transport factors while excluding inert molecules. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics and polymer density functional theory will be employed to model the pore environment using the synthesized structural data. The project is expected to provide a unified physical model of nucleocytoplasmic transport, explaining how mesoscale crowding and weak transient interactions generate emergent gating selectivity. This interdisciplinary effort integrates expertise from structural biology, polymer physics, and computational chemistry to elucidate these complex biological processes.
background_and_significance: The Nuclear Pore Complex (NPC) serves as a critical 110 MDa assembly mediating nucleocytoplasmic exchange through a central channel filled with intrinsically disordered FG-nucleoporins. While the rigid scaffold is well-characterized, the collective behavior of these proteins, which facilitates selective permeability without ATP consumption, remains poorly understood. Current research is fragmented, with structural data, biophysical phase models, and kinetic tracking studies existing in isolation. This project aims to synthesize these disparate datasets to develop a unified model of the NPC’s functional gate. By integrating high-resolution scaffold coordinates with NMR dynamics and single-molecule tracking, this study will investigate the transport paradox regarding how the pore maintains a barrier while allowing rapid receptor passage. Understanding this mesoscale emergence is expected to provide insights into viral entry mechanisms, drug delivery vectors, and neurodegenerative diseases associated with transport defects. This research will clarify how collective interactions within the confined pore geometry generate essential biological functions.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This study investigates how the mesoscale organization of tethered FG-nucleoporins generates a selective transport barrier that remains robust to noise while facilitating specific signaling. The research addresses whether the spatial distribution and grafting density of FG-repeat motifs dictate distinct transport pathways. It is hypothesized that cohesive GLFG repeats form a dense central plug, whereas FxFG repeats create a fluid peripheral zone, a phenomenon to be validated by synthesizing cross-linking mass spectrometry and super-resolution microscopy data. Furthermore, the project examines how mesoscale crowding influences transport thermodynamics, testing the hypothesis that selectivity emerges from an entropic barrier overcome by transient multivalent interactions. Finally, the study explores the paradox of rapidity by modeling the FG-meshwork near a critical point between gel and fluid states. This framework suggests that local melting and re-annealing facilitate rapid cargo passage, which will be validated by reproducing non-Gaussian diffusion behaviors and transit times observed in high-speed single-molecule fluorescence experiments.
methods_and_approach: This project employs a computational synthesis approach to model the nuclear pore complex (NPC) without generating new experimental data. The study integrates structural biology, polymer physics, and data science to construct a digital twin of the NPC. Data will be curated from the Protein Data Bank, BMRB, BioImage Archive, and MassIVE to harmonize structural scaffolds, NMR relaxation data, and single-molecule trajectories. An automated pipeline will standardize these disparate inputs, mapping sequence variants via UniProt to ensure consistency across model organisms. The core synthesis utilizes coarse-grained molecular dynamics and polymer density functional theory, employing the Martini 3 force field to accommodate mesoscale requirements. Machine learning will tune interaction parameters for disordered proteins, ensuring the model reflects specific sequence chemistry. Validation involves predicting held-out single-molecule tracking data and comparing simulated density profiles against independent Cryo-ET maps. This three-year effort will systematically integrate these datasets to refine the physical model of NPC transport dynamics.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to develop a validated, open-access digital twin of the Nuclear Pore Complex, providing a dynamic computational model that predicts transport behavior through synthesized physical principles. The study will produce a curated repository of structural and kinetic data, alongside a containerized simulator that enables researchers to model molecular transport based on size, charge, and hydrophobicity. A mechanistic model will be established to resolve existing debates regarding selective barrier function by integrating hydrogel and polymer brush frameworks into a unified mesoscale description. This research demonstrates how chaotic molecular interactions generate orderly gating, offering a template for analyzing other membraneless organelles. Furthermore, the model may facilitate the optimization of gene therapy vectors and identify novel antiviral targets by elucidating viral hijacking mechanisms. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed journals and training workshops, while long-term accessibility is ensured through the deposition of code and models in established public repositories to support ongoing biophysical research.
budget_and_resources: The requested budget provides the necessary personnel and computational infrastructure to execute this synthesis project, which requires no wet-lab reagents. Funding is allocated to human capital, specifically supporting two full-time postdoctoral fellows and one half-time graduate student. The fellows will develop coarse-grained models, implement PDFT theory, and manage machine learning pipelines, while the graduate student will curate literature and validate model outputs against biological controls. Computational resources, including cloud credits or national supercomputing allocations, will facilitate the extensive simulations and data storage required for this project. Furthermore, the budget supports biannual working group meetings to foster transdisciplinary collaboration and travel to major conferences for the dissemination of findings. Finally, resources are designated for open-access publication fees, website maintenance, and a mesoscale modeling workshop to train researchers in these synthesis tools. This allocation aligns with the NCEMS mandate by prioritizing the interdisciplinary expertise and computational power essential for synthesizing vast, existing datasets.

title: Mitochondrial Cristae Morphodynamics and the Emergence of Bioenergetic Efficiency
abstract: This research investigates how the complex folding of mitochondrial cristae influences respiratory efficiency and the assembly of respiratory supercomplexes. It is hypothesized that cristae geometry functions as a proton trap, representing an emergent phenomenon essential for efficient ATP synthesis. The study integrates electron tomography of mitochondrial ultrastructure, super-resolution imaging of respiratory chain complexes, and bioenergetic flux measurements. The central hypothesis suggests that specific cristae architectures optimize the spatial distance between proton pumps and ATP synthase, potentially establishing localized pH gradients that enhance metabolic efficiency beyond predictions of bulk membrane theory. Multiphysics simulations, incorporating diffusion and electrostatics, will be performed on membrane geometries derived from tomography data. These findings are expected to link mesoscale membrane architecture directly to metabolic output, providing insights relevant to the study of aging and metabolic diseases. This interdisciplinary project requires the collaboration of mitochondrial biologists, image analysis specialists, and biophysical modelers to achieve its objectives.
background_and_significance: The classical chemiosmotic theory attributes mitochondrial ATP synthesis to a bulk electrochemical proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane. However, this macroscopic model fails to explain the stability of respiration under fluctuating metabolic demands. Recent structural biology suggests that cristae invaginations create distinct sub-compartments, potentially giving rise to emergent mesoscale phenomena. While electron transport chain supercomplexes and membrane curvature are known to be coupled, the influence of specific mesoscale geometries on proton diffusion kinetics remains poorly quantified. Although cryo-electron tomography provides high-resolution ultrastructural snapshots, these data are rarely integrated with kinetic models to assess bioenergetic efficiency. This study investigates the hypothesis that cristae function as kinetic proton traps, where restricted diffusion and electrostatic focusing enhance energy transduction. By synthesizing existing structural datasets, this research aims to transition from qualitative descriptions of mitochondrial morphology to a quantitative biophysical framework. Such an approach may clarify how membrane morphodynamics maintain thermodynamic efficiency, providing insights into aging and metabolic disorders.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This research investigates the emergence of bioenergetic efficiency at the mesoscale through three interrelated questions. First, the study examines how membrane curvature dictates the supramolecular organization of the respiratory chain. It is hypothesized that high-curvature cristae ridges facilitate the assembly of ATP synthase dimers, while planar regions favor electron transport chain supercomplexes to minimize proton diffusion distances. Statistical analysis of tomograms is expected to reveal a non-random distribution of protein densities correlated with local curvature. Second, the project evaluates whether cristae geometries function as proton capacitors independent of the bulk intermembrane space. Narrow cristae junctions may create diffusion barriers that sustain local pH gradients, potentially allowing mitochondria to maintain ATP synthesis during substrate fluctuations. Finally, the study explores how pathological morphological changes compromise this efficiency. It is suggested that cristae linearization and junction widening uncouple proton sources and sinks, leading to increased dissipation and reduced ATP yield, which will be validated through comparative modeling of mutant datasets.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates structural biology, image analysis, and biophysical simulation to construct a mesoscale digital twin of mitochondrial cristae. High-resolution cryo-electron tomography datasets from EMPIAR, alongside atomic models from the PDB and EMDB, will be curated to represent diverse physiological states and genetic backgrounds. Raw tilt series will be processed via IMOD and AreTomo, with AI-driven segmentation generating geometrical scaffolds for subtomogram averaging. These data will inform finite element models in COMSOL or FEniCS, where Nernst-Planck and Poisson equations simulate proton diffusion and local pH microdomains. Agent-based modeling will further investigate whether membrane curvature drives protein segregation. Validation will be conducted through in silico cross-validation, comparing simulated ATP production rates against published oxygen consumption data from mutant cell lines. The interdisciplinary team, comprising a structural biologist, biophysicist, and data scientist, will execute this three-year study to synthesize a comprehensive Mito-Mesoscale Atlas, providing insights into the relationship between mitochondrial architecture and bioenergetic efficiency.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project establishes the Mito-Mesoscale Atlas, an open-access database that correlates mitochondrial geometries from EMPIAR with bioenergetic efficiency metrics to quantify the energetic quality of organelle morphology. A documented Python-based simulation pipeline will be provided, enabling users to input membrane meshes to model proton dynamics and facilitate broader access to mesoscale analysis. Furthermore, a theoretical framework will be developed to characterize cristae junctions as proton batteries, potentially resolving discrepancies between bulk chemiosmotic theory and observed metabolic efficiency. This research shifts the focus of mitochondrial biology from protein-centric models toward a mesoscale perspective, suggesting that membrane geometry acts as a primary regulator of metabolism. Such findings may provide a mechanistic basis for addressing mitochondrial diseases, where therapies targeting membrane curvature could prove as effective as enzyme-focused interventions. Finally, the project supports quantitative training through workshops and ensures long-term sustainability by archiving all data and computational tools on GitHub and Zenodo for future community-led research.
