budget_and_resources: The requested budget supports the collaborative, computational objectives of this synthesis project, focusing exclusively on human capital and infrastructure rather than wet-lab reagents. Two postdoctoral fellows will be appointed to lead the development of finite element models, reaction-diffusion simulations, and the implementation of artificial intelligence for image segmentation and dataset harmonization. A graduate student researcher will assist by curating bioenergetic parameters and validating findings against existing phenotypic data. Computational resources, including cloud services and high-performance computing, are required to train neural networks and execute intensive three-dimensional multiphysics simulations. Furthermore, funding is allocated for bi-annual working group meetings at the NCEMS center to facilitate interdisciplinary collaboration, alongside conference dissemination. Resources are also designated for open-access publication fees and the hosting of a mesoscale modeling workshop to ensure broad accessibility. This investment is expected to extract significant value from existing public microscopy and structural biology data through rigorous computational synthesis and analysis.

title: Ribosome Collisions and the Emergence of Translational Quality Control Mechanisms
abstract: This study investigates the emergent phenomenon of translational bursting and quality control mechanisms resulting from ribosome collisions on mRNA. Although translation is frequently modeled as a linear process, ribosomes often form mesoscale traffic jams that may serve as signals for mRNA degradation or protein folding stress. The research integrates ribosome profiling data, cryo-EM structures of colliding ribosomes, and transcriptomic decay rates to evaluate these interactions. It is hypothesized that the spatial patterning of ribosome queues functions as a mesoscale sensor for cellular stress, potentially integrating codon usage bias and tRNA availability into collective decision-making processes. Analytical models of traffic flow on mRNA tracks will be developed to predict collision probabilities and correlate them with cellular outcomes derived from public datasets. This project is expected to clarify how cells utilize the emergent statistics of ribosome traffic to regulate proteostasis by synthesizing genomics, structural biology, and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.
background_and_significance: The central dogma of molecular biology characterizes translation as the sequential polymerization of amino acids, traditionally modeled through mean-field approximations of codon optimality. This reductionist perspective often overlooks the mesoscale reality of polysomes, where multiple ribosomes occupy a single mRNA transcript. Emergent phenomena, particularly ribosome collisions, arise from these supramolecular assemblies and may function as sophisticated signaling nodes rather than mere translational errors. Specific collision geometries, such as disomes and trisomes, recruit quality control factors like ZNF598 or Hel2 to initiate ribosome-associated quality control. Although structural and genomic datasets exist, a quantitative synthesis connecting sequence-encoded risk landscapes to stochastic translational dynamics remains absent. This project will integrate Ribo-seq data, structural information, and transcriptomic decay profiles to model the grammar of ribosome collisions. By applying non-equilibrium statistical mechanics to existing genomic resources, this study aims to elucidate how mesoscale traffic dynamics influence cellular proteostasis, potentially providing insights into the mechanisms underlying neurodegenerative conditions and translational dysregulation.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This research investigates the polysome as a mesoscale computer that calculates cellular stress through collective ribosomal behavior. The study addresses three primary hypotheses using data synthesis. First, the traffic potential hypothesis suggests that specific non-optimal codon and amino acid combinations create high-friction motifs, which may statistically guarantee ribosome queuing. This will be tested by synthesizing Ribo-seq data across diverse organisms to determine if a Totally Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Process model predicts pile-up density. Second, the structural threshold hypothesis posits that collision interface geometry, identifiable via footprint lengths, dictates biological outcomes such as chaperone recruitment or mRNA decay. This will be validated by correlating Cryo-EM-defined footprint signatures with mRNA half-life datasets. Finally, the distributed sensor hypothesis proposes that global ribosome traffic undergoes a phase transition during stress, acting as a system-wide signal. By analyzing matched Ribo-seq and RNA-seq datasets, this project will investigate whether transcriptome-wide jamming transitions regulate resource reallocation and cell-state transitions under stress conditions.
methods_and_approach: This project utilizes a transdisciplinary synthesis of structural biology, genomics, and theoretical physics to analyze existing datasets without generating new experimental data. Genomic and Ribo-seq information will be harvested from repositories such as GWIPS-viz and the NCBI Sequence Read Archive, while structural coordinates will be extracted from the Protein Data Bank. A uniform Nextflow pipeline will harmonize these data, incorporating structural priors to categorize Ribo-seq reads by footprint size. The study will employ the Totally Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Process (TASEP) to model ribosome flow, integrating interaction terms derived from Cryo-EM data to simulate stall states. Unsupervised machine learning will further classify transcripts into distinct traffic regimes based on ribosome density profiles. Validation will rely on cross-dataset testing, comparing model predictions against independent cell types and knockdown conditions. This three-year effort aims to synthesize a comprehensive traffic atlas, ultimately providing a public web portal for exploring emergent mesoscale ribosome dynamics across diverse transcriptomic states.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to construct a comprehensive Ribosome Traffic Atlas, providing a dynamic, probabilistic perspective on protein synthesis regulation through physical crowding. The study will deliver an open-access database mapping collision hotspots across human and yeast transcriptomes, annotating genes by translatability and jamming risk. Furthermore, an open-source Python-based simulation suite will be developed to enable researchers to model ribosome traffic using RNA-seq data. Mechanistic models will be established to link codon usage to collision probability and subsequent mRNA decay. The research expects to demonstrate that translational bursting is an emergent property of ribosome density, suggesting that cells utilize jamming as a regulatory switch for protein output. These findings may offer significant insights for synthetic biology by optimizing transgene design and for medicine by identifying therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative diseases associated with ribosome stalling. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed journals and community workshops, with the atlas maintained on permanent infrastructure to ensure long-term accessibility.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget allocates resources exclusively to human capital, computational infrastructure, and collaborative activities, reflecting the requirements of a synthesis project devoid of wet-lab expenditures. Personnel costs, comprising 70% of the budget, support two postdoctoral fellows for 2.5 years to manage transcriptomic data processing and develop non-equilibrium statistical mechanics models. A graduate student researcher will focus on machine learning clustering and web development for the Ribosome Traffic Atlas over three years, while principal investigators receive partial salary support for project oversight. Computational resources, accounting for 10% of the budget, facilitate cloud-based processing of large-scale genomic datasets and extensive Monte Carlo simulations. Travel funding supports bi-annual working group meetings and conference dissemination to foster interdisciplinary collaboration. Finally, 5% of the budget is dedicated to open science initiatives, including hackathons for training and open-access publication fees. This investment strategy prioritizes the transdisciplinary expertise necessary to model emergent biological complexity at the genome scale.

title: Hydrodynamic Coupling and Emergent Synchronization Mechanisms in Ciliary Arrays
abstract: This study investigates the emergence of metachronal waves, characterized by coordinated beating patterns, within dense ciliary arrays found in airway and ventricular tissues. Although individual cilia possess intrinsic beat frequencies, macroscopic wave formation is considered an emergent property driven by hydrodynamic coupling. The research integrates high-speed video microscopy, structural axoneme data from the Protein Data Bank, and established fluid dynamics parameters. It is hypothesized that emergent synchronization remains robust against noise and individual defects due to long-range hydrodynamic interactions at the mesoscale. Computational fluid dynamics, coupled with elastic rod models, will be employed to simulate these ciliary fields. These investigations are expected to clarify the mechanisms underlying robust biological fluid transport and elucidate how disruptions in synchronization contribute to the pathogenesis of ciliopathies. This project requires a transdisciplinary approach, necessitating collaboration between fluid dynamicists, cell biologists, and computational physicists to analyze the complex interactions governing these biological systems.
background_and_significance: The biological mesoscale represents a critical domain where complex behaviors emerge from molecular components, exemplified by metachronal waves in ciliary arrays. Although the axoneme structure and macroscopic fluid transport are well-documented, the mechanism facilitating the spontaneous synchronization of thousands of cilia remains poorly understood. Current evidence suggests that this coordination arises from hydrodynamic coupling rather than centralized signaling, as individual ciliary beats exert drag forces on neighboring organelles. Existing research is currently bifurcated between high-resolution structural data and idealized fluid dynamic models that often lack biological realism. This project aims to bridge this gap by integrating disparate datasets, including atomic structures, high-speed microscopy, and rheological measurements, into a unified physics-based simulation. Such synthesis is essential for understanding ciliopathies, where individual motility persists despite a failure in collective synchronization. By mapping molecular stiffness to kinematic waveforms, this study will develop data-driven models to elucidate how robust order emerges from the stochastic activity of biological oscillators.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This research investigates the emergence of mesoscale synchronization by bridging molecular structure and tissue-level function through three interrelated inquiries. First, the study examines how axonemal stiffness, determined by molecular composition, constrains synchronization boundaries. It is hypothesized that the Sperm number dictates these limits, where variations in dynein structure may disrupt coherence. This will be validated by correlating calculated bending moduli from structural data with kinematic observations of ciliary arrays. Second, the project evaluates whether hydrodynamic coupling ensures metachronal wave robustness against stochastic noise and defects. The hypothesis suggests that long-range interactions provide a smoothing effect, buffering against localized failures. This will be tested using computational models informed by public image repositories to simulate lattice defects. Finally, the research explores how fluid rheology influences the transition to synchronized beating. It is expected that pathological viscoelasticity may sever hydrodynamic communication, independent of ciliary damage. This will be assessed by benchmarking model predictions against historical clinical clearance data.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates structural biology, computer vision, and computational fluid dynamics to synthesize publicly available data into a unified model of ciliary motion. Structural data from the RCSB Protein Data Bank and EM Data Bank will define the elastic moduli of axonemal components, while kinematic datasets from the BioImage Archive and open-access literature will provide high-speed video of ciliated tissues. Genetic associations from the Human Cell Atlas and ClinVar will further contextualize these structural defects. An OMERO-based pipeline will standardize heterogeneous video formats, utilizing U-Net architectures to generate a harmonized dataset of digital cilia waveforms. A multi-scale physics model will employ Finite Element Analysis to derive Kirchhoff Elastic Rod parameters, which are then driven by these waveforms and coupled via the Method of Regularized Stokeslets. Validation will involve leave-one-out cross-validation across diverse organisms and known ciliopathy mutants. This interdisciplinary effort aims to establish a robust, predictive framework for mesoscale ciliary fluid interactions.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project introduces the OpenCilia Synthesis Engine, an open-source computational framework designed to integrate molecular structure with fluid dynamics for predicting ciliary behavior. By utilizing parameters derived from public data repositories, this tool addresses limitations inherent in existing theoretical models. The study will produce a harmonized database of ciliary beat waveforms, transforming unstructured microscopy video into a queryable quantitative resource linked to genetic backgrounds. Furthermore, a validated biophysical model will define a phase diagram of emergence, mapping how stiffness, density, and viscosity influence synchronization. This framework may facilitate the development of virtual phenotype predictors, allowing clinicians to assess the severity of primary ciliary dyskinesia variants based on structural data. Ultimately, this research advances the understanding of biological emergence by elucidating the physical interactions governing cellular function. The project will also foster interdisciplinary expertise in data mining and computational physics, while disseminating findings through a dedicated web portal and academic workshops to support the broader scientific community.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget supports the intellectual synthesis and computational requirements for mesoscale simulations, excluding wet-lab reagents or equipment. Personnel funding of $450,000 covers two postdoctoral fellows for 2.5 years and one graduate research assistant for two years. The first fellow will develop Immersed Boundary/Stokeslets fluid models integrated with elastic rod theory, while the second will utilize U-Net pipelines to extract kinematic data from the BioImage Archive and PDB. The graduate assistant will manage documentation, workflow reproducibility, and community engagement. Computational resources totaling $60,000 provide access to high-performance computing for simulating interacting cilia and storing processed datasets. Travel funds of $40,000 facilitate bi-annual interdisciplinary meetings and conference dissemination, while $15,000 supports open-access publication and project infrastructure. This financial structure leverages NCEMS support to assemble a specialized team and computational framework, enabling the integration of disparate fields through intellectual and numerical synthesis that exceeds the scope of standard individual research grants.

title: Extracellular Matrix as Mechanical Memory: Emergent Reciprocity in Tissue Homeostasis
abstract: This research investigates the emergent reciprocity between cells and the extracellular matrix (ECM), which functions as a dynamic mesoscale material capable of accumulating mechanical memory through structural remodeling. The study integrates atomic force microscopy maps of tissue stiffness, RNA-seq data concerning matrix-remodeling enzymes, and histological imaging to characterize these interactions. A central objective involves determining how localized remodeling events integrate over time to generate stiffness gradients that influence cell migration and differentiation. Agent-based models will be employed, wherein cells modify a finite-element mesh representing the ECM based on local strain, thereby establishing a continuous feedback loop. It is expected that these findings will clarify how fibrosis may emerge as a runaway consequence of this mechanical memory process. This project requires support from the NCEMS to facilitate a multidisciplinary collaboration between tissue engineers, data scientists, and mechanobiologists to advance the current understanding of these complex cellular and mechanical dynamics.
background_and_significance: The extracellular matrix is increasingly recognized as a dynamic environment that actively regulates cellular behavior through mechanical signaling and bidirectional feedback loops. While molecular components and macroscopic tissue properties are well-documented, a significant knowledge gap persists regarding the mesoscale supramolecular architecture that facilitates mechanical memory. This phenomenon occurs when transient cellular forces induce permanent alterations in tissue topology, such as collagen fiber alignment and enzymatic crosslinking. Although these emergent properties are essential for tissue homeostasis, their dysregulation is frequently associated with fibrosis and cancer progression. Current research remains fragmented, with transcriptomic data, atomic force microscopy, and structural imaging existing in isolated silos. This study aims to synthesize these disparate datasets to establish a comprehensive model linking molecular remodeling to mesoscale structural outcomes. By integrating transcriptomic profiles with biophysical maps, this project will investigate how molecular inputs drive emergent mechanical phenomena, ultimately clarifying the mechanisms underlying self-perpetuating fibrosis and collective cell migration patterns.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates the emergent nature of extracellular matrix mechanical memory through the synthesis of existing datasets and computational modeling. The first objective examines how transient molecular expression patterns translate into permanent mesoscale topology, testing the hypothesis that mechanical memory requires a specific stoichiometric ratio of crosslinking enzymes and matrix metalloproteinases. By integrating spatial transcriptomics with histological fiber analysis, this study aims to define the quantitative parameters of this memory. The second objective explores whether mesoscale stiffness creates a feedback loop driving myofibroblast differentiation. Synthesizing longitudinal single-cell RNA sequencing with time-series atomic force microscopy may identify a critical stiffness threshold that sustains fibrotic states independently of inflammatory signaling. Finally, the project evaluates how mechanical memory guides collective cell migration. Agent-based models, parameterized by existing migration assays and traction force microscopy, will be used to determine if matrix modifications alone facilitate the transition from random cellular movement to ordered, stigmergic migration streams during development and metastasis.
methods_and_approach: This project employs a rigorous data synthesis and computational modeling strategy to investigate extracellular matrix (ECM)-cell reciprocity. Rather than generating new data, the study harmonizes heterogeneous datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus, Human Cell Atlas, Atomic Force Microscopy Data Bank, and BioImage Archive to parameterize a multi-scale model. A Common Coordinate Framework will integrate transcriptomic profiles, stiffness maps, and structural imaging into a unified digital tissue volume. The research utilizes a hybrid framework, coupling Finite Element Analysis for the viscoelastic ECM with an Agent-Based Model for cellular behavior. This approach simulates feedback loops where mechanical strain influences gene expression, subsequently modifying the local ECM architecture. Validation will be conducted through leave-one-out cross-validation, comparing model predictions against late-stage fibrosis datasets and live-cell imaging. This transdisciplinary effort, involving computational biologists, mechanobiologists, and mathematicians, is expected to elucidate the mechanisms of emergent reciprocity, providing a robust framework for understanding tissue remodeling and disease progression.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This synthesis project aims to advance molecular and cellular biosciences by providing integrated resources and theoretical frameworks. The Matri-Mechanics database will serve as a harmonized repository, linking transcriptomic profiles of matrix-remodeling enzymes with quantitative biophysical properties such as Young’s modulus and fiber alignment. Furthermore, the ECM-Memory engine, a containerized simulation framework combining agent-based and finite element modeling, will allow researchers to investigate how gene expression perturbations influence tissue-level mechanics. Predictive models of fibrosis will be developed to identify mechanical tipping points, potentially revealing new therapeutic windows for disease intervention. This work characterizes the extracellular matrix as an active, memory-encoding medium, bridging the gap between molecular biology and tissue physiology. By elucidating the mechanisms of mesoscale emergence, the study addresses how molecular crosslinking generates stiffness gradients. Finally, the project will facilitate interdisciplinary training and provide a blueprint for digital twin initiatives, while disseminating findings through open-access publications and workshops to inform future biomaterial design and regenerative medicine strategies.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget allocates resources exclusively to personnel and computational infrastructure, as the project involves no wet-lab experimentation. Funding for personnel, totaling $450,000 over three years, supports two full-time postdoctoral fellows and one graduate student to facilitate data synthesis and modeling. These researchers will manage transcriptomic data harmonization, spatial mapping, and the integration of atomic force microscopy data into coupled finite element and agent-based models. Computational requirements, estimated at $40,000, provide essential high-performance cloud resources for simulating complex local strain fields and maintaining secure, redundant storage for large-scale datasets. An additional $50,000 supports transdisciplinary collaboration through biannual synthesis meetings, conference dissemination, and open-access publication fees. Furthermore, the budget includes provisions for a mesoscale synthesis hackathon and training workshops to promote the utility of the developed simulation tools. This investment in human capital and open science infrastructure is expected to ensure the rigorous translation of biological data into predictive physical models for the broader scientific community.

title: The Glycocalyx Code: Emergent Immune Evasion Mediated by Bulky Glycan Shields
abstract: This study investigates the cell surface glycocalyx, a dense mesoscale carbohydrate layer, and its role in regulating immune cell accessibility. It is hypothesized that the physical height and density of this structure function as a kinetic trap for immune receptors, representing a biophysical barrier independent of chemical recognition. The research integrates glycomics data, atomic force microscopy measurements of surface topography, and immune cell adhesion assays. By modeling the steric repulsion and thermodynamic entropy of the polymer brush layer, the project aims to predict specific thresholds for immune evasion. These findings may elucidate how cancer cells utilize this emergent physical barrier to circumvent T-cell-mediated destruction, potentially informing future immunotherapeutic strategies. This interdisciplinary approach necessitates the synthesis of glycobiology, polymer physics, and immunology to characterize the mechanisms governing immune cell interactions. The resulting model is expected to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding how glycocalyx properties influence cellular immune responses.
background_and_significance: The cell surface is characterized by the glycocalyx, a complex mesoscale array of sugar chains extending up to 1000 nm from the membrane. Although molecular pathways of glycosylation are well-documented, the emergent physical properties of this collective structure remain poorly understood. Current immunological paradigms emphasize chemical recognition, often neglecting the physical barrier imposed by bulky glycoproteins like MUC1 and MUC16. These molecules form a dense polymer brush layer, where increased density and height exponentially elevate the entropic cost of membrane compression. This barrier function arises from the collective rigidity and hydration of the assembly rather than individual molecular interactions. Despite the availability of extensive transcriptomic and biophysical datasets, these domains remain siloed, obscuring the mechanism of immune evasion known as the kinetic trap. This project will synthesize disparate data types to model the glycocalyx as a biophysical shield, investigating how mesoscale organization prevents the close apposition required for immunological synapse formation and subsequent immune recognition.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This research investigates the glycocalyx as an emergent biophysical gatekeeper by synthesizing existing public datasets. The study first examines how the transcriptional landscape of glycosyltransferases and mucin core proteins dictates mesoscale topology. It is hypothesized that specific signatures, defined by the ratio of long-chain mucin expression to branching enzymes, predict cell surface polymer height and stiffness. Second, the project explores whether a thermodynamic phase transition in glycocalyx density renders immune receptor engagement energetically unfavorable. This threshold behavior suggests that when the entropic penalty of polymer compression exceeds the binding energy of the TCR-pMHC complex, immune cells are mechanically excluded. Finally, the study evaluates whether a derived biophysical barrier score predicts immunotherapy failure more effectively than tumor mutational burden. By leveraging inherent heterogeneity in public transcriptomic and clinical data, this work aims to validate whether the mesoscale physical barrier serves as a distinct mechanism of immune evasion, independent of tumor antigen load.
methods_and_approach: This project utilizes a transdisciplinary synthesis of bioinformatics, structural biology, and soft matter physics to construct a Virtual Glycocalyx pipeline. By integrating data from The Cancer Genome Atlas, GlyGen, and the Protein Data Bank, the study aims to harmonize transcriptomic, glycomic, and biophysical information. A machine learning model will be developed to infer glycan structures and densities from gene expression profiles. These parameters will inform Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics and Self-Consistent Field Theory simulations to represent the glycocalyx as a grafted polymer brush. The resulting steric potential, representing the energy required to compress the glycocalyx to the height of the T-cell receptor complex, will be used to calculate a Biophysical Barrier Score. This score is expected to predict T-cell exclusion and clinical responses to checkpoint inhibitors. Validation will involve correlating these scores with histological immune infiltration patterns and patient outcomes from existing clinical trial datasets, ultimately providing a framework for assessing tumor immune evasion.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to develop the Glyco-Barrier Atlas, a multidimensional map characterizing the biophysical properties of cell surfaces across diverse cancer types. The study will produce an integrated database linking gene expression, predicted glycan structures, and biophysical parameters for over 10,000 tumor samples. Furthermore, an open-source Python package, GlycoPhysics, will be developed to enable researchers to derive polymer brush parameters and immune evasion probabilities from RNA-seq data. A validated theoretical framework will also be established to describe how molecular glycosylation variations generate mesoscale exclusion zones, thereby regulating cell-cell interactions through emergent physical forces. This research suggests that transcriptomic profiles dictate cell surface physical barriers, potentially shifting the focus of immunology toward the glycocalyx. Clinically, identifying thresholds for immune exclusion may prevent the administration of ineffective immunotherapies. Therapeutic strategies could involve enzymatic modification of the glycocalyx to reduce physical barriers, which will be disseminated through academic publications, specialized conferences, and training workshops for the scientific community.
budget_and_resources: The requested budget facilitates the intellectual labor and computational infrastructure essential for high-level synthesis. Personnel funding supports two postdoctoral fellows, one specializing in bioinformatics and immunology for data integration, and another in soft matter physics for model development. A graduate student will assist with data curation and database construction, while a part-time scientific programmer will ensure code professionalization and containerization. Computational resources are allocated for cloud-based machine learning training and high-performance computing for physics simulations. Travel funds support bi-annual working group meetings and conference dissemination to foster transdisciplinary collaboration. Additionally, resources are designated for open-access publication fees, web hosting, and a virtual summer workshop on mesoscale data synthesis. This budget prioritizes personnel and computational capacity over material costs, aligning with the mandate for synthesis without new data generation. This investment in diverse expertise is expected to facilitate the cross-pollination of ideas required to address the emergent complexities of the glycocalyx.

title: Symmetry Breaking in the Centrosome and the Emergence of Spindle Bipolarity
abstract: This project investigates the emergent phenomenon of symmetry breaking during bipolar spindle assembly, a process wherein the centrosome must duplicate and separate to define the axis of cell division. The study integrates high-content screening image data of mitosis, phosphoproteomic time-course measurements, and protein interaction networks to characterize this transition. It is hypothesized that the shift from a monopolar to a bipolar state represents an emergent bifurcation driven by a threshold in motor protein forces and kinase activity gradients. Dynamical systems theory will be employed to model the stability landscape of spindle poles based on these integrated molecular datasets. This analysis is expected to identify the critical control parameters that ensure robust symmetry breaking, a mechanism frequently compromised in oncogenesis. The interdisciplinary research framework necessitates the collaboration of cell biologists, mathematicians, and image analysis experts to elucidate the regulatory principles governing spindle formation and its potential implications for cancer pathology.
background_and_significance: Accurate chromosome segregation during mitosis depends on the formation of a bipolar spindle, a process driven by the centrosome cycle. This symmetry-breaking event requires duplicated centrosomes to migrate to opposite nuclear poles, a mechanism often disrupted in aneuploidy and tumorigenesis. Although molecular components such as Eg5 and Nek2 are well-characterized, the principles governing their self-organization into robust bipolar structures remain poorly understood. Current evidence suggests that centrosome separation functions as a bi-stable system, indicating an underlying bifurcation in the forces regulating spindle assembly. Existing data from phenotypic screens, phosphoproteomic databases, and interaction networks remain fragmented, preventing a comprehensive understanding of the quantitative thresholds that dictate separation. This project aims to bridge these modalities by integrating static interaction maps with dynamic phenotypic data to model the mesoscale properties of the pericentriolar material. By analyzing these public repositories, the study will characterize the stability landscapes of spindle formation, providing insights into the emergent dynamics of mitotic symmetry breaking.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates the premise that spindle bipolarity emerges from the non-linear coupling of phosphorylation gradients and motor-driven forces. The study first examines the stability landscape of centrosome separation, hypothesizing that this transition represents a pitchfork bifurcation governed by the ratio of Eg5-mediated outward forces to inward-tethering cohesion. Analysis of MitoCheck imaging data and mass-spectrometry datasets is expected to reveal a discontinuity in separation velocities linked to specific linker protein phosphorylation thresholds. Second, the research explores how pericentriolar material (PCM) maturation influences symmetry breaking robustness. By utilizing volumetric data from public repositories, the study evaluates whether PCM density acts as a mechanical dampener that filters stochastic motor forces. Finally, the project assesses whether protein-protein interaction network topologies predict symmetry breaking failures in cancer. Mapping TCGA and DepMap expression data onto these networks may identify fragile motifs, which will be validated by cross-referencing predicted synthetic lethality with observed drug sensitivity in CRISPR screens.
methods_and_approach: This project employs a three-phase workflow to achieve community-scale synthesis of centrosome dynamics, integrating expertise from cell biology, mathematics, and data science. The initial phase involves data harmonization from the MitoCheck, MitoSys, PhosphoSitePlus, Phosida, BioGRID, IntAct, and Human Protein Atlas databases. These data will inform a Spindle-Knowledge-Graph, utilizing Graph Neural Networks to impute interaction weights and establish spatial constraints. Subsequently, a dynamical systems model will be constructed using differential equations to describe pole positioning, where force terms are derived directly from the integrated knowledge graph. Bifurcation analysis will be applied to identify stability transitions between monopolar and bipolar states. Finally, the model will be validated by simulating protein knockdowns and comparing predicted spindle phenotypes against historical RNAi and CRISPR screening data. An F1-score exceeding 0.8 is expected to confirm model accuracy. This interdisciplinary approach leverages complementary expertise to resolve complex biological mechanisms that remain inaccessible to individual research groups.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to develop the first multi-scale, quantitative model of centrosome symmetry breaking using exclusively public data. The study will produce an executable Python-based dynamical model, hosted on BioModels, which predicts spindle polarity outcomes based on molecular concentrations and phosphorylation states. Furthermore, a harmonized dataset linking protein network topology with quantitative phenotypic metrics will be generated through the re-analysis of raw images from the Image Data Resource. This research will identify critical control parameters, specifically molecular ratios that dictate bifurcation points, potentially explaining centrosome amplification in cancer cells. The study will demonstrate that spindle bipolarity remains robust to molecular noise up to a threshold defined by network topology, illustrating how lower-level molecular data explains higher-level organelle behavior. Finally, the identification of fragile nodes within the symmetry-breaking network may reveal therapeutic targets capable of inducing catastrophic multipolarity in cancer cells, while sparing healthy tissue. These findings will be disseminated through specialized workshops and peer-reviewed interdisciplinary publications.
budget_and_resources: The requested budget provides the necessary personnel and computational infrastructure to facilitate high-throughput data synthesis. Funding for human capital includes two full-time postdoctoral fellows tasked with developing image analysis pipelines, constructing graph networks, and performing dynamical systems modeling with bifurcation analysis. A graduate student will contribute fifty percent effort toward biological curation, literature cross-referencing, and the validation of model outputs. Computational resources, including cloud computing credits, are required to process extensive time-lapse imaging data from the Image Data Resource and to support the training of graph neural networks. Furthermore, funds are allocated for quarterly working group meetings to ensure interdisciplinary integration, alongside travel for the dissemination of findings at international conferences. Additional resources support open science initiatives, including hackathon hosting, open-access publication fees, and long-term data preservation. This allocation focuses exclusively on intellectual synthesis and computational integration, ensuring strict adherence to the mandate of the National Center for Excellence in Molecular Systems.

title: Mechanisms of Autophagosome Biogenesis via Emergent Membrane Remodeling from Protein Scaffolds
abstract: This research investigates the de novo formation of the autophagosome, a mesoscale organelle generated through the structural remodeling of membrane sheets. The study synthesizes data concerning Atg protein interactions, membrane curvature sensing, and lipid composition during cellular starvation responses. A primary objective is to determine how soluble protein machinery facilitates the topological transition required to transform a flat membrane into a closed vesicle. Analytical methods will employ Helfrich bending energy models integrated with protein density fields derived from quantitative fluorescence microscopy. This investigation is expected to elucidate the energetic requirements for mesoscale membrane remodeling and clarify how these processes are regulated by cellular energy states. The project requires an interdisciplinary approach, combining expertise from membrane biophysics, autophagy research, and computational geometry. These findings may provide a comprehensive understanding of the mechanical principles governing autophagosome biogenesis and the broader implications of membrane curvature in cellular homeostasis.
background_and_significance: Mesoscale cellular organization, situated between molecular structural biology and organelle-scale dynamics, represents a significant challenge in modern bioscience, particularly regarding autophagosome biogenesis. Although the molecular components of autophagy are well-cataloged and organelle dynamics are visualized via live-cell imaging, the physical principles governing the transition from protein-lipid assemblies to complex vesicles remain poorly understood. This study investigates the cup-to-sphere topological transformation by integrating disparate data from the Protein Data Bank, the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive, and the Image Data Resource. Current reductionist models fail to explain how transient interactions between Atg proteins and lipid bilayers facilitate sustained membrane curvature and fission. By synthesizing existing structural, kinetic, and imaging parameters, this research aims to develop a unified theoretical framework for membrane remodeling. This approach will characterize how protein wetting and scaffolding overcome energy barriers, providing a rigorous physical description of emergent system properties that individual protein analysis cannot currently predict.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This research project investigates the emergent physical properties of the expanding phagophore by testing three interrelated biophysical hypotheses. First, the study examines whether membrane curvature arises from a crowding pressure mechanism rather than the intrinsic curvature of individual proteins. By correlating protein density maps from the IDR with membrane geometry from EMPIAR, the analysis will determine if curvature scales non-linearly with density. Second, the project evaluates the energetic contribution of lipid composition to vesicle closure. Integrating lipidomics data from LipidMaps and PRIDE into a continuum membrane model may reveal how localized enrichment of cone-shaped lipids lowers the line tension energy barrier. Finally, the study explores how Atg2-mediated lipid flow stabilizes the growing membrane against collapse. A dynamic flux model will be constructed to assess whether known lipid transfer rates generate sufficient hydrodynamic pressure to maintain the phagophore’s cup shape. These integrated analyses are expected to clarify the mechanical equilibrium governing autophagosome formation and maturation.
methods_and_approach: This project constructs a digital twin of the mesoscale autophagosome by synthesizing heterogeneous public data through a transdisciplinary framework. Data are systematically harvested from repositories including the Protein Data Bank, EMPIAR, and the Image Data Resource to capture structural, ultrastructural, and omics information. These disparate inputs are harmonized into a Mesoscale Atlas, where spatial registration algorithms map atomic coordinates onto triangulated membrane meshes. Analytical methods incorporate Helfrich bending energy models, augmented by protein-lipid coupling terms, to characterize membrane mechanics. Furthermore, graph neural networks predict protein clustering behaviors, while phase-field simulations model temporal topological changes. The research team integrates expertise in cell biology, computational geometry, and biophysics to constrain these models. Validation relies on cross-modal consistency checks, comparing predicted curvature against cryo-electron tomography volumes and employing leave-one-out testing across yeast and mammalian datasets. This three-year study is expected to refine the digital twin through iterative parameter fitting, ultimately providing a comprehensive, data-driven representation of autophagosomal dynamics.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to develop a quantitatively rigorous, multi-scale physical model of autophagosome biogenesis using publicly available data. The primary deliverable is an open-source simulation framework, the Autophagy Digital Twin, which predicts membrane morphology based on Atg protein and lipid concentrations. This tool facilitates in silico genetic screens to evaluate how specific mutations influence membrane closure energetics. Furthermore, an integrated mesoscale dataset will harmonize PDB structures, EMPIAR volumes, and IDR imaging data to serve as a template for organelle organization. The study expects to define the energy budget of autophagy by quantifying the chemical and binding energy required for membrane deformation. These findings may shift the field toward quantitative membrane mechanics, potentially identifying physical constraints relevant to neurodegenerative conditions like Parkinson’s disease. Results will be disseminated through interdisciplinary journals and workshops, while long-term accessibility is ensured by depositing models and code in persistent repositories, thereby supporting future synthesis research in molecular and cellular biology.
budget_and_resources: This budget request prioritizes the intellectual infrastructure necessary for high-level synthesis over wet-lab consumables. Personnel funding supports two postdoctoral fellows, specializing in computational biophysics and bioinformatics, to harmonize datasets and construct models, alongside one graduate student dedicated to data curation and visualization. To facilitate interdisciplinary collaboration, the project includes three annual five-day working group meetings at NCEMS for twelve participants, covering travel, lodging, and facility expenses. Computational requirements involve cloud credits for training graph neural networks and hosting cryo-ET image datasets, supplemented by high-performance computing allocations for phase-field simulations. Dissemination efforts encompass open-access publication fees, maintenance of the Autophagy Digital Twin web portal, and conference travel for fellows. Finally, the budget provides forty thousand dollars to host a summer school on mesoscale data synthesis in the third year, training twenty graduate students in the developed methodologies. This allocation ensures the necessary human capital, computational resources, and collaborative frameworks required to achieve the project objectives.

title: Emergent Sorting Mechanisms in RNA Phase Separation Between Stress Granules and P-Bodies
abstract: This study investigates the mechanisms underlying the emergent immiscibility and selective sorting of RNA between stress granules and P-bodies. Although both organelles exhibit liquid-like properties, they maintain distinct molecular compositions that suggest a complex regulatory framework. The research integrates RNA-seq data from isolated granules, phase diagrams of RNA-binding proteins, and super-resolution imaging to characterize the coexistence of these condensates. It is hypothesized that the observed miscibility gap arises from the competition between specific RNA-RNA base pairing and non-specific protein-RNA interactions. To evaluate this, multicomponent Flory-Huggins solution theory will be adapted to model sequence-specific interactions and predict sorting behavior. This interdisciplinary approach, involving RNA biology, thermodynamics, and data science, is expected to elucidate the physical principles governing membrane-less compartmentalization within the cell. These findings may provide a comprehensive understanding of how cells spatially organize RNA processing pathways to maintain homeostasis under varying physiological conditions.
background_and_significance: Eukaryotic cellular organization relies on compartmentalization, particularly through membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation. Stress granules and processing bodies represent prominent ribonucleoprotein condensates that maintain distinct identities despite their shared biophysical properties. Although these structures frequently interact, they remain immiscible, suggesting that specific mechanisms govern the sorting of RNA and protein cargo. Current research remains fragmented, as isolated studies utilize inconsistent methodologies to characterize condensate composition. Consequently, a unified physical framework explaining the thermodynamic rules of transcript partitioning is currently absent. This project addresses this knowledge gap by synthesizing publicly available datasets, including high-throughput sequencing and biophysical phase diagrams. By integrating RNA biology, soft matter physics, and data science, this study aims to elucidate the emergent principles of ribonucleoprotein sorting. Understanding these mechanisms is expected to clarify how cells regulate gene expression under stress and provide insights into the pathological aggregation processes associated with neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates the mesoscale sorting of RNA by synthesizing existing datasets to address three fundamental questions regarding granule formation. First, the molecular grammar of RNA partitioning between stress granules and P-bodies is examined. It is hypothesized that transcript length, secondary structure, and specific sequence motifs dictate localization, with longer, structured RNAs favoring stress granules. Machine learning models trained on RIP-seq and CLIP-seq data will evaluate these predictive features. Second, the study explores whether the miscibility gap between these granules arises from the competition between non-specific and specific molecular interactions. The interaction network distance between granule scaffolds, derived from protein-protein interaction databases, will be mapped onto multicomponent Flory-Huggins phase diagrams to assess thermodynamic barriers. Finally, the project investigates how mesoscale properties like viscosity and surface tension enforce cargo sorting. RNAs acting as surfactants may localize to phase interfaces, a hypothesis that will be validated by correlating super-resolution imaging data with transcriptomic affinity metrics.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates bioinformatics, machine learning, and theoretical physics to synthesize publicly available data regarding stress granules and P-bodies. Transcriptomic data from GEO, ArrayExpress, and ENCODE, alongside proteomic datasets from PRIDE, BioGRID, and IntAct, will be harmonized using a Nextflow pipeline and Combat-seq. Biophysical parameters from PhaSePro and LLPSDB, combined with super-resolution imaging from the IDR, will populate a Neo4j-based Granule Knowledge Graph. Computational synthesis involves a Random Forest and Graph Neural Network classifier to predict RNA localization based on sequence features and secondary structure probabilities. Furthermore, multicomponent Flory-Huggins solution theory will be applied to simulate phase behavior and calculate the free energy of mixing for granule components. The three-year timeline encompasses data ingestion, model training, and physical validation. Validation will be conducted through leave-one-out cross-validation and testing against independent datasets, such as APEX-seq, to ensure the robustness of the predictive models and the theoretical framework regarding granule miscibility and structure.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to establish a comprehensive physical model of RNA sorting between membraneless organelles, transitioning the field from descriptive phenomenology toward predictive mechanics. The research will produce a Phase Sorting Atlas, an open-access database integrating transcriptomic and proteomic data for stress granules and P-bodies, annotated with relevant biophysical properties. Furthermore, the development of GranuleSort, an open-source computational tool, will enable researchers to predict RNA partitioning probabilities between these organelles and the cytoplasm. A theoretical framework describing the thermodynamic miscibility gap will also be formulated, providing insights applicable to diverse multiphase cellular systems. By elucidating the rules of mesoscale sorting, this study may clarify how cells organize biochemistry without membranes, with implications for understanding viral replication and neurodegenerative aggregation. Findings will be disseminated through interdisciplinary journals and technical workshops. Long-term accessibility of the developed tools and datasets will be ensured through permanent hosting on Zenodo and GitHub, facilitating continued utility for the broader scientific community.
budget_and_resources: The requested budget facilitates the intellectual labor and computational infrastructure necessary for comprehensive data synthesis. Personnel costs of $450,000 support two postdoctoral fellows specializing in computational biology and soft matter physics, who will oversee data harmonization, classifier development, and thermodynamic modeling. A graduate student will assist with data curation and literature annotation during summer rotations. Computational resources totaling $40,000 provide access to cloud platforms for deep learning and high-performance computing clusters for parallelized sequencing analysis. Travel funds of $35,000 enable biannual working group meetings at the NCEMS center and dissemination of findings at professional conferences. Additionally, $10,000 is allocated for open-access publication fees and the maintenance of the GranuleSort web-based tool. This financial plan prioritizes human capital and computational capacity, which are identified as the primary drivers of this research. In accordance with the NCEMS mandate, no funds are designated for wet-lab reagents, ensuring that all resources remain focused on the synthesis of existing data.

title: Emergent Proteostasis Failure and the Collapse of the Chaperone Network in Aging
abstract: This project investigates system-level protein folding failure, a phenomenon frequently associated with aging and disease progression. Although the chaperone network functions as a collective buffer, its capacity remains inherently finite. This study integrates proteomics data quantifying chaperone levels across various ages with existing protein aggregation and folding stability datasets. The research addresses whether a sharp percolation threshold exists, beyond which the chaperone network loses connectivity and triggers systemic collapse. The chaperone system is modeled as a flow network where capacity constraints may induce emergent congestion. This analysis is expected to define critical tipping points of proteostasis, potentially providing a theoretical framework for the sudden onset of age-related pathologies. Achieving these objectives requires an interdisciplinary approach involving systems biologists, network theorists, and gerontologists. By characterizing these network dynamics, the study aims to clarify the mechanisms underlying the transition from homeostatic protein maintenance to widespread proteostatic failure in biological systems.
background_and_significance: Proteostasis is essential for cellular viability, yet the mechanisms governing the mesoscale transition between individual molecular folding and systemic failure remain poorly understood. While thermodynamics of chaperone machines like Hsp70 are well-characterized, the collective, emergent behavior of the chaperome during aging requires further investigation. Current literature suggests that proteostasis collapse may represent a non-linear, catastrophic phase transition rather than a gradual accumulation of damage. This project aims to synthesize existing quantitative proteomics data from model organisms and human tissues with established protein aggregation and interaction networks. By modeling the chaperome as a capacity-constrained flow network, this study will investigate whether proteostasis failure corresponds to a percolation threshold where buffering capacity is saturated. Integrating these disparate datasets is expected to provide a predictive, mechanistic framework for identifying the tipping points of cellular health. Such an approach may facilitate the development of therapeutic strategies designed to reinforce the resilience of the entire mesoscale network.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This research investigates the emergent nature of proteostasis failure through three interconnected inquiries. First, the study examines whether the chaperone network exhibits a critical percolation threshold relative to the unfolded protein load. It is hypothesized that proteostasis collapse represents a phase transition, where functional connectivity is maintained until a specific ratio of unfolding load to chaperone capacity is exceeded, triggering non-linear aggregate formation. This will be validated by correlating age-stratified proteomics data with archival aggregation records. Second, the project explores whether keystone nodes within the chaperone network disproportionately influence system-wide stability. The hypothesis suggests that the depletion of specific hub co-chaperones drives network fragmentation more effectively than general abundance reductions. This will be tested using graph theory simulations on protein-protein interaction databases compared against existing CRISPR knockout screens. Finally, the study evaluates how age-related macromolecular crowding influences network topology by reducing chaperone diffusion rates, potentially providing more accurate kinetic models of protein aggregation.
methods_and_approach: This project employs a transdisciplinary synthesis of data engineering, network physics, and systems biology to investigate proteostasis using publicly available datasets. Data will be harvested from PRIDE, PaxDb, BioGRID, IntAct, AmyloGraph, CPAD, ProThermDB, and AlphaFold DB to characterize protein abundance, interactions, and stability across multiple species. These disparate sources will be harmonized into a unified SQL database, utilizing Uniprot identifiers and quantile normalization to ensure cross-species interoperability. Computational modeling will involve constructing weighted graphs where edges represent dynamic interactions between chaperones and client proteins. The network will be analyzed as a flow system, where folding demand is defined by unstable protein synthesis and folding capacity is provided by chaperone nodes. Percolation analysis will simulate aging by adjusting node abundances to identify connectivity thresholds. Validation will rely on retro-diction, testing whether model-predicted network collapse correlates with observed aggregation phenotypes in held-out datasets. This three-year study aims to refine a Proteostasis Risk Index through iterative cross-species validation.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to provide a theoretical framework for aging research by defining the Proteostasis Percolation Threshold, which quantifies the failure point of chaperone networks. By transitioning from qualitative descriptions of cellular decline to precise metrics of system collapse, this study addresses how individual protein interactions contribute to collective health. The research will produce the Harmonized Chaperome Atlas, an integrated dataset linking protein abundance, stability, and interaction data across aging trajectories to facilitate broader community analysis. Furthermore, the development of the Proteostasis Risk Calculator, an open-source computational tool, will enable users to derive network resilience scores from proteomic profiles, potentially clarifying mechanisms of selective neuronal degeneration. By bridging phase transition physics with cell biology, this work may identify keystone chaperones as therapeutic targets for stabilizing network topology. Findings will be disseminated through interdisciplinary publications and specialized workshops, ensuring that these synthesis methods are accessible for future investigations into complex biological systems.
budget_and_resources: This budget supports the intellectual synthesis of existing data, as no wet-lab reagents are required for the proposed research. Personnel funding of $450,000 covers two full-time postdoctoral fellows for three years, focusing on computational systems biology and network physics, alongside a research software engineer to manage code quality and database architecture. An allocation of $40,000 for cloud computing credits and storage ensures the necessary infrastructure for processing large-scale proteomics data and Monte Carlo simulations within a shared environment. Furthermore, $60,000 is designated for travel to facilitate transdisciplinary collaboration through bi-annual working group meetings, annual reporting at NCEMS headquarters, and dissemination of findings at major scientific conferences. Finally, $25,000 supports open science initiatives, including publication fees, data archiving, and the organization of virtual hackathons and training workshops for graduate students. This financial plan prioritizes human capital and computational resources, which are expected to be the primary drivers for transforming existing datasets into new scientific knowledge.

title: Influence of Matrix Architecture on Emergent Antibiotic Resistance in Bacterial Biofilms
abstract: This research investigates how the mesoscale architecture of the biofilm extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix confers emergent antibiotic resistance independently of genetic mutations. The study integrates structural data of biofilm matrices, antibiotic diffusion coefficients, and transcriptomic profiles of resident bacterial populations. It is hypothesized that the EPS matrix generates emergent nutrient and drug gradients, which may induce metabolic dormancy within specific spatial niches. Reaction-diffusion modeling applied to digitized biofilm architectures will be utilized to predict bacterial survival rates under varying conditions. These findings are expected to demonstrate that mesoscale spatial organization functions as a significant non-genetic mechanism of resistance. This interdisciplinary synthesis requires the collaborative expertise of microbiologists, materials scientists, and mathematical modelers to characterize the complex interplay between physical structure and physiological response. The resulting framework may provide a deeper understanding of how spatial heterogeneity contributes to the persistence of bacterial communities during antibiotic exposure.
background_and_significance: Antimicrobial resistance remains a significant biological challenge, particularly regarding the phenotypic tolerance observed in bacterial biofilms. While genetic mechanisms are well-characterized, the collective organization within an extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix likely drives the recalcitrance of chronic infections. Current research often isolates the diffusion barrier hypothesis from metabolic heterogeneity theories, failing to synthesize structural imaging with transcriptomic data. This project addresses the mesoscale gap by integrating existing datasets from the BioImage Archive, the Gene Expression Omnibus, and biophysical literature. By synthesizing confocal microscopy, transcriptomic profiles, and diffusion coefficients, this study investigates how supramolecular assembly dictates cellular phenotype. This approach treats biofilm tolerance as an emergent property, examining the interface where polymer architecture influences biological survival. The findings are expected to clarify how spatial organization generates resistance, providing insights that bridge microbial ecology, materials science, and soft matter physics. Ultimately, this synthesis of diverse public data may resolve long-standing questions regarding the mechanisms of bacterial persistence.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This study investigates how the mesoscale topology and chemical composition of the extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix generate emergent gradients that dictate antibiotic tolerance. It is hypothesized that the EPS matrix functions as a selective filter rather than a homogeneous barrier, where the ratio of extracellular DNA to polysaccharides determines mesh size and charge density. By meta-analyzing structural data and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching studies, this project will correlate composition with anomalous diffusion patterns. Furthermore, the research examines whether specific matrix architectures induce metabolic differentiation by creating oxygen and nutrient gradients that trigger dormancy-mediated tolerance. Transcriptomic data will be mapped onto spatial templates to determine if biofilm architecture predicts the expression of hypoxia and starvation markers. Finally, a predictive model will be developed to assess whether a calculated Tortuosity Index can forecast biofilm survival. This approach aims to demonstrate that antibiotic tolerance is an emergent property of mesoscale structural heterogeneity.
methods_and_approach: This project establishes a Digital Biofilm framework by synthesizing heterogeneous data into a unified computational model without requiring new experimental procedures. Structural data will be curated from the BioImage Archive and The Cell Image Library, targeting over 500 high-resolution 3D volumes of *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* and *Staphylococcus aureus* biofilms. Transcriptomic profiles will be mined from the Gene Expression Omnibus, while biophysical parameters, including antibiotic diffusion coefficients, will be extracted from literature. Image processing will utilize Napari and custom PyTorch-based scripts to segment matrix components and calculate mesoscale metrics such as porosity and fractal dimension. Transcriptomic data will be processed via Nextflow and integrated through Flux Balance Analysis to map metabolic states onto physical gradients. Finally, FEniCS or COMSOL Multiphysics will simulate reaction-diffusion systems to predict bacterial survival kinetics based on local drug concentrations. This interdisciplinary approach, supported by a diverse team of microbiologists, physicists, and computational biologists, is expected to elucidate emergent resistance mechanisms within complex biofilm architectures.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to advance the understanding of mesoscale biological organization by integrating soft matter physics with bacterial physiology. The study will produce the Biofilm Architecture Atlas, an open-access database linking three-dimensional biofilm structures with transcriptomic profiles and biophysical properties, categorized by topology rather than taxonomy. Additionally, the BioMatrixSim Python package will be developed to process confocal microscopy data, enabling reaction-diffusion simulations to predict antibiotic resistance scores. Findings regarding how matrix heterogeneity influences non-genetic resistance will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications. By quantifying how polymer assembly dictates population survival, this research illustrates emergent phenomena where resistance exceeds the sum of individual genetic contributions. These insights may inform the design of therapeutic adjuvants that disrupt biofilm architecture to restore antibiotic efficacy. Furthermore, the project supports workforce development in physical microbiology and ensures long-term data accessibility through permanent repositories, providing a standardized benchmark for future investigations into the systems-level dynamics of bacterial communities.
budget_and_resources: The requested budget provides the human capital and computational infrastructure required to synthesize complex, heterogeneous datasets across multiple research institutions. Personnel funding supports two postdoctoral fellows, specializing in computational image analysis and microbial genomics, to facilitate interdisciplinary collaboration. A data engineer will manage database architecture, ensure FAIR compliance, and maintain project repositories, while graduate students will assist with data curation. Computational resources, including cloud computing credits and long-term storage, are necessary for training deep learning models and executing high-throughput multiphysics simulations. Physical colocation through three intensive workshops at the NCEMS facility is expected to foster the integration of physical modeling and biological data. Furthermore, funds are allocated for open-access publication fees, website maintenance, and conference dissemination to ensure broad project visibility. This three-year investment of approximately $565,000 is expected to leverage existing data generation efforts, providing significant scientific returns by extracting emergent insights from established public resources through a collaborative synthesis framework.

title: Emergent Signaling Bias through Allosteric Regulation in GPCR Oligomerization Landscapes
abstract: This study investigates G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) oligomerization and the subsequent emergence of signaling bias within mesoscale receptor arrays. By synthesizing fluorescence resonance energy transfer and bioluminescence resonance energy transfer data regarding receptor proximity, this project integrates pharmacological response metrics with molecular dynamics simulations of receptor interfaces. The central hypothesis posits that the specific geometry of an oligomer may alter allosteric pathways, potentially generating signaling profiles, such as G-protein versus arrestin bias, that are absent in monomeric states. Statistical thermodynamic models will be employed to establish a quantitative link between diverse oligomer populations and observed signaling outputs. This multidisciplinary approach, requiring collaboration between pharmacologists, structural biologists, and computational chemists, is expected to elucidate the mechanisms of receptor assembly. Ultimately, these findings may facilitate the rational design of therapeutic agents specifically engineered to target distinct oligomeric states, thereby improving the precision of pharmacological interventions in complex biological systems.
background_and_significance: G-Protein Coupled Receptors (GPCRs) constitute the largest membrane protein family and serve as primary targets for approximately 35% of approved pharmaceuticals. Although traditionally viewed as monomeric switches, emerging evidence indicates that GPCRs organize into complex dimers and higher-order nanoclusters within the plasma membrane. This supramolecular architecture appears to modulate receptor trafficking, ligand binding, and signaling bias, where the oligomeric interface dictates downstream pathway activation through allosteric cross-talk. Despite these functional implications, current research is hindered by data fragmentation across structural, computational, and pharmacological domains. Static crystal structures, molecular dynamics simulations, and heterogeneous functional assays remain siloed, preventing a unified understanding of how mesoscale organization influences signaling outcomes. Integrating these disparate datasets is essential to elucidate the mechanisms by which receptor clustering functions as a logic gate. Addressing this synthesis gap may improve drug discovery success rates by accounting for oligomer-specific pharmacology, ultimately requiring a multidisciplinary approach to decode the emergent grammar of GPCR signaling.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates the fundamental nature of emergence at the membrane mesoscale by synthesizing existing data to transition from structural identification to dynamic mechanistic modeling. The study first examines whether conserved residue networks define GPCR oligomer geometry. It is hypothesized that co-evolved interface archetypes govern these assemblies, which may be validated by identifying higher co-evolutionary coupling scores at interface sites. Second, the research explores how oligomeric interfaces reshape allosteric landscapes to induce signaling bias. The study suggests that specific interfaces act as allosteric filters by mechanically modulating conformational fluctuations, such as TM6 movement, which may be confirmed by correlating MD simulation metrics with established pharmacological bias factors. Finally, the project evaluates whether mesoscale clustering explains tissue-specific pharmacological heterogeneity. By integrating scRNA-seq data with thermodynamic mass-action models, the study expects to demonstrate that receptor density and lipid composition dictate signaling outputs. These findings may confirm that mesoscale organization serves as a primary determinant of cellular phenotype.
methods_and_approach: This project investigates mesoscale GPCR organization through a multi-stage synthesis of existing data, utilizing high-performance computing and network theory. The study integrates structural data from the Protein Data Bank and GPCRmd, pharmacological metrics from IUPHAR and ChEMBL, and contextual expression data from the Human Cell Atlas. A Knowledge Graph will be constructed to harmonize these disparate datasets, employing the operational model of agonism to derive comparable bias factors. Computational geometry and Markov State Models will characterize interface stability, while dynamic network analysis is expected to quantify allosteric interference within oligomeric complexes. Furthermore, Graph Neural Networks will be trained to identify non-linear relationships between interface topology and signaling outcomes. Finally, systems biology models will simulate receptor population dynamics to predict net signaling outputs. This interdisciplinary approach, supported by a team of structural biologists, computational chemists, and pharmacologists, aims to synthesize these findings into a comprehensive framework for understanding GPCR oligomerization and functional signaling.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project establishes a quantitative framework linking mesoscale receptor organization to emergent functional outcomes, moving beyond monomeric paradigms to characterize signal transduction. The study will produce the GPCR OligomerAtlas, an open-access database mapping oligomer interfaces to allosteric effects, and the OligomerAllostery Python package, which utilizes graph neural networks to predict signaling bias from structural data. A synthesis publication will further detail the regulatory role of supramolecular assembly in signal transduction. These findings are expected to shift the understanding of signaling from a lock-and-key model to a network integration framework, explaining discrepancies between recombinant systems and native tissues. In drug discovery, this research may facilitate the design of interface-specific ligands that stabilize therapeutic dimer geometries. These analytical strategies are transferable to other membrane protein families, including ion channels. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and workshops, with the database integrated into the GPCRdb ecosystem to ensure long-term sustainability and community access.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget prioritizes personnel, computational resources, and collaborative efforts, as the project entails no wet-lab expenditures. Funding for human capital includes two postdoctoral fellows specializing in structural bioinformatics and systems pharmacology to conduct core modeling and data integration. A graduate research assistant will support data curation and reproducibility, while a data engineer will maintain the Knowledge Graph infrastructure and the OligomerAtlas web interface. Computational requirements involve significant cloud storage and high-performance computing allocations to facilitate the analysis of large molecular dynamics trajectories and the training of graph neural networks. Collaborative activities include biannual in-person synthesis meetings and conference presentations to foster team science. Furthermore, resources are allocated for open-access publishing, virtual training workshops, and the maintenance of project infrastructure. This financial structure reflects a strategic shift toward expertise-driven research, ensuring that the investment in personnel and computational power effectively extracts value from existing high-throughput datasets through rigorous, reproducible, and accessible scientific inquiry.

title: Nuclear Speckles as Splicing Hubs for the Emergent Amplification of Gene Expression
abstract: This study investigates the role of nuclear speckles as mesoscale reaction environments that potentially enhance pre-mRNA splicing efficiency. The research integrates spatial transcriptomics data, quantitative splicing metrics such as intron retention rates, and high-resolution imaging of speckle proximity. It is hypothesized that the elevated local concentration of splicing factors within these compartments provides a kinetic advantage for specific gene subsets, contingent upon their spatial relationship to the speckle. By correlating three-dimensional genomic distances with observed splicing kinetics across integrated datasets, this project aims to characterize a spatial regulatory code. These findings may demonstrate that nuclear positioning serves as a fundamental determinant of transcript processing efficiency. Achieving these objectives requires a multidisciplinary approach involving expertise in genomics, cell biology, and spatial statistics. The resulting data are expected to clarify how sub-nuclear architecture influences gene expression outcomes, providing a framework for understanding the spatial organization of the eukaryotic nucleus.
background_and_significance: Traditional models of gene regulation emphasize linear DNA sequences, often overlooking the influence of nuclear spatial compartmentalization. Nuclear speckles, previously characterized as passive storage sites for splicing factors, are now recognized as dynamic, membraneless organelles formed through liquid-liquid phase separation. This process creates a distinct physicochemical environment that concentrates splicing factors, potentially enhancing RNA processing kinetics beyond the influence of sequence motifs alone. Although high-transcription genes frequently associate with these structures, the quantitative relationship between spatial proximity and splicing efficiency remains poorly defined. This project integrates disparate datasets, including 4D Nucleome maps, ENCODE transcriptomics, and Human Cell Atlas single-cell data, to evaluate whether nuclear speckles function as active metabolic engines. By synthesizing these resources, the study investigates whether mesoscale organization acts as a physical catalyst for splicing amplification. This research aims to elucidate the spatial code of the genome, determining how nuclear architecture imposes non-linear regulatory layers on molecular events within the eukaryotic nucleus.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This study investigates the emergent properties of nuclear speckles at the mesoscale by synthesizing existing datasets to transition from correlation to mechanistic predictive modeling. The first objective examines whether a distance-dependent kinetic field enhances splicing efficiency. It is hypothesized that splicing fidelity exhibits a non-linear decay relative to the radial distance from speckle centers, potentially creating a gradient of influence. Integration of TSA-seq and nascent RNA-seq data is expected to reveal a sigmoid relationship, where genes within the speckle periphery demonstrate superior splicing fidelity. The second objective explores whether speckles facilitate the coordination of splicing for complex, multi-intron transcripts. This research posits that long genes are preferentially tethered to speckles to mitigate processing errors. Analysis of Hi-C contact maps and transcript metadata may demonstrate that mis-spliced isoforms originate from alleles lacking speckle association. Finally, the study evaluates whether cell-type-specific proteomic variations modulate the splicing landscape, suggesting that these mesoscale bodies function as tunable reaction crucibles.
