methods_and_approach: This project employs a high-throughput synthesis strategy to integrate 1D sequence, 3D genome structure, and proteomic data, constructing a multi-layered model of the nuclear mesoscale. The study utilizes high-quality public repositories, including the 4D Nucleome portal for TSA-seq and Hi-C data, ENCODE for eCLIP and RNA-seq, and GEO for nascent RNA measurements. Data harmonization focuses on K562 and GM12878 cell lines, mapping all inputs to the hg38 reference genome to ensure coordinate consistency. A unified "distance-splicing" tensor will be constructed, incorporating splicing efficiency, transcription rates, and protein binding density, with batch effects mitigated via quantile normalization. Analytical methods include Generalized Additive Models to characterize non-linear relationships between speckle distance and splicing, alongside Graph Neural Networks to predict splicing outcomes from 3D neighborhood embeddings. Biophysical models will evaluate whether phase separation kinetics explain splicing amplification. Finally, the study will utilize leave-one-chromosome-out cross-validation and testing on independent cell lines to ensure the robustness of these emergent properties.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to generate a quantitative, mesoscale map illustrating how nuclear architecture influences RNA processing kinetics, characterizing the nucleus as an emergent reaction chamber. The study will produce the Speckle-Splicing Atlas, an integrated database harmonizing 4DN and ENCODE data to map gene proximity to nuclear speckles alongside splicing efficiency. Furthermore, the development of the SpeckleKinetics computational toolkit and a Graph Neural Network will enable researchers to predict splicing outcomes based on 3D genome topology. A theoretical framework will be established to quantify the kinetic advantages conferred by phase separation, bridging soft matter physics and molecular biology. This research suggests that splicing fidelity is an emergent property of mesoscale organization rather than solely a product of molecular collisions. By synthesizing spatial and functional omics, the project provides a roadmap for leveraging legacy datasets. These findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, open-source repositories, and workshops to ensure long-term reproducibility and community engagement in transdisciplinary data analysis.
budget_and_resources: This budget supports a high-intensity computational synthesis effort, prioritizing human capital and infrastructure over laboratory consumables. Personnel costs, totaling $350,000 annually, fund two full-time postdoctoral fellows focused on genomic data harmonization and machine learning model development, alongside a graduate research assistant for data curation and web-tool development. Principal investigator salary support is included for project oversight and mentorship. Computational resources, allocated at $40,000 annually, provide necessary cloud-based storage and high-memory GPU instances for processing large-scale Hi-C contact maps. Travel funding of $25,000 facilitates biannual interdisciplinary synthesis meetings and trainee conference presentations to ensure effective dissemination of findings. Finally, $15,000 is designated for open-access publication fees, virtual workshop organization, and project infrastructure maintenance. This allocation reflects the labor-intensive nature of data harmonization and ensures that hardware constraints do not impede the analysis of terabyte-scale datasets. By strictly excluding wet-lab reagents, the project maintains its focus on the computational synthesis of existing biological data.

title: Thylakoid Stacking and the Emergence of Photosynthetic Robustness in Plant Systems
abstract: This research investigates the mesoscale stacking of plant thylakoid membranes and the resulting robustness of light-harvesting processes. The study integrates cryo-electron tomography data of thylakoid architecture with spectroscopic measurements of energy transfer and environmental stress responses. A central objective is to determine how the dynamic stacking and unstacking of membranes regulates energy distribution between Photosystem I and II, potentially serving as an emergent mechanism to mitigate photodamage. Excitonic energy transfer models will be applied to realistic membrane geometries to simulate these complex interactions. The findings are expected to clarify how plants manage fluctuating light environments through mesoscale structural remodeling. This interdisciplinary project requires the collaboration of plant biologists, quantum biologists, and structural modelers to synthesize diverse datasets. Ultimately, this work may provide a comprehensive understanding of the structural adaptations that maintain photosynthetic efficiency under variable conditions, offering insights into the fundamental mechanisms of plant photoprotection.
background_and_significance: Photosynthesis converts solar energy into chemical potential, yet the mesoscale organization of thylakoid membranes into grana and stroma lamellae remains poorly understood. While individual molecular components are well-characterized, the spatial arrangement that dictates light-harvesting efficiency and photoprotection requires further investigation. Current models suggest that lateral heterogeneity regulates electron transport, but the mechanisms by which 3D geometry ensures robustness under fluctuating light conditions remain unclear. Existing research often separates high-resolution cryo-electron tomography from spectroscopic data, failing to account for the complex, crowded nature of native membranes. This study integrates disparate datasets from repositories such as EMPIAR and the PDB to bridge the gap between structural snapshots and functional dynamics. By synthesizing these sources, the project examines how membrane remodeling acts as a molecular switch for energy redistribution and non-photochemical quenching. These findings may clarify emergent biological properties, potentially informing future bio-inspired solar energy technologies and strategies for enhancing crop resilience in changing climates.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This research investigates how mesoscale geometry dictates energy landscapes within thylakoid membranes. The first objective examines how grana stacking parameters, including membrane distance and curvature, modulate excitonic network connectivity between photosystems. It is hypothesized that thylakoid stacking generates a non-linear energy spillover network, where inter-membrane distance variations act as a tunable valve for excitation energy transfer. This will be validated by mapping excitonic models onto geometries derived from Cryo-ET data. The second objective evaluates whether mesoscale structural remodeling drives photosynthetic robustness during light stress, potentially preceding proteomic shifts. This study will synthesize time-resolved structural data with omics datasets to decouple physical remodeling from gene expression. Finally, the project explores whether structural irregularities, such as bifurcations, function as essential features that prevent energy traps and facilitate electron carrier diffusion. By comparing simulated transport efficiency in idealized versus native geometries, this work will determine if these structural features enhance the overall robustness of photosynthetic energy conversion.
methods_and_approach: This project utilizes a transdisciplinary framework to synthesize publicly available data, integrating structural biology, data science, and quantum biophysics to investigate thylakoid membrane function. Structural data will be acquired from the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive and the Protein Data Bank, while proteomics and transcriptomics will be sourced from PRIDE and NCBI GEO. A curated repository of spectroscopic data will be compiled from biophysical literature to support model validation. A mesoscale integration pipeline will process Cryo-ET tomograms into surface meshes, which are subsequently populated with molecular structures using packing algorithms constrained by stoichiometric data. This digital thylakoid model will facilitate geometric analysis and excitonic simulations using Quantum Master Equations and Förster Resonance Energy Transfer modeling. Unsupervised machine learning will identify conserved architectural motifs across species. Finally, predicted fluorescence decay kinetics will be compared against experimental values to evaluate the emergent role of mesoscale geometry in energy migration, with project completion expected within three years.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project establishes a comprehensive framework for analyzing thylakoid organization through three primary deliverables. The Digital Thylakoid Atlas will provide an open-access database integrating mesoscale geometries from cryo-electron tomography with photonic properties and proteomic states. Concurrently, the Thylakoid-Sim toolkit will offer a containerized software pipeline to predict energy transfer efficiencies from membrane geometries. Furthermore, a mathematically rigorous model will be developed to clarify how grana stacking mitigates photodamage, addressing the debate between statistical spillover and physically regulated connectivity. This research suggests that biological function emerges from mesoscale organization, establishing geometry as a primary determinant of quantum efficiency. These findings may inform the design of artificial photosynthetic systems and facilitate the breeding of crops with enhanced stress tolerance. Datasets and code will be archived in public repositories to support future artificial intelligence models. Dissemination efforts include publication in open-access journals and the organization of workshops to train researchers in utilizing these computational tools for structural analysis.
budget_and_resources: This three-year synthesis project requests funding to support human capital and computational infrastructure, as no wet-lab expenditures are required. Personnel costs of $450,000 will support two full-time postdoctoral researchers focused on computational biophysics and data science, alongside a graduate student dedicated to literature synthesis and website maintenance. Computational resources totaling $60,000 are allocated for cloud-based processing of large Cryo-ET volumes and the long-term storage of extensive simulation outputs. An additional $50,000 will facilitate bi-annual working group meetings to bridge disciplinary gaps between biology and physics, while supporting conference dissemination of findings. Finally, $25,000 is designated for open science initiatives, including publication fees, repository hosting, and a virtual training workshop for the Thylakoid-Sim toolkit. This budget prioritizes the integration of interdisciplinary expertise and the high-performance computing power necessary to simulate emergent mesoscale phenomena. These investments are expected to provide the essential framework required to synthesize complex biological data and advance current computational modeling capabilities.

title: Mechanisms of Exosome Loading and Sorting as Emergent Cellular Communication Packets
abstract: This project investigates the selective loading of cargo into exosomes to develop mesoscale vectors for intercellular communication. The study integrates vesicle content databases, such as ExoCarta, with comprehensive protein-lipid interaction and biogenesis pathway data. It is hypothesized that cargo sorting functions as an emergent property driven by membrane curvature sensing and microdomain partitioning at the budding site. Thermodynamic modeling will be employed to predict cargo enrichment patterns based on specific molecular properties. These investigations are expected to elucidate the addressing system of extracellular vesicles, which remains critical for understanding their functional roles in metastasis and therapeutic applications. Achieving these objectives requires a multidisciplinary approach involving expertise from vesicle biology, biophysics, and data science. The resulting framework may provide a predictive understanding of how molecular sorting mechanisms influence the biological activity of extracellular vesicles, ultimately facilitating the design of targeted delivery systems for future clinical interventions.
background_and_significance: The mesoscale organization of extracellular vesicles, particularly exosomes, represents a critical frontier in biological research. Although the molecular machinery of biogenesis is documented, the sorting mechanisms governing cargo packaging remain poorly understood. Current evidence suggests that cargo selection emerges from the collective physical properties of the budding membrane, including curvature and lipid phase separation. However, the field remains fragmented, as proteomic and transcriptomic datasets are rarely integrated with the structural and biophysical characteristics of constituent molecules. This study aims to bridge this gap by synthesizing high-throughput omics data with structural repositories to identify the rules of mesoscale assembly. By analyzing surface charge distributions and curvature-sensing domains, this project will investigate whether thermodynamic negotiations between membrane energy and chemical potential dictate cargo partitioning. Establishing this biophysical model may clarify how cells encode information for long-distance communication, providing insights into cancer metastasis and the development of therapeutic delivery vectors through the systematic analysis of public data.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This study investigates the mechanisms of exosome cargo sorting by synthesizing proteomic, lipidomic, and structural data to address three fundamental questions. First, the research examines whether a universal biophysical sorting code exists, hypothesizing that exosomal proteins possess structural motifs, such as BAR domains, that facilitate partitioning into high-curvature membrane regions. This will be tested by training a machine learning classifier on biophysical features derived from ExoCarta and structural databases to distinguish cargo from non-cargo. Second, the project explores how the stoichiometry of sorting machinery, specifically ESCRT versus lipid-dependent pathways, dictates vesicle heterogeneity. By correlating Human Cell Atlas transcriptomic data with EV proteomic profiles, the study expects to demonstrate that imbalanced biogenesis factor expression drives vesicle diversity. Finally, the research evaluates whether loading efficiency is determined by interactome connectivity and phase-separation potential. Network models will assess if disordered proteins are recruited via piggybacking on membrane-bound drivers, with validation provided by analyzing experimental knockout datasets.
methods_and_approach: This project aims to elucidate the mesoscale mechanisms of exosome biogenesis by developing a "Virtual Vesicle" synthesis engine that integrates heterogeneous data without generating new experimental results. The study will curate high-resolution datasets from ExoCarta, Vesiclepedia, and the ERCC exRNA Atlas, while retrieving structural data from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold DB, and LIPID MAPS. These sources will be harmonized within a Neo4j graph database, utilizing UniProt identifiers and standardized housekeeping proteins for contextual normalization. Biophysical features, including surface charge and membrane curvature potential, will be extracted to parameterize coarse-grained thermodynamic models of membrane budding. Furthermore, Graph Neural Networks will be trained to predict exosomal cargo inclusion based on structural interactions and protein abundance. The model’s predictive power will be validated through cross-system testing and in-silico knockouts of known sorting proteins. This transdisciplinary effort, involving biologists, biophysicists, and data scientists, is expected to reveal universal principles governing vesicle formation and cargo selection.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project establishes a biophysically grounded framework for understanding exosome composition, transitioning the field from descriptive phenomenology toward mechanistic analysis. The study will deliver ExoPhys-DB, a public database linking extracellular vesicle protein cargo to over fifty biophysical parameters and structural models. Furthermore, an open-source predictive model, Vesicle-Sort AI, will be developed to estimate protein loading probabilities based on sequence and structural features. A series of publications, the Mesoscale Sorting Atlas, will define universal rules for membrane-mediated sorting, specifically addressing the roles of curvature and molecular crowding. By mapping the thermodynamic landscape of vesicle budding, this research will elucidate how macroscopic vesicle properties constrain microscopic sorting decisions. These findings are expected to provide design principles for engineering therapeutic delivery systems, such as Cas9 encapsulation, and improve the interpretation of liquid biopsies by clarifying the biophysical basis of marker export. Project outputs will be disseminated through training workshops and maintained via persistent cloud-based repositories for long-term accessibility.
budget_and_resources: This project requests $1.2 million over three years to support the personnel and computational infrastructure required for community-scale synthesis. Personnel costs of $850,000 will fund two postdoctoral researchers specializing in data science and computational biophysics, one graduate student for data curation, and a part-time programmer to ensure software sustainability. Working group activities, allocated $200,000, will facilitate semi-annual in-person meetings for ten core members and rotating experts to foster transdisciplinary collaboration. Computational infrastructure, requiring $100,000, will cover cloud hosting for graph databases, high-memory machine learning tasks, and long-term storage for terabyte-scale datasets. Finally, $50,000 is designated for open science dissemination, including open-access publication fees, workshop organization, and data archiving. This budgetary strategy prioritizes human capital and collaborative engagement, which are expected to be the primary drivers of successful synthesis research. By integrating these resources, the study aims to establish a robust framework for data harmonization, thermodynamic modeling, and the long-term maintenance of essential computational tools for the broader scientific community.

title: Predictive Modeling of Emergent Life-like Behaviors Through Synthetic Cell Component Integration
abstract: This project conducts a meta-synthesis of data derived from bottom-up synthetic biology to identify the minimal requirements for emergent life-like behaviors, including motility, division, and homeostasis. The study integrates findings from diverse synthetic cell initiatives, such as liposome encapsulation and minimal genome reconstitution, to establish a comprehensive dataset. Machine learning models will be trained on these data to predict which combinations of energy, information, and containment modules facilitate system-level stability rather than collapse. This investigation serves as a rigorous test of current understanding regarding the transition from non-living matter to autonomous living systems. Achieving these objectives necessitates a multidisciplinary collaboration between synthetic biologists, systems theorists, and artificial intelligence researchers to define the fundamental design rules of life at the mesoscale. The resulting framework is expected to clarify the conditions under which emergent biological properties arise, thereby advancing the theoretical foundations of synthetic life research.
background_and_significance: The construction of synthetic cells from non-living components represents a significant challenge in modern biology, testing the understanding of mesoscale emergence between molecular interactions and cellular behavior. Although extensive data exist regarding cell-free protein synthesis, liposome encapsulation, and minimal genomes, these findings remain fragmented across siloed repositories. Current research is limited by a lack of integration, as combining genetic circuits with membrane encapsulation frequently results in emergent failure modes, such as membrane lysis or transcriptional stalling. These mesoscale phenomena, involving energy flux and spatial organization, cannot be predicted by studying individual components in isolation. This project aims to aggregate existing datasets to construct a holistic model of synthetic cells, thereby defining the fundamental design rules of life. By transitioning from trial-and-error methods toward rational design, this transdisciplinary approach will clarify the minimal requirements for self-replication. Such integration is essential to bridge the gap between molecular lists and the functional complexity of cellular life.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This research investigates three interrelated questions concerning mesoscale emergence in synthetic systems. First, the stability of encapsulated genetic systems may be defined by the ratio of metabolic energy production to macromolecular crowding. It is hypothesized that a phase boundary exists where osmotic stress from waste accumulation exceeds membrane expansion, leading to rupture. This will be investigated by synthesizing data from liposome leakage assays, turnover rates, and membrane tension studies. Second, spatial heterogeneity in uniform mixtures may emerge from feedback loops between reaction-diffusion networks and membrane curvature. By applying Turing-like instability models to existing fluorescence microscopy data, critical concentration thresholds for spontaneous organization will be identified and validated against historical image datasets. Finally, homeostatic resilience is expected to be an emergent property of gene regulatory network topology rather than specific protein identities. Analysis of gene expression noise and synthetic oscillator datasets will determine if specific feedback-to-feed-forward ratios predict a system's capacity to recover from environmental perturbations.
methods_and_approach: This project utilizes computational integration and machine learning to identify mesoscale design rules by synthesizing publicly available data. Data will be harvested from repositories including BioModels, BRENDA, LipidMaps, the Membrane Protein Data Bank, SynBioHub, and NCBI archives. To address data heterogeneity, metadata will be standardized using the Synthetic Biology Open Language and Resource Description Framework, facilitating the construction of a Meta-SynCell Knowledge Graph. Analytical methods include Graph Neural Networks to predict interaction strengths and Physics-Informed Neural Networks to model reaction-diffusion dynamics within confined volumes. Bayesian inference will be employed to quantify kinetic parameter uncertainty and assign confidence intervals to stability predictions. The synthesis of a virtual cell will be treated as a constraint satisfaction problem, validated through leave-one-out cross-validation and the analysis of negative data from failed constructs. Spanning 2.5 years, the study will progress from data harmonization to model training and final validation, supported by an interdisciplinary team of systems biologists, biophysicists, and computer scientists.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This research establishes a comprehensive, quantitative framework for synthetic cell design, transitioning the field toward a rigorous engineering discipline. The project delivers the SynCell-Atlas, an open-access database integrating kinetic, structural, and omics data to support bottom-up synthetic biology. Furthermore, the Life-Design Engine, a pre-trained machine learning model, will enable in silico testing of molecular combinations to predict stability and emergent behaviors before experimental implementation. A white paper will define biophysical constraints, including energy and crowding, to address fundamental mesoscale puzzles. By identifying phase boundaries of stability and symmetry breaking, this study provides a mechanistic explanation for the transition from non-living matter to living systems. These tools are expected to reduce experimental failure rates in drug delivery and bio-manufacturing while informing theories on abiogenesis. Long-term sustainability is ensured through integration with global standards and dissemination via open-access platforms, providing a template for analyzing complex biological systems such as organoid development and microbiome interactions.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget allocates resources exclusively to personnel and computational infrastructure, excluding wet-lab reagent expenditures. Personnel funding of $450,000 supports two postdoctoral fellows for 2.5 years, specializing in biophysics and machine learning to facilitate data curation and model architecture development, alongside a data engineer tasked with maintaining database standards. Computational requirements, estimated at $80,000, provide necessary GPU acceleration for training graph neural networks and physics-informed models, while covering cloud storage and repository maintenance. An allocation of $50,000 supports biannual in-person working group meetings and synthesis workshops, which are expected to foster cross-disciplinary collaboration, as well as trainee travel for conference presentations. Finally, $20,000 is designated for open science initiatives, including data synthesis hackathons, open-access publication fees, and long-term archiving services. These investments are intended to ensure the project maintains a sustainable legacy and supports the workforce development objectives of the NCEMS program through rigorous data management and collaborative synthesis efforts.

title: Emergent Phase Separation Grammar: Sequence Patterns of Intrinsically Disordered Regions Driving Mesoscale Condensate Properties
abstract: Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence, where intrinsically disordered proteins self-organize into membraneless organelles with properties unpredictable from individual components. This project aims to decode the sequence grammar connecting protein features to emergent condensate behaviors by integrating diverse public datasets, including the Protein Data Bank, MobiDB, PhaSePro, and the Human Cell Atlas. The central hypothesis suggests that specific combinations of sequence motifs create interaction networks that dictate material properties and cellular function. Natural language processing and graph neural networks will be employed to identify synergistic motifs that predict condensate viscosity, surface tension, and client recruitment. Furthermore, integrating GWAS data may link protein variants to disease states through altered mesoscale organization. This transdisciplinary effort is expected to establish a predictive framework for condensate behavior and provide mechanistic insights into disease-related dysregulation. All resulting analysis pipelines, models, and datasets will be disseminated according to FAIR principles to facilitate broader scientific utility.
background_and_significance: Biomolecular condensates represent a fundamental organizing principle of cellular architecture, forming through liquid-liquid phase separation of proteins and nucleic acids. While individual sequence features promoting this process are documented, the rules governing how these elements synergistically determine emergent material properties remain largely undeciphered. This project addresses critical knowledge gaps by integrating heterogeneous data from structural repositories, disorder databases, and cellular imaging archives. By synthesizing information from the Protein Data Bank, MobiDB, and the Human Protein Atlas, the study aims to decode the grammar of phase separation. The research will investigate how linear sequence information encodes dynamic, mesoscale structures that influence cellular phenotypes. This interdisciplinary effort requires collaboration between computational biophysicists, machine learning specialists, and cell biologists to link molecular features to disease states. Ultimately, this synthesis is expected to provide a predictive framework connecting sequence-level variation to the emergent properties of condensates, thereby clarifying their role in neurodegeneration, cancer, and aging.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how sequence motifs within intrinsically disordered regions dictate protein phase separation and mesoscale condensate properties. It is hypothesized that proteins follow specific grammatical rules, where motif arrangement—rather than mere composition—determines condensate behavior. Machine learning models will be developed to classify these proteins, with predictions validated against experimental data from the PhaSePro and LLPSDB databases. Furthermore, the study examines how molecular interaction networks scale to influence condensate viscosity and client recruitment, utilizing graph neural networks to analyze scaffold-client complementarity. By integrating single-cell RNA-seq data from the Human Cell Atlas, the research will explore how cell-type-specific expression of these grammatical classes generates organizational diversity. Finally, the project assesses whether disease-associated variants preferentially disrupt these grammatical patterns, potentially shifting condensate states toward pathological aggregation or dissolution. This framework is expected to elucidate the mechanisms transforming linear sequence information into functional mesoscale organization, providing a predictive basis for understanding condensate-related disease phenotypes.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates data from eleven public repositories, including PDB, MobiDB, DisProt, and the AlphaFold Database, to characterize intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). By harmonizing structural, cellular, and population genetics data, the study aims to establish a unified schema for analyzing protein phase separation. Data quality will be managed through systematic filtering and identifier mapping to UniProt accessions, with relationships stored in a Neo4j graph database. Analytical methods include sequence feature extraction, transformer-based language models, and grammatical pattern discovery to identify motifs associated with phase behavior. Furthermore, graph neural networks will be employed to predict emergent material properties, while statistical genetics will assess the clinical significance of sequence variants. Validation will rely on cross-validation, temporal testing, and benchmarking against established proteins like FUS and TDP-43. This multidisciplinary effort, spanning three years, is expected to produce predictive models linking sequence features to condensate formation, ultimately providing a comprehensive framework for understanding the genetic basis of protein-mediated cellular organization.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to elucidate mesoscale emergence in biomolecular condensates through five primary deliverables. First, the CondensateAtlas will integrate sequence features, structural data, and genetic variants for the human proteome into a harmonized, publicly accessible database. Second, a grammatical classification system will categorize intrinsically disordered regions based on sequence motifs, mapping these patterns to emergent material properties. Third, a suite of machine learning models, including language models and graph neural networks, will be developed to predict phase behavior, scaffold-client interactions, and variant impacts. Fourth, standardized software pipelines will facilitate sequence feature extraction and network analysis, while a knowledge base will document mechanistic insights into condensate dysregulation. Collectively, these resources will bridge the gap between linear sequence information and mesoscale organization. By enabling predictive modeling and rational protein design, this study may provide significant insights into neurodegenerative disease mechanisms and cellular regulation, ultimately establishing a robust framework for future investigations into complex biological systems.
budget_and_resources: The proposed three-year budget of $1,100,000 supports the personnel, computational, and collaborative requirements of this interdisciplinary synthesis project. Personnel costs, comprising 65% of the total, fund two postdoctoral researchers for machine learning and data integration, two graduate students for biophysical and genetic analysis, and a research software engineer to ensure tool sustainability. Computational resources, accounting for 16% of the budget, provide necessary cloud-based GPU capacity for transformer model training, alongside institutional high-performance computing and redundant data storage. Travel and workshop allocations, totaling 14%, facilitate quarterly team meetings, conference dissemination, and annual training events to support the NCEMS mission. Finally, 5% of the budget is dedicated to open science infrastructure, including web hosting, repository fees, and publication costs, ensuring long-term accessibility of project outputs. This comprehensive financial plan is expected to provide the essential human and technical resources required to execute this complex, multi-institutional research synthesis effectively over the project duration.

title: Temporal Dynamics of Ribosome Clustering through Integrated Cryo-ET and Ribosome Profiling for Emergent Translation Factories
abstract: Translation occurs within dynamic mesoscale clusters known as polysomes, where ribosome cooperation generates emergent properties. This project investigates how ribosome clustering facilitates enhanced processivity, coordinated protein folding, and localized mRNA regulation, which remain unpredictable from isolated ribosome behavior. The study integrates cryo-electron tomography from EMPIAR and EMDB, Ribo-seq data from GEO, structural data from PDB, and proteomics from PRIDE to characterize these systems. Computational methods include spatial statistics, kinetic modeling, and agent-based simulations to correlate polysome architecture with translation efficiency. Machine learning will identify organizational features predictive of translation output and co-translational assembly, while integration with STRING and BioGRID networks clarifies nascent chain interactions. This research aims to establish principles governing polysome architecture and the quantitative relationship between mesoscale organization and translational output. Expected outcomes include open-source analysis tools, curated datasets, and predictive models, providing insights into translation dysregulation and potential applications in synthetic biology.
background_and_significance: Protein synthesis consumes significant cellular energy, yet translation is increasingly understood to occur within organized mesoscale structures known as polysomes. These clusters represent a critical frontier where emergent properties arise from collective ribosome behavior, potentially enhancing processivity, facilitating co-translational protein folding, and creating specialized regulatory microenvironments. Although cryo-electron tomography and ribosome profiling have generated extensive datasets regarding ribosome organization and translational dynamics, these modalities remain largely unintegrated. Consequently, current quantitative frameworks fail to connect polysome geometry to translation output or explain the rules governing assembly configurations. This project will systematically integrate structural data from the EMDB and translational dynamics from the GEO to elucidate how mesoscale architecture influences gene expression. By applying machine learning to these diverse datasets, this study aims to establish quantitative principles of translation factory behavior. These findings may clarify the mechanisms underlying translation dysregulation in disease and provide essential insights for synthetic biology applications requiring precise control over protein expression.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how mesoscale ribosome organization generates emergent translational properties through four interconnected research questions. The study integrates publicly available cryo-ET and Ribo-seq datasets to test hypotheses regarding polysome architecture, elongation dynamics, co-translational assembly, and predictive modeling. It is hypothesized that polysome geometry follows predictable rules determined by mRNA sequence and cellular context, potentially facilitating co-translational assembly of protein complexes. Furthermore, ribosome spacing patterns may reflect coordinated elongation dynamics, where inter-ribosome distances correlate with Ribo-seq pausing signatures. The research will examine whether polysome organization enables emergent nascent chain interactions, positioning exit tunnels to favor complex assembly. Finally, the project will evaluate whether machine learning models incorporating mesoscale features outperform traditional single-ribosome-based predictions of protein output. These investigations are expected to elucidate the biophysical principles of polysome self-organization and establish architectural regulation as a critical layer in gene expression, bridging the gap between molecular mechanisms and cellular phenotypes across diverse organisms.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates cryo-electron tomography, ribosome profiling, protein structural data, and quantitative proteomics to model emergent translation factory behavior. By harmonizing heterogeneous datasets across diverse organisms and experimental conditions, the study aims to reconcile structural and functional translation metrics. Initial efforts involve retrieving over 500 tomograms and 200 ribosome profiling datasets to establish a comprehensive baseline. Computational pipelines will employ deep learning for polysome segmentation and graph neural networks to classify ribosome connectivity patterns. Spatial statistics and stochastic kinetic models will subsequently characterize ribosome clustering and translation dynamics, with agent-based simulations predicting emergent properties like collision frequencies. Machine learning models will then integrate these features to predict protein abundance, with uncertainty explicitly quantified throughout the workflow. Validation strategies include cross-modality consistency checks and the use of held-out test sets. This collaborative framework is expected to elucidate the relationship between polysome architecture and translation efficiency, ultimately providing a predictive understanding of cellular protein synthesis.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to advance the understanding of emergent translation factory behavior by generating five categories of research resources. An integrated polysome architecture atlas will catalog over 50,000 annotated structures, while a cross-referenced database will link mRNA sequences to translation metrics. Computational tools, including deep learning segmentation and stochastic simulation frameworks, will be released to facilitate spatial and kinetic analysis. Furthermore, validated predictive models will characterize the relationship between polysome geometry and translation efficiency, supported by curated training datasets. These outputs are expected to establish quantitative principles of mesoscale ribosome organization, suggesting that polysome architecture reflects functional optimization and coordinated dynamics. By bridging structural and systems biology, this work may reveal a regulatory layer at the mesoscale, enhancing protein abundance predictions and synthetic biology applications. Long-term sustainability will be ensured through deposition in established repositories, open-source software maintenance, and community-driven training initiatives, providing a lasting foundation for future investigations into cellular translation.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget allocates $940,000 over three years to support a multidisciplinary synthesis project requiring diverse expertise and collaborative infrastructure. Personnel costs, totaling $720,000, fund two postdoctoral researchers for cryo-ET analysis and translation biology, two graduate students for mathematical and machine learning modeling, and a research software engineer to ensure code sustainability. Computing resources of $90,000 provide necessary GPU-hours for deep learning and 100TB of cloud storage for large-scale tomographic data. Travel and collaboration funds of $60,000 facilitate quarterly team meetings, conference presentations, and laboratory visits to maintain project cohesion. Furthermore, $40,000 supports workshops to disseminate methods and foster community synthesis, while $30,000 ensures open science infrastructure through database hosting, DOI registration, and documentation. Finally, $10,000 covers open-access publication fees. This investment is expected to enable a community-scale synthesis effort that integrates structural, computational, and biological data, ensuring that project outputs remain accessible, reproducible, and impactful for the broader scientific community over the three-year duration.

title: Integrated Structural, Biophysical, and Transport Modeling of Collective Gating Mechanics in the Nuclear Pore Complex
abstract: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) serves as a model for mesoscale emergence, where approximately 500 intrinsically disordered FG-nucleoporins establish a selective barrier with properties exceeding individual protein behaviors. This project integrates diverse public datasets, including cryo-EM structures, molecular dynamics trajectories, single-molecule kinetics, and proteomic data, to investigate how collective FG-nup dynamics facilitate selective cargo transport. It is hypothesized that this selectivity emerges from mesoscale network properties, such as transient crosslinks and cargo-induced reorganization, rather than simple additive binding. The methodology employs coarse-grained molecular dynamics, network theory, and machine learning to characterize these collective states. Furthermore, phosphoproteomics and cross-species comparative analyses will be utilized to identify regulatory mechanisms and conserved principles of barrier function. This interdisciplinary effort aims to establish mechanistic models of NPC selectivity, ultimately providing insights for the design of synthetic barriers. All simulation protocols and analytical code will be made publicly available to facilitate community-driven refinement.
background_and_significance: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) functions as a mesoscale selective barrier, facilitating rapid bidirectional transport while excluding non-specific macromolecules. Although cryo-electron microscopy has resolved the scaffold architecture, the intrinsically disordered phenylalanine-glycine nucleoporins (FG-nups) forming the central transport channel remain poorly characterized. Current research integrates single-molecule kinetic data with molecular dynamics simulations to investigate how collective FG-nup behavior generates emergent transport properties. Despite these efforts, a comprehensive framework linking atomic-scale interactions to millisecond translocation events is currently lacking, leaving competing models of barrier function unresolved. This study aims to synthesize disparate data types, including structural information from the Protein Data Bank and quantitative abundance data, to bridge these multiscale gaps. By reconciling these datasets, this project may elucidate the mechanisms of disordered protein assemblies. Such insights are expected to clarify the role of NPC dysfunction in disease and provide foundational principles for designing synthetic selective barriers in future biotechnological applications.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates emergent selectivity in nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) by analyzing FG-nucleoporin (FG-nup) collective states, network topology, and post-translational modifications. It is hypothesized that FG-nup meshworks occupy metastable collective states, with transitions occurring on microsecond to millisecond timescales. Markov state modeling of existing molecular dynamics trajectories will be used to identify these states and correlate energy barriers with experimental transport kinetics. Furthermore, the study examines whether selective transport emerges from specific network properties, such as small-world connectivity, which may be conserved across species despite sequence divergence. Sequence analysis and structural predictions will evaluate how these topological features facilitate cargo navigation. Finally, the research explores how phosphorylation modulates meshwork cohesion and permeability. Machine learning models will be trained on phosphoproteomics data to predict transport phenotypes based on modification patterns. This framework is expected to elucidate how collective dynamics, rather than static structures, govern NPC selectivity and provide insights into broader intrinsically disordered protein assemblies.
methods_and_approach: This project employs a multi-scale computational framework to synthesize heterogeneous public datasets, facilitating a comprehensive analysis of nuclear pore complex (NPC) transport. The study integrates structural data from the Protein Data Bank and Cryo-ET maps with sequence information from UniProt and OrthoDB to characterize nucleoporin dynamics. Molecular dynamics trajectories, single-molecule transport kinetics, and proteomic datasets are harmonized into a relational database using UniProt identifiers and custom ontologies. Analytical methods include coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, network analysis of FG-nup contact topologies, and machine learning models to identify collective meshwork states. Evolutionary conservation patterns are assessed through ancestral sequence reconstruction and phylogenetic profiling. Validation strategies involve comparing model predictions against independent crosslinking mass spectrometry data and published transport measurements. This 36-month initiative leverages a multidisciplinary team of structural biologists, polymer physicists, and data scientists to elucidate transport mechanisms. The resulting framework is expected to provide mechanistic insights into NPC function through rigorous cross-dataset validation and systematic computational modeling.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to advance the understanding of nuclear pore complex (NPC) emergence by generating integrated data resources and computational tools. A harmonized database will consolidate structural, kinetic, and post-translational modification data from over 500 entries and 100 species to facilitate programmatic access. Furthermore, a suite of coarse-grained simulation models and Markov state models will be developed to characterize FG-nup assembly dynamics and free energy landscapes. Predictive machine learning tools will be employed to identify determinants of transport selectivity, while a cross-species atlas will delineate conserved barrier functions. These efforts are expected to establish quantitative principles regarding how collective protein dynamics generate emergent functional properties. The resulting framework, which links sequence features to network topology, may be applicable to diverse mesoscale systems such as phase-separated condensates and cytoskeletal networks. Dissemination will occur through peer-reviewed publications, community workshops, and the long-term hosting of curated data and simulation models in established repositories to support future research.
budget_and_resources: This synthesis research project requests $750,000 over three years to support data integration, computational modeling, and community engagement. Personnel costs, totaling $480,000, provide essential expertise in computational biology, machine learning, and software engineering, alongside graduate student training. These roles are expected to facilitate complex Markov state modeling and the development of robust machine learning pipelines. Computing resources, allocated at $120,000, will support scalable cloud-based simulations and high-performance computing requirements to ensure reproducibility. Furthermore, $75,000 is designated for travel and collaborative meetings, which are necessary to integrate diverse expertise across institutions. Training initiatives, including workshops and online materials, will receive $45,000 to foster workforce development and community capacity. Finally, $30,000 is allocated for open science infrastructure, ensuring long-term data accessibility and independent verification of results. This budget structure prioritizes human expertise and collaborative synthesis, ensuring that project deliverables remain sustainable and impactful for the broader scientific community beyond the initial three-year funding period.

title: Integrative Modeling of Emergent Nuclear Organization Through Chromatin Compartmentalization Dynamics, Hi-C, Imaging, and Epigenomic Data
abstract: Chromatin organization into A/B compartments, topologically associating domains, and nuclear bodies emerges from complex DNA-protein interactions. This project integrates multi-modal data, including Hi-C contact maps, super-resolution imaging, ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and single-cell multi-omics, to elucidate how molecular modifications drive nuclear compartmentalization. The central hypothesis posits that phase separation, facilitated by multivalent interactions among histones and reader proteins, generates mesoscale domains with distinct biochemical environments. Integrative computational frameworks will be developed, combining polymer physics models, machine learning, and spatial statistics to analyze the relationship between contact frequencies and physical distances. Network analysis will further characterize hierarchical chromatin communities and their correlation with transcriptional output. By comparing diverse cell types, this study aims to distinguish conserved organizational principles from cell-specific patterns. The research is expected to provide quantitative models of compartmentalization, identify key molecular drivers of nuclear structure, and clarify the causal influence of spatial organization on gene expression within the nucleus.
background_and_significance: The eukaryotic nucleus exhibits emergent organization where molecular interactions between DNA, histones, and proteins generate mesoscale structures. Although Hi-C and super-resolution microscopy have provided extensive data on chromatin architecture, the quantitative rules linking molecular modifications to these structures remain poorly defined. Current research often analyzes contact frequencies, spatial imaging, and epigenomic profiles in isolation, limiting a comprehensive understanding of nuclear organization. This project aims to synthesize these disparate data modalities to resolve discrepancies between Hi-C contact frequencies and physical distances. Furthermore, the study will investigate the combinatorial logic of histone modifications in driving phase separation and assess whether cell-to-cell variability reflects stochastic fluctuations or functional heterogeneity. By integrating datasets from the 4DN Consortium, ENCODE, and the Human Cell Atlas, this research will model chromatin compartmentalization as a multi-scale phenomenon. Such an integrative approach is expected to clarify how molecular-level interactions translate into the functional nuclear architecture essential for transcriptional regulation and DNA repair.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates the emergence of chromatin compartmentalization through four interconnected research questions using publicly available data. First, the relationship between Hi-C contact frequencies and physical distances will be analyzed across cell types, testing whether power-law exponents reflect chromatin compaction states. Discrepancies between imaging and contact data are expected to reveal systematic deviations in heterochromatic regions. Second, machine learning models will determine if a minimal set of histone modifications and accessibility data can predict compartmentalization with high accuracy, evaluating potential synergistic effects between specific markers. Third, single-cell multi-omics data will be utilized to assess whether variability in chromatin accessibility at compartment boundaries correlates with transcriptional heterogeneity, potentially identifying discrete organizational states. Finally, cross-cell-type meta-analysis will distinguish conserved hierarchical principles from lineage-specific organizational features. These investigations are expected to establish quantitative rules for chromatin architecture, identifying minimal molecular determinants and biophysical parameters that govern emergent nuclear organization while providing a predictive framework for future studies.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates 50 terabytes of data from six major repositories, including 4DN, ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, HCA, IDR, and the Cell Image Library. The harmonization strategy involves mapping datasets to reference genomes, aligning cross-modality signals, and applying batch correction to ensure data consistency. Computational methods will utilize polymer physics modeling to simulate chromatin organization, constrained by Hi-C contact maps via approximate Bayesian computation. Machine learning models, including gradient-boosted trees and neural networks, will predict compartment identity from epigenomic features, with feature importance assessed through SHAP values. Spatial statistics will characterize chromatin domain organization from super-resolution imaging, while network analysis will identify multi-scale structural communities. Furthermore, maximum entropy approaches will integrate contact frequencies and imaging-derived distances to infer 3D structures. Validation will rely on cross-dataset testing, functional correlation with RNA-seq data, and benchmarking against established literature. This collaborative effort combines expertise in chromosome biology, polymer physics, image analysis, machine learning, and bioinformatics to achieve a comprehensive understanding of nuclear architecture.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to advance the understanding of emergent nuclear organization by generating harmonized, multi-modal datasets and computational tools for the chromatin biology community. Integrated resources will link Hi-C contact maps, epigenomic profiles, and imaging data across fifty human cell types, facilitating the analysis of compartmentalization and chromatin states. A suite of software, including predictive machine learning models and polymer physics simulations, will be released to characterize hierarchical chromatin communities. These tools are expected to elucidate the molecular determinants of phase separation and organizational variability. By integrating molecular-level data with mesoscale observations, the study will identify the minimal features necessary to predict nuclear structure and its influence on transcriptional heterogeneity. Furthermore, the developed methodological paradigms may be generalized to other cellular systems, such as membraneless organelles and cytoskeletal networks. Long-term sustainability will be ensured through public data repositories, open-source software distribution, and comprehensive documentation to support future research in developmental and cancer biology.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget of $1,100,000 over three years supports a multidisciplinary synthesis project requiring significant personnel, computational, and infrastructure resources. Personnel costs, comprising 65% of the total, fund three postdoctoral researchers, two graduate students, and a research software engineer to facilitate data integration, machine learning development, and chromatin modeling. Computational requirements, totaling 16% of the budget, provide necessary cloud and high-performance computing allocations for processing over 50 TB of data and executing molecular dynamics simulations. Travel and workshop funding, representing 14% of the budget, will support quarterly team meetings, conference dissemination, and community training events to ensure broad engagement. Finally, 3% of the budget is allocated to open science infrastructure, including long-term data storage, repository fees, and open-access publication costs. This investment is expected to enable the integration of heterogeneous datasets across multiple laboratories, addressing complex computational challenges that exceed the capacity of individual research grants while advancing the broader mission of NCEMS.

title: Discovery of Long-Range Communication Networks in Protein Complexes via Structural Database Mining
abstract: Allosteric regulation in multi-subunit protein complexes manifests as emergent behavior, where binding events influence distant sites through collective conformational changes absent in isolated subunits. This project systematically characterizes these emergent networks by integrating structural data from the Protein Data Bank, molecular dynamics trajectories, hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, and deep mutational scanning datasets. The study investigates whether specific mesoscale organizational features, such as interface geometries and dynamic coupling patterns, facilitate long-range communication across 10–100 nm distances. Computational methods, including graph-theoretical analysis, normal mode analysis, and machine learning, will identify allosteric pathways and co-evolving residue networks. By correlating these findings with disease mutation databases, the research aims to link disrupted allostery to pathological phenotypes. Expected outcomes include a comprehensive atlas of allosteric networks and predictive models for site identification. These resources will be publicly released to support the rational design of allosteric modulators and elucidate the principles governing complex-level protein assembly.
background_and_significance: Allostery, the regulation of protein activity via distant ligand binding, is a fundamental biological mechanism that facilitates cellular responses to environmental stimuli. While classical models focused on individual proteins, contemporary research suggests that sophisticated allosteric behaviors emerge primarily within multi-subunit complexes. These assemblies function at the mesoscale, where cooperative binding and long-range conformational propagation arise from complex subunit interactions. Although vast repositories like the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold, and MaveDB provide extensive structural and functional data, significant gaps persist regarding the principles governing emergent allostery. Current limitations include an incomplete understanding of the structural features, evolutionary constraints, and dynamic mechanisms that define these communication networks. This project will synthesize multi-dimensional datasets to identify predictive models for allosteric sites. By integrating structural, evolutionary, and biophysical expertise, the study aims to elucidate how complex-level properties arise from molecular assembly, ultimately informing therapeutic strategies and clarifying the role of allosteric disruption in human disease.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates the structural, dynamic, and evolutionary determinants of emergent allostery in multi-subunit protein complexes. By comparing allosteric complexes from the Allosteric Database with size-matched controls, the study evaluates whether specific interface geometries and residue interaction network topologies distinguish allosteric systems. Conformational dynamics are assessed through normal mode analysis and molecular dynamics trajectories, testing the hypothesis that correlated motions and low-frequency modes facilitate long-range communication. Furthermore, the research examines evolutionary constraints by analyzing sequence conservation, coevolutionary signatures, and deep mutational scanning data to identify functional dependencies within allosteric pathways. Finally, machine learning models will be developed to predict allosteric sites and communication networks based on integrated structural and evolutionary features. These predictions will be validated against independent datasets, including disease-associated mutations and hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry profiles. This comprehensive framework aims to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms governing allosteric regulation and to establish predictive models for identifying functional sites in complex protein assemblies.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates heterogeneous data from structural, dynamic, evolutionary, and phenotypic repositories to characterize allosteric mechanisms. Structural data from the Protein Data Bank and AlphaFold will be harmonized using UniProt identifiers and SIFTS mappings to ensure consistent residue numbering. The study will employ graph-theoretical network analysis and normal mode modeling to represent protein structures as residue interaction networks and characterize collective motions. Machine learning ensemble classifiers, trained on structural, evolutionary, and dynamic features, will be developed to predict allosteric sites. Furthermore, evolutionary analysis and perturbation propagation algorithms will identify allosteric pathways. Validation strategies include cross-referencing predictions with hydrogen-deuterium exchange data, mutational fitness landscapes, and disease-associated variants from ClinVar and COSMIC. Well-characterized systems will serve as positive controls to ensure methodological robustness. This multidisciplinary effort, spanning three years, will culminate in a web-accessible atlas of allosteric pathways, providing insights into protein regulation and the functional impact of disease-related mutations across the human proteome.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to advance the understanding of emergent allostery through four primary deliverables. First, the AlloAtlas database will catalog allosteric sites, communication pathways, and network properties for over 10,000 protein complexes, expanding current data fivefold. Second, a suite of open-source computational tools, including AlloPath, AlloPredict, AlloNet, and AlloDyn, will be released to facilitate structural and dynamic analysis. Third, the study will distill mechanistic principles of emergent allostery, identifying quantitative criteria for interface properties, network topologies, and evolutionary constraints. Finally, disease-allostery connection maps will be generated to identify mutations that disrupt communication networks, potentially highlighting new therapeutic targets. By characterizing these mesoscale phenomena, the project will elucidate how protein assembly enables functional properties absent in individual subunits. These findings are expected to provide foundational insights for drug discovery, protein engineering, and evolutionary biology. The project will ensure long-term utility through stable database hosting, comprehensive documentation, and broad dissemination via peer-reviewed publications and community workshops.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget of $1,000,000 over three years supports a collaborative synthesis project requiring significant personnel, computational, and infrastructure resources. Personnel costs, comprising 68% of the total, fund three postdoctoral researchers embedded across laboratories to facilitate cross-disciplinary integration in bioinformatics, machine learning, and evolutionary dynamics. Two graduate students will contribute to disease mutation analysis and visualization tool development, while a part-time software engineer will ensure long-term code sustainability. Computational requirements, totaling 12% of the budget, provide cloud-based scaling for the analysis of over 200,000 protein structures and machine learning model training. Travel and collaboration funds, representing 9% of the budget, support annual working group meetings at NCEMS, conference presentations, and PI coordination. Finally, 11% of the budget is allocated to community workshops, online training development, and open science infrastructure, including database hosting and data archiving. This comprehensive financial plan is expected to enable the synthesis of existing data beyond the capacity of individual laboratories.

title: Integration of Structural and Live-Cell Data for Modeling Emergent Mechanical Properties of Mesoscale Cytoskeletal Crosstalk
abstract: The cytoskeleton exhibits emergent mechanical properties derived from mesoscale interactions between actin filaments, microtubules, and intermediate filaments. This project investigates how cytoskeletal crosstalk generates cellular mechanics by integrating diverse public datasets, including cryo-ET from EMPIAR, super-resolution microscopy, atomic force microscopy, proteomics, and transcriptomics. The study addresses how mesoscale interactions produce stiffness, viscosity, and active stress generation beyond the capacity of individual filaments. It is hypothesized that crosslinker proteins facilitate mechanical coupling through dynamic networks dependent on mesoscale organization. The analytical framework employs finite element modeling, agent-based simulations, and machine learning to predict mechanical properties from network topology. Standardized image analysis pipelines will quantify cytoskeletal architecture, while network analysis identifies critical nodes influencing emergent mechanics. By connecting these findings to cell migration and morphogenesis, the study aims to establish predictive models and principles for engineering cellular mechanics. All developed tools, code, and curated datasets will be disseminated to support future mechanobiology research.
background_and_significance: The eukaryotic cytoskeleton comprises actin microfilaments, microtubules, and intermediate filaments, which interact at the mesoscale to generate emergent mechanical properties. While individual components are well-characterized through in vitro studies, the principles governing their collective organization remain poorly understood. Current structural data from cryo-electron tomography and super-resolution microscopy reveal complex physical interconnections, yet the translation of these molecular interactions into cellular mechanics is unclear. This project addresses the critical gap between nanometer-scale molecular interactions and micrometer-scale bulk mechanics. By integrating heterogeneous datasets from repositories such as EMPIAR, IDR, and BioPlex, this study will investigate how network topology and crosslinker dynamics determine mechanical outcomes. Evidence suggests that organization, rather than composition, dictates cellular phenotypes, including strain-stiffening and active stress generation. Synthesizing these diverse data types is expected to elucidate the mechanical principles underlying development, disease, and morphogenesis. This interdisciplinary approach will provide a comprehensive framework for understanding how cytoskeletal architecture governs emergent cellular behavior.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates emergent cytoskeletal mechanics at the mesoscale by addressing three interconnected research questions through existing public data. The first objective examines how network topology, rather than filament density alone, determines mechanical properties such as stiffness and viscosity. Hypotheses suggest that specific topological motifs, including actin-microtubule junctions, act as mechanical amplifiers that disproportionately influence global cellular behavior. The second objective identifies critical crosslinker proteins governing mechanical coupling between cytoskeletal systems. It is hypothesized that a small subset of proteins with high betweenness centrality, particularly those with dual-binding capabilities, facilitates emergent mechanical coupling that exceeds additive models. The third objective links mesoscale organization to functional outcomes like migration and morphogenesis. This study suggests that mechanical heterogeneity and intermediate filament reorganization are essential for adaptive behaviors and morphological stability. All hypotheses will be validated using cross-dataset integration, employing known crosslinker knockouts as benchmarks to ensure that observed correlations exceed those expected by chance.
methods_and_approach:
This project integrates structural imaging, super-resolution microscopy, mechanical measurements, proteomics, and transcriptomics to characterize cytoskeletal organization. Data will be aggregated from public repositories, including EMPIAR for cryo-electron tomography, the Image Data Resource for microscopy, and the BioPlex and GEO databases for molecular profiles. A three-tiered harmonization strategy will be employed: standardizing modalities, registering cross-scale descriptors, and modeling transitions between molecular interactions and mechanical properties. 

Computational workflows include the CytoMesh pipeline for image segmentation, finite element modeling via FEniCS, and agent-based simulations using Cytosim. Machine learning models, specifically graph neural networks, will be developed to predict mechanical phenotypes from structural and proteomic features. Validation will involve cross-dataset testing and sensitivity analyses to ensure robustness. Over a three-year period, this collaborative effort aims to synthesize multi-scale data into predictive models of cytoskeletal mechanics. By bridging diverse research communities, this study is expected to elucidate the organizational principles governing cellular architecture and mechanical behavior.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to advance the understanding of emergent cytoskeletal mechanics by generating integrated resources for the research community. The study will develop CytoMechDB, a public database linking mesoscale organizational features to mechanical properties across diverse cell types. Concurrently, the CytoMesh pipeline will provide standardized image analysis tools for quantifying cytoskeletal networks from various imaging modalities. Validated computational models will be constructed to predict mechanical properties, such as stiffness and viscosity, based on network topology and crosslinker dynamics. Furthermore, a key crosslinker atlas will identify critical molecular nodes governing mechanical coupling, while a synthesis of general principles will clarify how mesoscale organization dictates emergent cellular behaviors. These deliverables are expected to transform mechanobiology from a descriptive field into a predictive, mechanistic discipline. By integrating heterogeneous data, this project will establish a template for studying emergent phenomena, ultimately providing frameworks to investigate mechanical dysfunction in disease and guiding future research in synthetic biology and tissue engineering.
budget_and_resources: This three-year project requires $1,600,000 to support data synthesis, computational analysis, and open science objectives. Personnel costs, comprising 75% of the budget, fund two postdoctoral researchers for computational mechanobiology and bioimage informatics, two graduate students for systems biology and transcriptomics, and a research software engineer to ensure tool sustainability. Undergraduate support and PI salary allocations further facilitate project leadership and workforce training. Computing resources, accounting for 11% of the budget, provide cloud-based infrastructure for large-scale image processing, machine learning, and high-performance simulations. Travel and collaboration funds support quarterly meetings, conference presentations, and laboratory visits to foster interdisciplinary integration. Additionally, 9% of the budget is dedicated to annual synthesis workshops and online training development to promote community engagement. Finally, 6% covers open science infrastructure, including repository archiving, documentation, and open-access publication fees. This allocation is expected to provide the necessary expertise and technical capacity to achieve the project’s synthesis goals effectively.

title: Decoding Signaling Fidelity through the Synthesis of Phosphoproteomics and Structural Data in Kinase-Substrate Networks
abstract: Cellular signaling networks achieve specificity through mesoscale organization, including scaffolds, localization, and temporal dynamics, rather than intrinsic kinase-substrate affinity alone. This project investigates these emergent properties by integrating large-scale phosphoproteomic, structural, and cell biology datasets from sources such as PhosphoSitePlus, PDB, and the Human Protein Atlas. Computational frameworks will be developed to combine sequence-based kinase predictions with spatial and temporal context, utilizing machine learning to model phosphorylation events based on network topology and scaffold interactions. Dynamic models will test whether spatial constraints are required for signaling fidelity, while time-series analysis may reveal how temporal ordering influences pathway specificity. Furthermore, integration with disease mutation data from COSMIC and ClinVar will examine how disrupted organization contributes to aberrant signaling. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of signaling specificity and the identification of key organizational features, with all predictive pipelines and datasets released to facilitate future research into rational pathway intervention.
background_and_significance: The human kinome regulates cellular processes through phosphorylation, yet a paradox persists where kinases with similar catalytic domains achieve distinct signaling outcomes. While biochemical and structural studies have characterized intrinsic molecular recognition, these data fail to explain how specificity emerges in vivo. Current prediction algorithms, relying primarily on sequence motifs, achieve limited accuracy because they neglect the mesoscale organizational features that govern signaling fidelity. This project investigates how scaffold-mediated interactions, subcellular localization, and temporal dynamics collectively constrain kinase activity. By integrating extensive datasets from the Protein Data Bank, PhosphoSitePlus, and the Human Protein Atlas, this research will synthesize information on protein-protein interactions and spatial organization. The study aims to establish quantitative principles of emergent specificity, addressing how cells maintain signaling precision despite the inherent promiscuity of molecular components. These findings may clarify the relationship between mesoscale dysfunction and disease, ultimately informing the development of more precise therapeutic kinase inhibitors.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates emergent specificity in kinase-substrate networks by evaluating how mesoscale organizational features influence signaling beyond intrinsic sequence recognition. The study tests whether subcellular co-localization, scaffold-mediated concentration, and network topology improve phosphorylation prediction accuracy compared to sequence-only models using data from the Human Protein Atlas, BioGRID, and STRING. Temporal organization is examined through time-series phosphoproteomic data from PRIDE, testing whether kinetic proofreading and structural constraints dictate signaling order in pathways like MAPK and PI3K/Akt. Furthermore, the research explores how disease-associated mutations in scaffolds or kinases disrupt these organizational features, potentially altering signaling specificity. These hypotheses will be validated through rigorous statistical analysis of existing datasets, employing cross-validation and computational controls to ensure robustness. The findings are expected to quantify the relative contributions of localization, scaffolding, and temporal dynamics to signaling fidelity. Ultimately, this work may shift the understanding of cellular signaling from a molecule-centric perspective toward a comprehensive, organization-centric framework.
methods_and_approach:
This project integrates data from eight major public resources, including PhosphoSitePlus, PRIDE, and the Protein Data Bank, to analyze kinase-substrate specificity. The study harmonizes heterogeneous datasets by mapping proteins to UniProt accessions and constructing a unified knowledge graph that links phosphorylation events, protein interactions, and subcellular localization. A multi-layer integration framework will facilitate quality control, weighting interactions by confidence scores and filtering phosphosites by evidence level. 

Computational efforts will employ machine learning, including gradient-boosted trees and graph neural networks, to quantify the contribution of sequence, structural, and network features to phosphorylation prediction. Temporal dynamics will be investigated using Bayesian network inference and ordinary differential equation models to assess how spatial constraints influence signaling fidelity. Furthermore, the project will evaluate how disease-associated mutations disrupt mesoscale organization. These models will be validated through temporal hold-out sets and cross-dataset comparisons, ultimately identifying conserved organizational principles across species and providing insights into the regulatory mechanisms of cellular signaling pathways.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to elucidate emergent specificity in kinase-substrate networks by developing five primary deliverables. These include an integrated knowledge graph of the human kinome, the MesoKinase prediction tool, and parameterized ordinary differential equation models for major signaling pathways. Furthermore, the study will produce a mesoscale disruption atlas linking disease-associated mutations to organizational dysfunction and provide reproducible Snakemake analysis workflows. This research investigates how signaling fidelity arises from mesoscale context, such as localization and scaffolding, rather than molecular interactions alone. It is expected that organizational features contribute significantly to predictive power and that disease-associated dysfunction often stems from structural disruption. These frameworks may be extended to other regulatory systems, including transcription factor networks. By providing accessible computational tools and mechanistic insights, this project will facilitate future research in structural biology and drug development. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, open-source repositories, and community workshops to ensure long-term utility and integration with existing biological databases.
