budget_and_resources: The proposed budget supports a transdisciplinary synthesis project requiring specialized personnel, extensive computational resources, and robust open science infrastructure. Two postdoctoral researchers will lead machine learning model development and dynamical systems modeling, while a graduate assistant and a software engineer will facilitate data curation and sustainable tool development. Computing funds are allocated for cloud-based GPU processing of graph neural networks, large-scale data storage, and essential software licenses. Travel expenses prioritize quarterly team meetings to ensure deep integration across collaborating institutions, alongside conference dissemination and NCEMS workshop participation. Furthermore, the budget covers annual training workshops and the maintenance of web-based prediction tools to foster community access. By prioritizing computational expertise and digital infrastructure over traditional wet-lab instrumentation, this financial plan enables the synthesis of eight major databases. These resources are expected to facilitate the development of scalable machine learning frameworks, ensuring that project outputs remain accessible and sustainable beyond the initial funding period.

title: Integration of Structural, Metabolomic, and Interactome Data for Metabolon Assembly and Emergent Metabolic Channeling
abstract: Metabolons represent transient enzyme assemblies that facilitate substrate channeling, potentially enhancing metabolic efficiency beyond the predictions of isolated enzyme kinetics. This study systematically characterizes metabolon organization by integrating diverse public datasets, including protein-protein interactions from BioGRID and IntAct, structural data from the PDB, and metabolomics from MetaboLights. The research investigates how mesoscale enzyme clustering generates emergent properties, such as increased flux and pathway insulation, which isolated enzymes may not achieve. The project employs constraint-based metabolic modeling, molecular docking, and kinetic simulations to evaluate how enzyme stoichiometry and spatial arrangement influence these microenvironments. Algorithms will be developed to identify putative metabolons, with predictions validated against metabolomic signatures of channeling. Furthermore, machine learning will assess metabolon formation propensity across varying cellular conditions. The expected outcomes include a comprehensive metabolon atlas and predictive models of channeling efficiency, providing insights into metabolic engineering and diseases associated with metabolic dysfunction.
background_and_significance: Cellular metabolism relies on the assembly of enzymes into dynamic supramolecular complexes known as metabolons, which facilitate substrate channeling. This mesoscale organization enables enhanced pathway flux and intermediate protection, properties that are not predictable from isolated enzyme kinetics. Although metabolons have been identified across diverse pathways, a systematic understanding of their assembly principles and functional consequences remains elusive. Current knowledge is fragmented, as relevant data reside in disparate databases, including BioGRID, the Protein Data Bank, and various metabolomics repositories. This project aims to integrate these extensive datasets to construct a comprehensive atlas of metabolon organization and predictive models of channeling efficiency. By bridging the gap between molecular and organelle scales, this research will elucidate how spatial arrangement dictates metabolic function. Such insights may clarify the role of metabolon disruption in metabolic diseases and inform the engineering of microbial cell factories, ultimately requiring a transdisciplinary approach to synthesize these complex biological data.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates metabolon organization and emergent metabolic channeling at the mesoscale through four interconnected research questions. First, a comprehensive metabolon atlas will be generated by integrating protein-protein interaction data with metabolic pathway annotations. This study hypothesizes that metabolon formation is enriched in pathways involving labile intermediates or kinetic coordination, with core architectures likely conserved across eukaryotes. Second, structural principles governing assembly will be identified by analyzing enzyme interfaces, surface electrostatics, and channel geometries. Machine learning models are expected to predict metabolon propensity based on these structural features. Third, quantitative models will link metabolon architecture to emergent kinetic properties, such as enhanced flux and reduced intermediate pools. It is hypothesized that channeling efficiency depends on active site proximity and local intermediate concentrations. Finally, the dynamic regulation of metabolons in response to metabolic demands will be assessed by integrating transcriptomic and post-translational modification data. These findings will establish fundamental principles of mesoscale cellular organization.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates six primary data categories—protein interactions, structures, metabolomics, enzyme kinetics, proteomics, and post-translational modifications—into a unified computational framework to characterize metabolon organization and emergent channeling. The study proceeds through four phases: data harmonization, metabolon identification, kinetic modeling, and cross-species comparative analysis. Initially, large-scale datasets from repositories such as BioGRID, PDB, and BRENDA will be standardized using UniProt identifiers and Frictionless Data schemas. Subsequently, network-based algorithms and machine learning classifiers, including graph neural networks, will identify putative metabolons by integrating structural docking and co-expression modules. Kinetic properties will be investigated through constraint-based metabolic modeling and ordinary differential equation simulations, which will be validated against measured intermediate concentrations from MetaboLights. Finally, cross-species comparisons and condition-dependent assembly analyses will be conducted to identify conserved architectures and lineage-specific innovations. This multidisciplinary approach is expected to provide a comprehensive atlas of metabolon organization, offering insights into the regulatory mechanisms of metabolic channeling across diverse biological systems.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project will generate four foundational resources for the metabolism and systems biology communities. First, a comprehensive Metabolon Atlas will provide a searchable database of curated annotations, structural models, and condition-dependent assembly profiles for metabolic pathways across five model organisms. Second, validated computational models, including machine learning classifiers and kinetic simulations, will be developed to predict metabolon formation and substrate channeling efficiency. Third, reproducible analysis pipelines implemented as Snakemake workflows will facilitate metabolon detection and structural characterization. Finally, the project will produce peer-reviewed publications and training materials to disseminate these findings. By quantifying emergent properties at the mesoscale, this study will establish general principles governing spatial organization and structure-function relationships. These outcomes are expected to advance metabolic engineering, elucidate disease mechanisms, and inform drug discovery. Furthermore, the project will provide a framework for future research, ensuring long-term sustainability through open-access data, permissive software licensing, and the establishment of a community-led steering committee.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget of $950,000 over three years supports a transdisciplinary synthesis project requiring specialized personnel, computational infrastructure, and community engagement. Personnel costs, comprising 76% of the total, fund two postdoctoral researchers to lead metabolon detection and structural analysis, alongside two graduate students for database and genomic tasks. A part-time scientific programmer will ensure code reproducibility and infrastructure maintenance. Computational requirements, totaling $90,000, utilize cloud and high-performance computing to facilitate large-scale data processing and machine learning model training. Travel funds support annual working group meetings and conference dissemination, while $40,000 is allocated for community workshops and training materials. Open science infrastructure, including database hosting and open-access publication fees, ensures long-term project sustainability. This budget reflects the necessity of integrating diverse expertise and resources that exceed the capacity of individual laboratories. Consequently, this funding is expected to enable the comprehensive synthesis of metabolomics data through sustained, collaborative, and reproducible scientific efforts.

title: Emergent Selectivity of Autophagy Receptors: Integration of Structural and Proteomic Data for Decoding Cargo Recognition Networks
abstract: Selective autophagy achieves cargo specificity through receptor proteins that bridge substrates to autophagosomes via multivalent mesoscale interactions. This project investigates how these receptors generate emergent selectivity by integrating structural biology, proteomics, and cell biology datasets. Structural data from the Protein Data Bank, autophagy interactomes, and organelle proteomics will be synthesized to examine how avidity, coincidence detection, and cooperative binding facilitate cargo recognition. It is hypothesized that receptor oligomerization and phase separation create condensates that amplify weak individual interactions. Computational approaches, including structural modeling and machine learning, will predict cargo selectivity based on receptor and cargo features. Coarse-grained simulations will further evaluate how receptor density and geometry influence clustering. By integrating disease mutation data, the study aims to link disrupted recognition to pathological accumulation. These findings are expected to provide mechanistic models of selectivity, identify key recognition features, and establish principles for engineering autophagy pathways, with all data released publicly.
background_and_significance: Selective autophagy functions as a sophisticated quality control mechanism, facilitating the targeted degradation of organelles, protein aggregates, and pathogens. Unlike bulk autophagy, this process relies on receptor proteins that bridge cargo to the autophagosomal membrane. Although individual receptor-cargo interactions exhibit weak micromolar affinities, the system achieves high specificity through emergent mesoscale phenomena. Recent structural and proteomic data, including over 200 receptor structures and thousands of documented interactions, suggest that oligomerization and multivalent engagement amplify these weak signals. Despite this extensive data, the mechanisms governing how receptors distinguish between substrates with overlapping features remain unclear. This project will synthesize structural, proteomic, and functional datasets to elucidate the principles of mesoscale selectivity. By integrating information from the Human Protein Atlas, CRISPR screens, and disease databases, the study aims to define the thresholds for cargo recognition. These findings may provide a conceptual foundation for therapeutic interventions in autophagy-related disorders and establish paradigms for understanding emergent biological systems.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how mesoscale organization, including oligomerization, coincidence detection, and phase separation, generates emergent selectivity in autophagy receptors. It is hypothesized that receptor oligomerization creates avidity through geometric matching, where larger assemblies preferentially target extensive cargo structures. Coarse-grained modeling of ubiquitin-binding domains is expected to demonstrate that spatial complementarity between receptors and cargo surfaces maximizes multivalent engagement. Furthermore, the study examines how receptors achieve coincidence detection by integrating multiple cargo signals, suggesting that multi-domain receptors exhibit increased selectivity at the expense of sensitivity. Network analysis of interactomes may reveal that disease-associated mutations disrupt specific cargo-recognition domains, leading to distinct phenotypic outcomes. Finally, the research explores whether liquid-liquid phase separation establishes concentration thresholds that discriminate between cargo and bystanders. By integrating structural, proteomic, and phenotypic data, this study aims to establish quantitative relationships between receptor architecture and cargo selectivity, ultimately identifying the fundamental parameters that govern autophagy outcomes across diverse cellular pathways.
methods_and_approach:
This project integrates heterogeneous data from structural, proteomic, and cell biology repositories to elucidate mechanisms of selective autophagy. Data acquisition encompasses atomic-resolution structures from the PDB and AlphaFold, protein-protein interactions from BioGRID and IntAct, and post-translational modifications from PhosphoSitePlus. Subcellular localization, disease variants, and functional CRISPR screens are also incorporated to provide a comprehensive biological context. Systematic harmonization involves mapping identifiers to UniProt accessions and normalizing interaction scores to ensure consistency across datasets.

Analytical methods include data-driven docking and integrative modeling to construct mesoscale receptor-cargo assemblies. Coarse-grained simulations using the MARTINI force field will investigate how receptor density and cargo geometry influence avidity. Furthermore, machine learning models, including graph neural networks, will be trained to predict cargo selectivity based on structural and network features. Validation will rely on cross-dataset comparisons and established disease phenotypes. This transdisciplinary study leverages expertise in autophagy biology, computational biophysics, and systems biology to develop a predictive framework for selective autophagy pathways.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to elucidate emergent selectivity in autophagy by developing four primary resources: the AutoSelectDB database, mechanistic models of mesoscale organization, predictive computational tools, and curated benchmark datasets. AutoSelectDB will integrate structural, proteomic, and functional data to facilitate analysis of receptor-cargo interactions. Mechanistic models will quantify how multivalent recognition and phase separation drive selectivity, while machine learning tools will predict cargo specificity and mutation impacts. These outputs will address fundamental questions regarding how weak molecular interactions scale to produce cellular outcomes through avidity and coincidence detection. The findings are expected to generalize to other mesoscale systems, including immune signaling and membrane trafficking. Furthermore, the project will support therapeutic development and synthetic biology applications by providing a framework for engineering autophagy receptors. All resources will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, workshops, and sustainable repositories, ensuring long-term accessibility for the research community to generate and validate new hypotheses regarding selective autophagy.
budget_and_resources: The project budget supports a multidisciplinary team of two postdoctoral researchers, a graduate student, and a research software engineer to conduct structural modeling, machine learning, and data curation. Personnel costs reflect the intellectual requirements of synthesis research, while computing resources, including cloud infrastructure and high-performance computing, facilitate large-scale simulations and database management. Persistent data storage ensures the long-term availability of derived datasets. Travel funds are allocated for quarterly team meetings to maintain collaboration and for conference dissemination to engage the broader scientific community. Furthermore, the budget covers two training workshops designed to disseminate mesoscale modeling methods and project tools to external participants. Open science infrastructure, including repository hosting and open-access publication fees, is prioritized to ensure the sustainability and accessibility of all project outputs. Collectively, these expenditures are expected to provide the necessary human and technical capacity to integrate heterogeneous data sources and advance the understanding of emergent selectivity in autophagy.

title: Integration of Structural Dynamics and Systems-Level Oscillations in Emergent Circadian Protein Network Timing
abstract: Circadian rhythms represent a form of mesoscale emergence where system-level periodicity arises from non-oscillatory protein interaction networks. This project integrates structural biology, proteomics, and systems biology datasets to elucidate how post-translational modifications and protein-protein interactions generate 24-hour oscillations. Data from the Protein Data Bank, BioGRID, CircaDB, and published phosphoproteomic time-series will be synthesized to investigate the hypothesis that emergent timing results from coupled feedback loops within mesoscale protein complexes. Computational methods, including mathematical modeling and molecular dynamics simulations, will be employed to identify structural features governing interaction kinetics and assembly-driven delays. Furthermore, comparative analysis across species and tissues will clarify how conserved mechanisms and expression patterns influence period variability. The study is expected to provide mechanistic models linking molecular interactions to emergent periodicity and identify organizational features that modulate circadian rhythms. These findings may offer insights into chronotherapy and metabolic disease management, with all resulting datasets and models released publicly.
background_and_significance: Circadian rhythms emerge from molecular networks lacking intrinsic timing, presenting a fundamental challenge in understanding mesoscale biological organization. While the core mammalian transcription-translation feedback loops involving CLOCK, BMAL1, PER, and CRY proteins are well-characterized, the mechanism maintaining stable 24-hour periods remains elusive. Current research suggests that mesoscale organization, including multi-protein complexes and post-translational modifications, generates the necessary temporal delays. Although structural data from the Protein Data Bank and extensive phosphoproteomic datasets from PRIDE provide detailed molecular insights, these findings are often analyzed in isolation. This project integrates heterogeneous structural, proteomic, and transcriptomic data to bridge the gap between atomic-level features and systems-level oscillatory dynamics. By synthesizing information from databases like CircaDB and BioGRID, this study will investigate how mesoscale protein interactions create emergent timing and ensure robustness against molecular noise. Ultimately, this synthesis aims to elucidate the principles of mesoscale emergence, explaining how identical molecular components generate diverse, tissue-specific circadian periods across various biological systems.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how mesoscale molecular organization generates emergent circadian timing through four interconnected research questions. It is hypothesized that delays necessary for 24-hour oscillations arise from cooperative protein complex assembly and sequential phosphorylation cascades. Structural features extracted from the Protein Data Bank will be correlated with kinetic measurements to validate these mechanisms. Furthermore, the study examines how interface flexibility and allosteric networks influence interaction kinetics, potentially explaining period-altering mutations. By integrating tissue-specific expression data from GTEx and BioGRID interaction networks, the research will assess whether differential network topology accounts for period variations across mammalian tissues. Finally, cross-species structural and network analyses will be conducted to identify conserved organizational principles that maintain robust timing despite molecular divergence. This study is expected to elucidate how mesoscale protein assembly, phosphorylation dynamics, and network architecture collectively tune circadian periods, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding the emergence of temporal properties in diverse biological systems.
methods_and_approach:
This project synthesizes heterogeneous data from structural biology, proteomics, transcriptomics, and systems biology to elucidate emergent circadian timing. By integrating information across scales—from atomic-resolution structures to tissue-level oscillations—the study employs computational methods to bridge these domains. All analyses rely exclusively on publicly available datasets, ensuring no new experimental data generation.

The methodology involves harmonizing diverse data sources through unified identifiers and standardized temporal annotations. Structural analysis utilizes interface characterization and molecular dynamics simulations to assess allosteric coupling, while phosphoproteomic data are analyzed via time-series algorithms to map modification cascades. Furthermore, tissue-specific interaction networks are reconstructed and integrated into ordinary differential equation models to simulate complex formation. Machine learning approaches, including graph neural networks, are expected to predict interaction kinetics and structural determinants of period-altering mutations. Validation strategies involve cross-dataset testing, leave-one-out procedures, and comparisons against established literature. This transdisciplinary effort aims to provide a comprehensive, integrated circadian data resource and validated mathematical models of clock mechanisms.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to elucidate emergent circadian timing by integrating structural, proteomic, and systems-level data into a comprehensive framework. The study will produce the CircaMeso database, which harmonizes structural annotations, phosphoproteomic time-series, and tissue-specific interaction networks across species. Validated mathematical models will be developed to investigate how mesoscale protein complex assembly generates temporal delays and period diversity. Furthermore, the research will establish a structural-kinetic atlas and reproducible computational pipelines to map molecular features to system-level oscillations. These efforts are expected to demonstrate that cooperative assembly, sequential modifications, and network topology function as fundamental mechanisms for biological timing. Beyond circadian biology, this synthesis provides transferable paradigms for studying emergent phenomena in signal transduction and metabolic control. By bridging molecular structure with system-level dynamics, the project will generate testable hypotheses for chronotherapy and establish a robust infrastructure for future transdisciplinary research, supported by open-access dissemination, community-driven workshops, and long-term maintenance of all computational resources.
budget_and_resources: This three-year project requests $1,200,000 to support a transdisciplinary synthesis study requiring expertise across structural biology, systems modeling, and computational data analysis. Personnel costs, comprising 65% of the budget, will fund two postdoctoral researchers, two graduate students, and a part-time research software engineer to ensure robust code development and data integration. Computational requirements, totaling 15% of the budget, will utilize cloud and high-performance computing resources to facilitate molecular dynamics simulations, machine learning, and scalable data processing. Travel and collaboration expenses are allocated to support annual working group meetings, conference dissemination, and intensive laboratory exchanges. Furthermore, 10% of the budget is dedicated to training initiatives, including annual workshops and online materials, to foster synthesis research skills. Finally, 4% of the funding will maintain open science infrastructure, covering data storage, software maintenance, and open-access publication fees. This investment is expected to enable the integration of diverse datasets, exceeding the capabilities of individual laboratories.

title: Integration of Cryo-ET and Bioenergetic Data for Modeling Mesoscale Energy Transduction in Mitochondrial Cristae
abstract: Mitochondrial cristae architecture facilitates emergent proton gradients that enhance ATP synthesis efficiency beyond the capacity of flat membrane models. This project investigates how mesoscale cristae geometry influences bioenergetic properties by integrating structural, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets from repositories including EMPIAR, PDB, and MitoCarta. It is hypothesized that cristae microcompartments generate local proton concentrations exceeding bulk predictions, while respiratory chain supercomplex organization optimizes proton delivery to ATP synthase. The methodology employs finite element modeling of proton diffusion, molecular simulations of supercomplexes, and systems biology modeling of oxidative phosphorylation. Image analysis pipelines will quantify cristae morphology across diverse cell types to correlate architecture with bioenergetic output and disease-related dysfunction. This interdisciplinary study aims to establish quantitative models of emergent proton gradients and identify architectural features that optimize ATP synthesis. The resulting analysis pipelines and integrated datasets will be made publicly available to support further research into mitochondrial function, aging, and metabolic disease.
background_and_significance: Mitochondria generate the majority of cellular ATP via oxidative phosphorylation, yet the influence of inner mitochondrial membrane architecture on bioenergetic efficiency remains poorly understood. While cristae are known to form distinct microcompartments, the relationship between their mesoscale geometry and emergent bioenergetic properties requires further investigation. Current research is hindered by the isolation of structural, proteomic, and metabolic datasets, which prevents a comprehensive understanding of how cristae morphology regulates proton gradients and respiratory supercomplex function. This project will integrate diverse data from repositories such as EMPIAR, PDB, and MitoCarta to systematically correlate morphological parameters with bioenergetic output. By synthesizing these disparate datasets, the study aims to validate theoretical models of proton concentration and elucidate how genetic variants disrupt mitochondrial function. These findings may provide a framework for understanding the role of cristae abnormalities in metabolic diseases and neurodegeneration, ultimately identifying potential therapeutic targets for conditions associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and aging.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how mesoscale cristae morphology facilitates emergent proton concentration gradients and ATP synthesis rates unattainable by flat membranes. The study evaluates quantitative relationships between cristae geometry and bioenergetic efficiency, hypothesizing that smaller junction diameters and higher surface area densities correlate with increased oxidative capacity. Respiratory chain supercomplex organization is expected to optimize proton delivery, with supercomplexes potentially localizing to high-curvature regions to minimize diffusion distances. Finite element modeling will be employed to determine if cristae constraints generate local proton concentrations exceeding bulk thermodynamic predictions, thereby enhancing ATP synthesis. Furthermore, the research examines how pathogenic mutations and metabolic perturbations alter cristae architecture, potentially linking structural deficits to clinical phenotypes. Finally, the study explores the evolutionary convergence of cristae morphology across species based on metabolic demand. These hypotheses will be validated through the synthesis of existing EMPIAR tomograms, respirometry data, metabolomic profiles, and clinical databases, providing a comprehensive mechanistic assessment of mitochondrial bioenergetics.
methods_and_approach: This project employs a multi-scale computational synthesis approach to integrate structural, proteomic, metabolomic, and bioenergetic data for predictive modeling of emergent proton gradients within mitochondrial cristae. The methodology proceeds through four interconnected phases: systematic data harmonization, quantitative morphological analysis, multi-scale computational modeling, and integrative validation. Initially, cryo-ET tomograms, high-resolution respiratory complex structures, and mitochondrial protein datasets will be retrieved and standardized using a metadata ontology to mitigate experimental heterogeneity. Subsequently, automated deep learning pipelines will extract morphological parameters from tomograms, while subtomogram averaging will map respiratory complex localization. These data will inform finite element models of proton diffusion and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to assess the influence of membrane curvature on complex organization. Finally, the study will validate model predictions against independent respirometry and biochemical datasets. This framework is expected to elucidate how cristae architecture dictates bioenergetic efficiency and may provide insights into the functional consequences of disease-associated morphological variations.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to elucidate emergent bioenergetic properties at the mesoscale by developing five integrated resources. The study will establish CristaeDB, a comprehensive database of quantitative morphological parameters derived from cryo-ET tomograms, alongside CristaeMorph, an open-source pipeline for automated structural analysis. Computational models will be generated to predict proton concentration profiles and ATP synthesis rates based on specific cristae geometries, providing a framework to link mesoscale architecture to bioenergetic function. Furthermore, a structure-function correlation atlas and a disease-morphology-function map will be produced to identify architectural determinants of mitochondrial efficiency and the mechanistic consequences of genetic variants. By integrating structural, proteomic, and functional data, this research addresses how mesoscale organization influences biochemical outcomes. These findings are expected to provide generalizable principles for studying membrane-bound compartments. Ultimately, the project will offer a robust methodological template for investigating emergent phenomena, supporting future translational research into mitochondrial pathologies and facilitating broader community access to quantitative bioenergetic analysis.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget supports a multi-disciplinary synthesis project requiring specialized personnel, computational resources, and collaborative infrastructure. Two postdoctoral researchers will lead finite element modeling of proton diffusion and the development of the CristaeMorph deep learning pipeline, respectively. Two graduate research assistants will facilitate data curation and biological interpretation, while a research software engineer will ensure the long-term maintainability of developed tools. Computational requirements include cloud-based GPU and CPU allocations for simulations and deep learning, alongside secure storage for large-scale cryo-ET datasets. Travel funds are allocated for bi-annual working group meetings, conference dissemination, and collaborative laboratory visits to foster team science. Furthermore, the budget covers annual training workshops, webinar infrastructure, and open science platforms to ensure community engagement and long-term data preservation. These expenditures reflect the project’s reliance on human expertise and scalable digital infrastructure, prioritizing collaborative synthesis over experimental data generation to maximize the impact and accessibility of the research outputs.

title: Integration of Structural and Immunopeptidomic Data for Modeling Emergent Epitope Generation in the Immunoproteasome
abstract: The immunoproteasome generates MHC-presented peptides through cleavage patterns distinct from constitutive proteasomes, suggesting that subunit composition influences processing outcomes at the mesoscale. This project investigates how immunoproteasome assembly facilitates emergent epitope generation by integrating structural biology and immunopeptidomics. Data from EMDB, IEDB, SysteMHC Atlas, and UniProt will be synthesized to examine how allosteric communication and cooperative effects among catalytic sites dictate substrate threading. Computational modeling and machine learning will be employed to predict cleavage sites and correlate proteasome subunit expression with immunopeptidome composition across various cell types and disease states. This analysis aims to elucidate how altered proteasome architecture shifts epitope generation, potentially informing vaccine design and cancer immunotherapy. Expected outcomes include predictive models of antigen processing and the identification of key subunit interactions. All developed algorithms, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be made publicly available to support further research into immune recognition mechanisms.
background_and_significance: The eukaryotic proteasome is a 2.5 MDa complex that functions as the primary engine for intracellular protein degradation. While the constitutive proteasome utilizes specific β-subunits for peptide cleavage, interferon-γ stimulation induces the incorporation of immunoproteasome variants, which fundamentally alters the resulting peptide repertoire. This shift represents an emergent phenomenon where the assembled mesoscale architecture dictates cleavage specificity through allosteric communication and cooperative active site interactions. Despite extensive structural data in the EMDB and immunopeptidomic records in the IEDB, the mechanisms linking proteasome architecture to functional outcomes remain poorly understood. This project will integrate heterogeneous datasets from structural biology, immunopeptidomics, and transcriptomics to model how proteasome composition influences epitope generation. By synthesizing these diverse data types, the study aims to decode the rules governing antigen processing. These findings may provide foundational insights for vaccine development, cancer immunotherapy, and the management of autoimmune conditions by enabling the rational manipulation of peptide presentation.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates the emergent properties of immunoproteasome-mediated antigen processing at the mesoscale. The study addresses how complete immunosubunit incorporation generates non-additive cleavage specificities, potentially driven by allosteric communication within the proteasome barrel. By correlating scRNA-seq data with immunopeptidome profiles, the research evaluates whether fully induced immunoproteasomes produce unique peptide signatures absent in partial-incorporation states. Furthermore, the project examines how mesoscale architecture, including channel geometry and gate dynamics, influences substrate threading and processing outcomes. Molecular modeling is expected to demonstrate that immunoproteasome-specific channel configurations dictate substrate orientation, thereby shaping cleavage patterns independently of catalytic site chemistry. Finally, the study explores how these emergent cleavage properties optimize epitope generation for MHC binding and T cell recognition. By integrating transcriptomic and immunopeptidomic datasets, the analysis will assess whether altered proteasome composition in disease states correlates with predictable shifts in immunogenicity. These findings may establish a framework for understanding how molecular machine assembly dictates functional outcomes in immune responses.
methods_and_approach:
This project integrates heterogeneous data from public repositories, including structural biology, immunopeptidomics, transcriptomics, and immunology, to elucidate proteasome function. Structural data from the Protein Data Bank and Electron Microscopy Data Bank will be systematically cataloged, while immunopeptidomic datasets from IEDB and SysteMHC Atlas will provide experimental context. Transcriptomic profiles from GEO and TCGA will be utilized to map proteasome subunit expression across diverse physiological and pathological states.

A multi-layer harmonization framework will align structural, sequence, and expression data to enable cross-modal analysis. Computational pipelines will extract active site geometries and conformational ensembles, while deep learning models, utilizing protein language models, will be trained to predict proteasome cleavage sites. Network analysis will further characterize epitope generation patterns. This synthesis aims to correlate structural features with functional outcomes and predict altered epitope generation in disease contexts. Validation will rely on independent datasets, known positive controls, and temporal cross-validation to ensure model robustness and predictive accuracy.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to elucidate emergent immunoproteasome function through five primary deliverables. First, an integrated database will link proteasome structures to functional annotations, facilitating structural analysis via standardized features and visualization tools. Second, machine learning models will be developed to predict cleavage specificity based on substrate sequence and subunit composition, providing uncertainty estimates for user assessment. Third, an expression-immunopeptidome atlas will map transcriptomic data to peptide repertoires, enabling the prediction of antigen processing outcomes across diverse cellular contexts. Fourth, a mechanistic framework will be articulated to explain how mesoscale architecture and allosteric networks govern cooperative catalysis. Finally, curated datasets will be released to support future benchmarking of cleavage prediction algorithms. By quantifying compositional emergence, architectural constraints, and allosteric integration, this study will establish general principles for mesoscale molecular machines. These findings are expected to advance structural biology, proteomics, and immunology, ultimately providing a robust computational infrastructure to catalyze future research and therapeutic development.
budget_and_resources: The project budget supports a transdisciplinary synthesis approach, prioritizing human expertise and computational infrastructure over experimental costs. Personnel requirements include two postdoctoral researchers for structural bioinformatics and machine learning, a graduate student for pipeline development, and a research software engineer to ensure tool sustainability. Principal investigators will provide essential scientific oversight across immunology and computational biology. Computational resources, including cloud services and high-performance computing, are allocated for large-scale data processing and molecular modeling. Travel funds facilitate in-person collaboration and the dissemination of findings at major disciplinary conferences. Furthermore, the budget covers two workshops to train researchers in synthesis methods and promote community engagement. Open science infrastructure, including repository hosting and permanent archiving, ensures the long-term accessibility of project outputs. Finally, publication fees and specialized software licenses support the dissemination and execution of the research. This allocation reflects the project’s commitment to rigorous, reproducible, and accessible scientific synthesis.

title: Integration of Structural and Transport Data for Modeling CRM1-Mediated Cargo Recognition in Nuclear Export
abstract: CRM1-mediated nuclear export facilitates the selective transport of numerous cargoes through mesoscale complex assembly rather than simple binary interactions. This project investigates the mechanisms of emergent export selectivity by integrating structural biology, proteomics, and transport kinetics. Data from the Protein Data Bank, NESdb, ValidNES, and the Human Protein Atlas will be synthesized alongside published single-molecule kinetic studies. It is hypothesized that emergent selectivity arises from conformational selection, where RanGTP binding induces allosteric changes in CRM1 that differentially stabilize cargo complexes based on specific NES properties. The computational framework employs molecular dynamics simulations, machine learning for export efficiency prediction, and kinetic modeling of assembly dynamics. This research aims to identify sequence and structural determinants of selectivity while correlating export disruption with pathological phenotypes. The resulting predictive models and curated datasets are expected to elucidate principles of cargo recognition, providing insights into diseases characterized by protein mislocalization and facilitating future therapeutic modulation.
background_and_significance: Nuclear transport is a fundamental eukaryotic process regulated by the CRM1 receptor, which facilitates the movement of diverse protein cargoes across the nuclear envelope. While CRM1-mediated export is often attributed to binary interactions with leucine-rich nuclear export signals, this model fails to account for the observed variability in transport kinetics and cargo affinity. Emergent selectivity likely arises from mesoscale assembly dynamics within the ternary CRM1-RanGTP-cargo complex, rather than static binding interactions alone. This project will synthesize heterogeneous data from structural biology, proteomics, and single-molecule kinetics to elucidate the mechanisms governing these complex assemblies. By integrating these disparate datasets, the study aims to construct predictive models of export efficiency that transcend current binary frameworks. Such insights are expected to clarify the functional consequences of disease-associated mutations and improve the clinical application of CRM1 inhibitors. Ultimately, this transdisciplinary approach will provide a comprehensive understanding of how mesoscale dynamics dictate selective nuclear transport in health and disease.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how CRM1 achieves emergent selectivity for diverse cargoes through mesoscale ternary complex formation with RanGTP. The study addresses four research questions to determine how structural features, allosteric states, and kinetic parameters govern export efficiency. First, NES structural properties, including secondary structure propensity and flanking region dynamics, are hypothesized to modulate ternary complex assembly kinetics beyond simple binding affinity. Second, RanGTP-induced allostery in CRM1 may create distinct conformational substates that facilitate cargo-specific selection. Third, export efficiency is expected to depend on kinetic signatures, such as assembly and RanGAP-stimulated disassembly rates, rather than equilibrium thermodynamics alone. Finally, disease-associated mutations are hypothesized to disrupt these emergent mechanisms by altering conformational or kinetic parameters. By integrating structural data from the PDB, kinetic measurements, and subcellular localization datasets, this research aims to establish a comprehensive framework for nuclear export, shifting the current understanding from binary binding models toward a nuanced, mesoscale systems perspective.
methods_and_approach: This project employs a multi-layered data synthesis approach to construct comprehensive models of emergent export selectivity by integrating structural, sequence, localization, kinetic, and disease mutation data. The study proceeds through four interconnected phases: data harmonization, structural analysis, computational modeling, and disease integration, utilizing exclusively publicly available datasets. Initially, structural data from the Protein Data Bank and NES sequences from established databases will be curated and standardized. Subcellular localization scores from the Human Protein Atlas and kinetic parameters from literature will be integrated to quantify export efficiency. Structural analysis will characterize CRM1 conformational states and NES binding geometries, while machine learning models will be developed to predict export efficiency based on physicochemical and evolutionary features. Kinetic modeling will further elucidate the export cycle, with a Bayesian framework managing data integration and uncertainty. Finally, the study will validate these models against known substrates and analyze the impact of disease-associated mutations on export selectivity.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This synthesis project aims to elucidate emergent selectivity in nuclear export through five integrated deliverables. A comprehensive CRM1-CargoAtlas will aggregate structural, kinetic, and clinical data for over 500 cargo proteins to serve as a community resource. Machine learning models will be developed to predict export efficiency from sequence and structural features, targeting high accuracy in binary and quantitative classifications. A structural atlas of CRM1 conformational states will map allosteric pathways, while kinetic models will identify rate-limiting steps in the export cycle. Furthermore, the analysis of over 1,000 disease-associated mutations will clarify mechanisms of pathogenicity and therapeutic sensitivity. By integrating these data, the study will establish principles of mesoscale emergent phenomena, demonstrating how conformational selection and kinetic assembly dictate functional outcomes. These findings are expected to provide a template for studying other transport systems, inform precision medicine for export-related diseases, and facilitate the engineering of synthetic protein localization circuits for future biotechnological applications.
budget_and_resources: This project requests $750,000 over three years to support a community-scale synthesis initiative requiring extensive interdisciplinary coordination and computational infrastructure. Personnel costs, totaling $480,000, prioritize human expertise in computational biology, structural chemistry, and programming to facilitate data integration, kinetic modeling, and database maintenance. Graduate research assistants will contribute to specific project components while receiving specialized training. Computational requirements, budgeted at $120,000, utilize cloud services and high-performance computing to manage large-scale machine learning models, structural simulations, and long-term data storage. An allocation of $75,000 for travel and collaboration supports quarterly working group meetings and conference dissemination, ensuring deep intellectual integration. Furthermore, $45,000 is designated for annual training workshops and tutorial development to foster community engagement. Finally, $30,000 supports open science infrastructure, including database hosting and persistent data archiving. This budget is expected to provide significant value by synthesizing existing public data, thereby maximizing research efficiency and enabling broad community access to project outcomes.

title: Emergent Cooperativity in Transcription Factor Clusters: Integrating ChIP-seq, Structural, and Imaging Data for Enhancer Activation Modeling
abstract: Transcription factor (TF) clustering at enhancers facilitates emergent transcriptional outputs through cooperative DNA binding and co-activator recruitment, representing mesoscale phenomena beyond the capacity of isolated factors. This project integrates genomics, structural biology, and imaging datasets to decode emergent TF cooperativity. By synthesizing ChIP-seq data, PDB structural information, and super-resolution imaging, the study investigates how assemblies of 10–100 TF molecules drive transcriptional activation. It is hypothesized that emergent cooperativity arises from multivalent interactions, DNA-mediated communication, and phase separation. The computational framework employs thermodynamic modeling, machine learning, and spatial simulations to predict enhancer activity from TF binding patterns. Furthermore, single-cell transcriptomics and GWAS data will be analyzed to link TF cluster heterogeneity to transcriptional noise and disease phenotypes. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent cooperativity and predictive principles for transcriptional output. These findings may provide significant insights into developmental biology and gene therapy, with all developed models and datasets released publicly.
background_and_significance: Transcriptional regulation relies on the collective orchestration of gene expression by transcription factors (TFs), yet the mechanisms governing their mesoscale clustering at enhancers remain poorly understood. Although genomics and imaging have identified TF clusters containing tens to hundreds of molecules, the structural basis for this emergent cooperativity is not fully characterized. Current research suggests that phase separation, driven by intrinsically disordered regions, may facilitate these assemblies, though the link between condensate formation and transcriptional output requires further investigation. This project aims to integrate disparate datasets, including ChIP-seq, structural PDB entries, and single-cell transcriptomics, to elucidate the rules governing cooperative binding. By synthesizing genomic binding patterns with structural constraints and disease-associated variants, this study may clarify how mesoscale organization bridges molecular interactions and cellular phenotypes. Such an integrative approach is expected to reveal how cells achieve precise transcriptional control and identify potential therapeutic targets for diseases characterized by dysregulated gene expression.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how transcription factor (TF) clustering at enhancers facilitates emergent transcriptional activation. The study addresses four research questions regarding the structural and functional mechanisms of TF cooperativity. First, structural configurations enabling cooperative binding are examined by integrating ChIP-seq data with PDB structural models to determine how DNA geometry and protein interfaces influence transcriptional output. Second, the role of intrinsically disordered regions in phase separation is evaluated by correlating TF sequence features with transcriptional nonlinearity and super-resolution imaging data. Third, the relationship between TF cluster heterogeneity and transcriptional noise is analyzed using single-cell RNA-seq to determine how enhancer architecture buffers against stochasticity. Finally, the impact of disease-associated genetic variants on cooperative TF configurations is assessed by comparing GWAS data with structural predictions of binding disruption. Collectively, this research is expected to establish a comprehensive model of mesoscale transcriptional regulation, identifying the structural rules, phase separation contributions, noise-buffering principles, and disease-relevant variants that define emergent TF cooperativity.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates genomic, structural, imaging, transcriptomic, and genetic variation data to model transcription factor (TF) regulatory mechanisms. Publicly available datasets, including ENCODE, ReMap, JASPAR, FANTOM5, PDB, AlphaFold, and the Human Cell Atlas, will be harmonized to a GRCh38 coordinate framework. A multi-layer integration strategy will extract structural features, establish enhancer-gene linkages, and construct a graph-based representation of regulatory relationships. Analytical methods include thermodynamic modeling of cooperative binding, machine learning for enhancer activity prediction, and agent-based simulations of TF clustering dynamics. Furthermore, transcriptional noise will be quantified using single-cell data, while genetic variants will be assessed for their impact on TF binding and cooperative configurations. Validation will rely on cross-dataset comparisons, known regulatory controls, and orthogonal data from published CRISPRi screens. This three-year initiative involves a multidisciplinary team of experts in transcriptional regulation, structural biology, computational genomics, imaging, and statistical genetics to ensure comprehensive model development, documentation, and tool deployment.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to advance the understanding of emergent transcription factor (TF) cooperativity at enhancers by generating comprehensive resources and quantitative models. The study will develop the TF-CoopDB, a database linking genomic binding sites with structural parameters, cooperative potential scores, and enhancer-gene linkages. Computational tools, including predictive software for binding configurations, agent-based simulations, and pipelines for analyzing transcriptional noise and variant effects, will be released as documented packages. Furthermore, the project will establish thermodynamic and machine learning models to predict enhancer activity, alongside a curated super-resolution imaging dataset and a catalog of disease-associated variants. By elucidating how molecular interactions drive mesoscale organization and transcriptional outcomes, this research addresses fundamental questions regarding collective molecular behaviors. These findings are expected to provide general principles for gene regulation, inform synthetic biology applications, and improve the interpretation of disease-relevant genetic variants. Dissemination will occur through peer-reviewed publications, workshops, and long-term maintenance of open-access repositories to ensure sustained community utility.
budget_and_resources: This three-year project requests $1,200,000 to support transdisciplinary synthesis research. Personnel costs, totaling $780,000, provide for two postdoctoral researchers focused on genomic integration and biophysical modeling, two graduate students for transcriptomics and imaging analysis, and a part-time software engineer to ensure tool sustainability. Computing resources of $180,000 are required for cloud-based machine learning, high-performance spatial simulations, and extensive data storage. Travel and collaboration expenses of $120,000 facilitate biannual team meetings, conference dissemination, and inter-laboratory exchanges essential for distributed synthesis efforts. An allocation of $60,000 supports annual training workshops and online tutorials, aligning with workforce development goals. Furthermore, $30,000 is designated for open science infrastructure, including repository fees and web hosting, while $30,000 covers publication costs, software licenses, and miscellaneous supplies. This budget structure prioritizes the human capital and computational infrastructure necessary to integrate large-scale datasets, ensuring that project outcomes remain accessible, robust, and impactful for the broader scientific community throughout the research period.

title: Integrative Modeling of Viral Capsid Geometry Through Cryo-EM and Sequence Data Analysis
abstract: Viral capsid assembly represents an emergent mesoscale process where protein subunits self-organize into precise icosahedral structures. This project investigates how local protein-protein interactions dictate global geometry by integrating cryo-EM structural data, protein sequences, assembly kinetics, and evolutionary information. It is hypothesized that emergent geometry arises from conformational switching at quasi-equivalent positions, allowing identical proteins to achieve specific curvature. The methodology employs coarse-grained molecular dynamics, graph-theoretical analysis, and machine learning to derive interaction rules from structural datasets. These models will be tested to determine if minimal rule sets can recapitulate observed capsid architectures. Furthermore, evolutionary analysis will examine how assembly constraints influence protein diversification, while deep mutational scanning links assembly defects to viral fitness. This interdisciplinary study aims to establish general principles of emergent assembly and predictive sequence-to-structure models. The resulting algorithms, simulation code, and curated datasets will be made publicly available to support future research in antiviral design and nanotechnology.
background_and_significance: Viral capsids serve as a model for understanding emergent mesoscale organization, where protein subunits self-assemble into precise icosahedral structures. Although the Caspar-Klug theory provides a geometric framework for these shells, the molecular rules governing specific assembly outcomes and polymorphism remain poorly understood. Current structural, sequence, and fitness databases offer vast, untapped resources for addressing these fundamental questions. This project aims to synthesize heterogeneous data from the EMDB, PDB, and MaveDB to bridge the gap between molecular interactions and global geometric assembly. The study will investigate the mechanisms of conformational switching, the predictability of T-number selection, and the evolutionary constraints on capsid proteins. By integrating structural, kinetic, and fitness data, this research seeks to establish a unified framework for mesoscale assembly. These findings may elucidate general principles applicable to diverse protein cages, providing insights into the collective behaviors that emerge at the critical 20–200 nanometer scale where atomistic and continuum descriptions often fail.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This study investigates the emergent mesoscale organization of viral capsid assembly through four interconnected research questions. It is hypothesized that capsid geometry arises from minimal local interaction rules, which may be extracted from structural data to predict global assembly outcomes. The project will analyze protein-protein interfaces from cryo-EM and PDB datasets to identify discrete conformational states and convergent evolutionary solutions. Furthermore, the study explores whether protein sequences encode conformational plasticity, using machine learning to predict T-number geometry from sequence features. Evolutionary constraints will be assessed by examining residue covariation and mutational epistasis, suggesting that assembly requirements impose distinct selective pressures on capsid proteins. Finally, the research examines kinetic pathways, proposing that assembly fidelity is governed by intermediate structures and rate-limiting nucleation steps. By integrating structural, evolutionary, and kinetic data, this project aims to establish a universal grammar of capsid assembly, providing mechanistic insights into how mesoscale organization emerges from molecular interactions.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates structural, sequence, and functional data from public repositories to analyze viral capsid assembly. Structural data from EMDB and PDB, alongside sequence information from UniProt and NCBI, will be harmonized into a relational PostgreSQL database. This framework will incorporate fitness measurements from MaveDB and kinetic parameters derived from systematic literature mining. Automated pipelines using Snakemake will ensure data quality and reproducibility. Computational analysis will employ graph-theoretical methods to characterize capsid topology and PDBe PISA algorithms to quantify protein-protein interfaces. Machine learning models, including gradient boosting and ESM-2 embeddings, will be trained to predict assembly properties from sequence features. Furthermore, coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations will test whether extracted interaction rules recapitulate observed assembly pathways. Evolutionary constraints will be assessed through direct coupling analysis and phylogenetic modeling. The study will validate these predictions via cross-family benchmarking and structural consistency checks, ultimately establishing a comprehensive framework for understanding the principles governing viral capsid formation.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to elucidate emergent mesoscale organization in viral capsids by integrating structural, sequence, kinetic, and evolutionary data. The study will produce the Capsid Assembly Database, a comprehensive resource for icosahedral viruses, alongside three open-source software packages: CapsidGraph for topological analysis, AssemblyPredict for machine learning-based assembly forecasting, and CapsidSim for coarse-grained dynamic modeling. These tools will facilitate the development of quantitative mechanistic models describing interaction grammars, sequence-assembly relationships, and evolutionary constraints. By establishing viral capsids as a model system, this research will identify general principles of mesoscale emergence applicable to bacterial microcompartments and engineered protein cages. Furthermore, the project will provide actionable insights for antiviral drug development and the rational design of nanotechnological delivery vehicles. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, community workshops, and long-term hosting via established repositories like EMBL-EBI. This synthesis framework is expected to provide a robust template for investigating complex assembly phenomena across diverse biological systems.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget of $950,000 over three years supports a multidisciplinary team dedicated to structural bioinformatics, machine learning, computational biophysics, and evolutionary biology. Personnel costs, totaling $720,000, facilitate the systematic analysis of capsid structures, the development of predictive assembly models, and the maintenance of sustainable research software. Computational requirements, estimated at $90,000, provide necessary cloud-based GPU and CPU resources for large-scale data processing, alongside secure database hosting and 50 TB of storage for project reproducibility. Travel and workshop allocations of $100,000 support quarterly team meetings, conference dissemination, and two specialized training workshops designed to maximize community engagement and tool adoption. Furthermore, $40,000 is designated for open science infrastructure, including long-term data archiving, professional documentation, and usability testing to ensure broad accessibility. These expenditures reflect the project’s commitment to synthesis-driven research, where human expertise and collaborative integration are essential for advancing the understanding of capsid assembly principles and ensuring the long-term impact of all generated outputs.

title: Integration of Structural and Lipidomic Data for Modeling Collective BAR Domain Behavior in Emergent Membrane Curvature Sensing
abstract: BAR domain proteins facilitate membrane curvature through collective mesoscale behaviors that emerge from oligomerization and remodeling processes. This project integrates structural biology, lipidomics, and biophysical datasets to investigate how these proteins generate 10–100 nm membrane deformations. It is hypothesized that cooperative oligomerization on curved membranes creates a positive feedback loop between protein binding and curvature generation. The methodology employs coarse-grained molecular dynamics, continuum mechanical modeling, and machine learning to correlate structural features with curvature preferences. By synthesizing data from the Protein Data Bank, LIPID MAPS, and the Human Protein Atlas, the study aims to connect in vitro emergent behaviors to in vivo membrane remodeling. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of curvature sensing and the identification of principles governing protein function. These findings may clarify mechanisms underlying endocytosis, cell division, and neurological pathologies. All developed algorithms, simulation code, and curated datasets will be made publicly available to support further research.
background_and_significance: Membrane curvature is a fundamental organizing principle in cell biology, yet the mechanisms by which Bin/Amphiphysin/Rvs (BAR) domains generate emergent mesoscale remodeling remain poorly understood. Although structural data characterize individual BAR domain dimers, these static snapshots fail to capture the collective behavior observed in ordered lattices and helical scaffolds. This project integrates fragmented datasets from the Protein Data Bank, LIPID MAPS, and LipidBank to investigate how cooperative binding and lipid heterogeneity drive curvature sensing. By synthesizing biophysical measurements of membrane remodeling kinetics with lipidomic profiles, the study aims to decode the principles governing these complex assemblies. Computational approaches, including machine learning and coarse-grained molecular dynamics, will be employed to bridge the gap between molecular structure and mesoscale organization. This research is expected to elucidate how BAR domain dysfunction contributes to neurological disorders and provide a framework for engineering membrane-remodeling proteins in synthetic biology, ultimately clarifying the emergent properties that facilitate essential cellular processes like endocytosis.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates the emergence of mesoscale properties through collective protein-membrane interactions, specifically focusing on BAR domain superfamily dynamics. Four research questions address how structural features, lipid composition, and evolutionary specialization govern curvature sensing and membrane remodeling. It is hypothesized that BAR domain curvature preferences are modulated by electrostatic potential and amphipathic helix insertion, while oligomerization propensity drives non-linear, cooperative binding behavior. Furthermore, membrane lipid composition, particularly phosphatidylinositol phosphate species and cholesterol content, is expected to regulate the nucleation and mechanical activity of these protein assemblies. The study will evaluate whether universal principles of cooperative binding apply across BAR, N-BAR, F-BAR, and I-BAR families, despite variations in spatial organization. Finally, these in vitro mechanisms will be correlated with in vivo localization and post-translational regulation. These hypotheses will be tested through meta-analysis of structural data from the PDB, lipid properties from LIPID MAPS, and cellular annotations from the Human Protein Atlas to characterize emergent mesoscale phenomena.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates heterogeneous data from structural biology, lipidomics, proteomics, and cell biology repositories to elucidate BAR domain-mediated membrane remodeling. Established databases, including the Protein Data Bank, LIPID MAPS, and the Human Protein Atlas, will provide the foundational datasets for this synthesis. Data harmonization will utilize standardized ontologies to ensure consistency in nomenclature and physical units across all parameters. The analytical framework employs coarse-grained molecular dynamics and continuum elasticity models to investigate BAR domain assembly and membrane deformation. Furthermore, machine learning architectures will be trained to predict curvature preferences based on structural, electrostatic, and sequence-derived features. Network analysis of protein-protein interactions will identify organizational principles within cellular complexes. Validation strategies rely on cross-validation, benchmarking against well-characterized proteins, and comparison with independent literature. This transdisciplinary study aims to synthesize existing molecular properties into a comprehensive model of emergent curvature sensing, ultimately providing a unified framework for understanding BAR domain function across diverse biological contexts.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to advance the understanding of emergent membrane curvature sensing through four primary deliverables. First, the BAR Domain Database (BAR-DB) will integrate structural features, lipid sensitivities, and localization data for over 200 proteins, providing a centralized resource for the research community. Second, validated multi-scale computational models, ranging from machine learning to continuum mechanics, will be developed to predict curvature preferences and membrane deformation. Third, the study will articulate quantitative principles governing collective BAR domain behavior, identifying structural determinants of cooperativity and lipid-dependent organization. Finally, a curated literature compendium will organize biophysical measurements to facilitate future experimental design. By elucidating how molecular properties drive mesoscale emergent phenomena, this work provides a framework for analyzing membrane remodeling in endocytosis, cell division, and neurological function. These findings will be disseminated through open-access publications, workshops, and sustainable digital repositories, ensuring that the developed tools and datasets remain accessible for hypothesis generation and synthetic biology applications.
budget_and_resources: The proposed project requires an annual budget of $535,000 to support transdisciplinary research across the BAR domain superfamily. Personnel costs include two postdoctoral researchers for structural analysis and membrane biophysics, two graduate students for data science and bioinformatics, and a research software engineer to ensure code sustainability. Principal investigators will provide scientific leadership and mentorship throughout the three-year duration. Computational requirements, estimated at $45,000 annually, utilize cloud-based infrastructure for large-scale simulations and machine learning, alongside database hosting and software licensing. Travel funds facilitate quarterly team meetings, conference dissemination, and specialized workshops to foster collaboration and professional development. Furthermore, $25,000 is allocated annually for training initiatives, including workshops and online tutorials, to promote community adoption of synthesis methods. Finally, $15,000 supports open science infrastructure, covering data publication, documentation, and reproducibility tools. This comprehensive budget ensures the necessary resources for high-impact, community-scale synthesis research while maintaining a commitment to accessible and reproducible scientific outputs.

title: Integration of Cryo-EM Structures and Clinical Data for Modeling Prion Fibril Architecture and Pathology
abstract: Prion strains exhibit distinct pathological properties, including incubation periods and tissue tropisms, which are thought to emerge from mesoscale fibril architectures rather than primary sequence variations. This project investigates how fibril structure dictates these emergent strain properties by integrating cryo-EM data from the EMDB, clinical cohorts, neuropathological descriptions, and UniProt sequences. It is hypothesized that strain-specific behaviors arise from fibril surface features, fragmentation propensities, and cellular interaction interfaces defined by core architecture. The methodology employs structural analysis of fibril polymorphs, machine learning to correlate architectural features with clinical phenotypes, and kinetic modeling of propagation. Comparative analysis across prion-like proteins, such as α-synuclein and tau, may reveal shared principles of strain determination. Expected outcomes include predictive models linking fibril architecture to emergent pathology and the identification of structural determinants for disease progression. These findings may inform future diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for neurodegenerative conditions, with all analytical pipelines and datasets released publicly.
background_and_significance: Prion diseases illustrate how identical protein sequences encode diverse phenotypes through distinct mesoscale structural conformations. This strain diversity, characterized by varying incubation periods and neuropathological profiles, suggests that biological information is encoded within three-dimensional assemblies spanning 10 to 1000 nanometers. While cryo-electron microscopy has provided high-resolution structures of various amyloid fibrils, a significant gap remains in connecting these architectures to emergent pathological properties. Current research is often siloed, separating structural biology from clinical and neuropathological datasets. This project proposes a systematic synthesis of existing structural data from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank with extensive clinical and neuropathological archives. By integrating these heterogeneous sources, this study aims to develop quantitative models that predict how specific fibril features influence disease progression and regional vulnerability. Such an approach may elucidate fundamental principles of biological information encoding, offering insights applicable to a broad spectrum of neurodegenerative conditions characterized by protein misfolding and strain-like behavior.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how mesoscale fibril architecture dictates strain-specific pathological properties across prion and prion-like proteins. The study addresses three primary questions regarding the structural determinants of clinical phenotypes, propagation kinetics, and conserved architectural principles. It is hypothesized that quantifiable features, such as core compactness and surface electrostatic profiles, predict disease duration and tissue tropism. Furthermore, fragmentation propensity and secondary nucleation efficiency are expected to govern strain replication and spatial spread patterns. The research also explores whether common structural descriptors, including twist periodicity and core burial, facilitate strain emergence across diverse amyloidogenic proteins like tau and α-synuclein. These hypotheses will be validated using existing cryo-EM structures from the EMDB and clinical data from established surveillance cohorts. Through cross-dataset validation and machine learning, this project aims to establish mathematical relationships between fibril architecture and pathology. Ultimately, the study may reveal whether biological information is encoded through universal structural principles within protein assembly architectures.
methods_and_approach:
This project integrates heterogeneous data from structural biology, clinical medicine, and neuropathology repositories to investigate the relationship between amyloid fibril architecture and disease phenotypes. The study will systematically aggregate approximately 200 high-resolution cryo-EM structures and associated atomic models from the EMDB and PDB. Clinical and neuropathological data will be extracted from established surveillance cohorts and brain bank studies, while sequence variants and transcriptomic datasets will be sourced from UniProt, ClinVar, and GEO. 

Data harmonization will utilize standardized ontologies, such as the Human Phenotype Ontology, to link structural descriptors—including twist, surface electrostatics, and interface stability—to clinical outcomes. The analytical framework will employ the Fibril Architecture Analysis Toolkit to extract geometric and energetic features for machine learning models. These models will evaluate whether mesoscale architecture predicts phenotypic variation. Furthermore, kinetic modeling will simulate fibril propagation dynamics. The study will be validated through rigorous cross-validation and independent testing, ultimately aiming to elucidate the structural determinants of protein misfolding diseases.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to advance the understanding of emergent prion strain properties through five primary deliverables. The PrionStrainDB will provide a publicly accessible, integrated database linking amyloid fibril structures to clinical and pathological phenotypes. The Fibril Architecture Analysis Toolkit (FAAT) will offer an open-source Python package for the automated extraction of structural features from cryo-EM data. Furthermore, machine learning models will be developed to predict clinical outcomes from structural descriptors, while a kinetic modeling framework will relate fibril architecture to propagation dynamics. These resources will be supported by comprehensive synthesis publications detailing the principles of mesoscale information encoding. By establishing quantitative structure-emergence relationships, this study will investigate how mesoscale organization dictates biological function beyond primary sequence. These findings are expected to provide insights into neurodegenerative disease mechanisms, inform diagnostic development, and identify potential therapeutic targets. Ultimately, these tools and frameworks will facilitate future research into protein assemblies, fostering a deeper understanding of emergent phenomena in molecular biology.
budget_and_resources: The project budget supports a multidisciplinary team, including two postdoctoral researchers, a graduate student, and a software engineer, to facilitate structural analysis, machine learning, and data curation. Principal investigators will provide essential oversight across prion biology, structural modeling, and neuropathology. Computational requirements include cloud-based elastic resources for large-scale analysis and institutional high-performance computing for intensive molecular dynamics. Persistent storage will ensure data accessibility and reproducibility. Travel funds are allocated for annual team meetings, conference dissemination, and collaborative laboratory visits to foster cross-disciplinary integration. A two-year workshop series will provide training on analytical pipelines and promote community engagement among structural biologists and clinicians. Open science infrastructure, including persistent identifiers and web-based interfaces, will ensure long-term tool adoption and FAIR compliance. Finally, publication fees and standard research supplies are included to support broad dissemination. This budget reflects the intellectually intensive nature of synthesis research, prioritizing personnel and collaborative infrastructure to integrate complex biological datasets.

title: Modeling Symmetry Breaking in Emergent Cell Polarity Through Integrated Imaging and Interactome Data Analysis
abstract: Cell polarity originates from protein localization networks that spontaneously break symmetry, representing a mesoscale phenomenon driven by molecular interactions. This project investigates how reaction-diffusion networks generate spatial organization within 1–10 μm domains from initially homogeneous distributions.
