The study integrates diverse datasets, including the Human Protein Atlas, BioGRID interaction networks, and phosphoproteomics from PhosphoSitePlus, to analyze polarity establishment. It is hypothesized that emergent polarity arises from positive feedback loops, mutual antagonism, and scaffolding interactions that amplify initial asymmetries. The methodology combines reaction-diffusion modeling, machine learning, and image analysis to identify the network motifs necessary for symmetry breaking. Furthermore, single-cell RNA-seq integration may clarify how expression heterogeneity influences polarity variability across different cell types. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of polarity dynamics, the identification of minimal network requirements, and principles for cellular engineering. These findings may provide insights into developmental biology, oncology, and tissue engineering, with all models and datasets released publicly.
background_and_significance: Cell polarity represents a fundamental emergent behavior where asymmetric organization arises spontaneously from homogeneous protein distributions. Although molecular components such as PAR proteins and Rho GTPases are well-characterized, a quantitative understanding of how these networks generate spatial organization remains elusive. Current theoretical frameworks, including reaction-diffusion models, often rely on simplified systems that fail to capture the complexity of cellular regulatory networks. This project aims to bridge the gap between molecular data and systems-level models by synthesizing heterogeneous datasets from resources like the Human Protein Atlas, BioGRID, and PhosphoSitePlus. By integrating these diverse data types, the study will develop predictive models of emergent polarity at the mesoscale. Such insights are expected to clarify the mechanisms underlying cancer metastasis, tissue engineering, and asymmetric stem cell division. Ultimately, this research will establish general principles of self-organization, providing a foundational framework for understanding how collective dynamics emerge from molecular interactions within complex biological systems.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This project investigates how reaction-diffusion networks of polarity proteins generate emergent mesoscale spatial organization from homogeneous distributions. The study addresses four research questions using existing public datasets to validate specific hypotheses regarding symmetry breaking, expression variability, evolutionary conservation, and predictive modeling. 

Minimal network motifs, including positive feedback, mutual antagonism, and scaffolding, are hypothesized to drive symmetry breaking. The research will correlate membrane-cytoplasm exchange rates, phosphorylation-mediated antagonism, and scaffold-mediated clustering with observed polarity patterns. Furthermore, the study examines how cell-to-cell expression variability influences the robustness of polarity, testing whether stoichiometric imbalances and expression noise correlate with domain positioning defects. 

Comparative analyses across cell types will determine if core network motifs are conserved or if distinct mechanisms predominate in specific contexts. Finally, machine learning models will be trained to predict polarity outcomes from integrated molecular and imaging data. Validation relies on cross-dataset comparisons, established positive controls, and literature-based verification to ensure robust, evidence-based conclusions regarding emergent biological organization.
methods_and_approach:
This project integrates heterogeneous data from public repositories to investigate polarity protein networks. The study synthesizes immunofluorescence images, protein-protein interactions, phosphoproteomics, gene expression, and structural data to construct a unified model of polarity establishment. Data harmonization utilizes UniProt mapping, Bayesian frameworks for interaction scoring, and standardized normalization pipelines for expression and imaging datasets. 

Analytical methods include partial differential equation models of protein dynamics, graph-theoretic network analysis, and machine learning to link molecular features to polarity outcomes. Automated image analysis pipelines will quantify asymmetry and domain dynamics. The research aims to test mechanistic hypotheses by parameterizing reaction-diffusion models with interaction kinetics and validating predictions against localization patterns and single-cell expression variability. This transdisciplinary approach identifies conserved versus specialized polarity mechanisms across epithelial, migrating, and stem cells. The project will culminate in a comprehensive synthesis of polarity regulation, supported by cross-validation against established phenotypes and literature benchmarks, ultimately providing predictive insights into the emergent properties of cellular polarity.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This synthesis project aims to advance the understanding of emergent cell polarity by integrating molecular-scale interactions with micrometer-scale spatial organization. The study will produce a comprehensive, publicly accessible database of polarity-associated proteins, interaction networks, and phosphorylation sites. Furthermore, parameterized reaction-diffusion models and machine learning tools will be developed to predict polarity outcomes and quantify symmetry-breaking mechanisms. By identifying minimal network motifs, the project will establish general principles of self-organization, such as positive feedback and mutual antagonism, which may apply to broader biological systems. These computational frameworks and automated image analysis pipelines are expected to bridge the gap between molecular binding events and cellular-scale behaviors. Beyond polarity, the findings will provide insights into cancer progression, tissue engineering, and developmental morphogenesis. The project will disseminate these resources through peer-reviewed publications, workshops, and sustainable repositories, ultimately providing the research community with a robust infrastructure to investigate emergent phenomena and validate quantitative predictions in diverse biological contexts.
budget_and_resources: The project budget prioritizes personnel to facilitate data integration and computational analysis, reflecting the study’s focus on synthesis rather than experimental data generation. Two postdoctoral researchers will lead machine learning development, database construction, and mechanistic reaction-diffusion modeling. A graduate student will develop image analysis pipelines, while a research software engineer will ensure code sustainability and infrastructure maintenance. Computational requirements include cloud resources for large-scale processing and high-performance computing for systematic parameter exploration. Dedicated storage will ensure long-term data persistence and accessibility. Travel funds support essential in-person collaboration, conference dissemination, and inter-institutional visits to integrate complex findings. Furthermore, the budget covers a methods workshop and a scientific symposium to foster community engagement and training. Open science infrastructure, including repository fees and documentation hosting, will ensure the transparency of all outputs. Finally, open-access publication fees are allocated to maximize the reach of the anticipated findings within the broader scientific community.

title: Integration of Structural and Proteomic Data for Decoding Emergent Specificity in Ubiquitin Chain Recognition
abstract: The ubiquitin code suggests that signaling specificity emerges from mesoscale polyubiquitin chain conformations rather than simple receptor binding. This project investigates how chain ensembles spanning 5–50 nm facilitate signaling outcomes unattainable by monoubiquitin. By integrating structural data from the Protein Data Bank, proteomics from PhosphoSitePlus, and interactomes from BioGRID, the study examines how chain-specific conformational ensembles enable avidity-based discrimination by multivalent receptors. Computational methods, including molecular dynamics simulations and machine learning, will be employed to correlate structural features with receptor selectivity across K48, K63, linear, and branched chains. Furthermore, network analysis and disease mutation data will link disrupted recognition to pathological phenotypes. This collaborative effort aims to establish predictive models for ubiquitin signaling and identify key conformational determinants of receptor binding. These findings may inform the development of targeted protein degradation therapies, with all analysis pipelines and curated datasets being made publicly available to the scientific community.
background_and_significance: Ubiquitination regulates diverse eukaryotic processes through the attachment of ubiquitin chains, which encode distinct cellular fates via specific linkage types. Although individual ubiquitin-binding domains exhibit limited selectivity, cellular responses remain highly specific, suggesting that emergent mesoscale properties of polyubiquitin chains dictate signaling outcomes. This project investigates how conformational ensembles and multivalent receptor interactions generate this specificity, addressing a critical gap in current ubiquitin biology. By integrating heterogeneous data from the Protein Data Bank, proteomic repositories, and molecular dynamics simulations, this study will elucidate the relationship between chain dynamics and receptor selectivity. The research aims to clarify how chain length, branching, and disease-associated mutations influence signaling fidelity. These findings are expected to provide mechanistic models for the rational design of targeted protein degradation technologies, such as PROTACs. Ultimately, this synthesis research may reveal how dysregulated ubiquitin recognition contributes to the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative, oncological, and inflammatory disorders, thereby identifying new therapeutic opportunities.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how mesoscale polyubiquitin chain conformations generate emergent signaling specificity unattainable by monoubiquitin. The study addresses four primary research questions regarding conformational signatures, receptor binding selectivity, chain-length modulation, and disease-associated mutations. First, conformational ensembles for various linkage types will be characterized using structural data from the Protein Data Bank and molecular dynamics simulations, with validation provided by NMR and SAXS profiles. Second, machine learning models will be developed to determine if receptor selectivity correlates with the geometric complementarity between binding sites and chain conformations. Third, the influence of chain length on specificity will be evaluated, testing the hypothesis that a critical threshold of three to four ubiquitins facilitates multivalent receptor engagement. Finally, the impact of disease-linked mutations on recognition interfaces will be analyzed to correlate altered selectivity with specific clinical phenotypes. These integrated analyses are expected to establish a predictive framework for the ubiquitin code, elucidating the mechanistic basis of signaling specificity.
methods_and_approach: This study integrates heterogeneous data from structural, proteomic, interactomic, and functional genomic repositories to characterize ubiquitin-dependent signaling. Structural data from the Protein Data Bank and BMRB will be combined with molecular dynamics trajectories and AlphaFold2 predictions to map conformational landscapes. Proteomic datasets, including PhosphoSitePlus and quantitative mass spectrometry, will be harmonized with BioGRID interactome data and CRISPR-based functional screens. A unified relational database will employ ontology-based annotations, utilizing UniProt identifiers and FATCAT structural alignments to ensure consistency. Computational pipelines will extract conformational descriptors, such as Euler angles and solvent-accessible surface areas, to facilitate principal component analysis and Gaussian mixture modeling. Machine learning architectures, including graph neural networks and transformer-based models, will be trained to predict receptor-chain binding selectivity. Network topology metrics and structural bioinformatics tools, such as HADDOCK and Rosetta, will further elucidate functional modules and mutation effects. Finally, model performance will be validated against orthogonal experimental data, established positive controls, and existing biochemical literature.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to elucidate emergent specificity in ubiquitin signaling by integrating structural, conformational, and functional data into the UbiChainAtlas database. This resource will provide curated polyubiquitin chain structures, binding affinities, and disease mutation annotations to facilitate systematic analysis. Concurrently, a machine learning tool, the UbiSpecificity Predictor, will be developed to estimate receptor selectivity based on structural features. Quantitative models will describe conformational ensembles, while formalized principles will define how mesoscale properties dictate chain recognition. These outputs will generate comprehensive maps linking receptor mutations to disease phenotypes, offering mechanistic insights into clinical variants. By establishing relationships between molecular features and mesoscale properties, this study addresses fundamental questions regarding emergent signaling phenomena. The resulting framework is expected to advance targeted protein degradation, synthetic biology, and the interpretation of pathogenic variants. All data, models, and software will be disseminated through open-access platforms, ensuring long-term utility for the broader scientific community.
budget_and_resources: The proposed three-year budget of $960,000 supports a synthesis-focused research program requiring specialized personnel, computational infrastructure, and collaborative dissemination. Personnel costs, comprising 75% of the total, fund two postdoctoral researchers for structural bioinformatics and machine learning, two graduate students for data integration and biological analysis, and a research software engineer to maintain project sustainability. Computational requirements include $90,000 for cloud-based machine learning model training and national high-performance computing resources for molecular dynamics trajectories. Travel funds facilitate quarterly cross-institutional collaboration meetings and trainee presentations at major scientific conferences. Furthermore, $45,000 is allocated for annual workshops and training materials to promote community engagement with synthesis methods. Open science infrastructure, including database hosting and Zenodo archiving, ensures long-term data accessibility. Finally, $15,000 covers open-access publication fees and specialized software licenses. This budget structure is designed to maximize scientific output and provide comprehensive training in collaborative, data-driven research practices while maintaining a focus on computational synthesis.

title: Integration of Spatial Transcriptomics and RNA Structure Data for Modeling Emergent mRNA Targeting Networks
abstract: mRNA localization facilitates emergent spatial gene expression patterns through mesoscale RNA-protein networks, achieving precision beyond individual binding events. This project integrates spatial transcriptomics from the Human Cell Atlas, SHAPE-MaP structural data, ENCODE eCLIP interaction datasets, and Human Protein Atlas localization profiles to decode these mechanisms. The study investigates how RNA-binding protein (RBP) networks generate subcellular targeting within 100–1000 nm granules. It is hypothesized that emergent localization arises from combinatorial RBP binding, RNA secondary structure, and phase separation that integrates multiple weak signals. Computational methods, including machine learning and spatial statistics, will model targeting complexes and quantify localization precision. By incorporating translation data, the research will link localization to local protein synthesis across diverse cell types. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent RNA targeting and identified principles for engineering gene expression. These findings may provide insights into neurological disease mechanisms and the development of mRNA-based therapeutics, with all data and pipelines released publicly.
background_and_significance: The spatial organization of mRNA at the mesoscale represents an emergent biological phenomenon where collective RNA-protein interactions generate subcellular precision. While reductionist studies have identified individual localization elements and binding proteins, they fail to explain how weak, promiscuous molecular interactions achieve high specificity. This project will synthesize diverse, publicly available datasets—including spatial transcriptomics, eCLIP interaction maps, and transcriptome-wide secondary structure data—to address this paradox. By integrating these resources, the study aims to define the combinatorial logic of RNA-binding proteins and the role of RNA structure in governing localization. This research is expected to elucidate how phase-separated RNA granules facilitate local protein synthesis, a process critical for neuronal plasticity and cellular polarity. Furthermore, the findings may clarify the mechanisms underlying neurodegenerative diseases linked to granule dysfunction. Ultimately, this integrative approach will transform descriptive spatial data into a predictive framework, providing essential insights for optimizing mRNA-based therapeutics and understanding fundamental principles of cellular organization.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates how RNA-binding protein (RBP) networks generate emergent mRNA targeting at the mesoscale. The study addresses four hypotheses regarding the mechanisms of subcellular precision. First, it is hypothesized that mRNA localization is determined by combinatorial RBP binding codes rather than individual interactions, with specificity arising from clusters of 3–5 binding sites. Second, RNA secondary structure is expected to modulate RBP accessibility, sequestering non-functional motifs within base-paired regions. Third, RNA granule composition may emerge from shared RBP-mRNA interaction networks, facilitating phase separation through collective binding profiles. Finally, the study explores whether mRNA localization and local translation are coordinated by shared RBP regulators, influencing protein synthesis efficiency. These hypotheses will be tested by integrating ENCODE eCLIP data, spatial transcriptomics, SHAPE-MaP reactivity, and ribosome profiling. The findings are expected to establish a predictive framework for RNA organization, elucidating the structural grammar and regulatory coupling that govern subcellular mRNA distribution and subsequent protein synthesis.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates diverse public datasets to elucidate the regulatory mechanisms governing subcellular mRNA localization. The study synthesizes spatial transcriptomics, RBP-RNA interaction maps, RNA structure profiles, and protein localization data to construct a comprehensive regulatory framework. Data harmonization involves mapping transcripts to GENCODE v38, implementing platform-specific normalization, and applying rigorous quality control to ensure cross-dataset consistency. A multi-modal deep learning architecture will be developed to predict localization patterns by integrating sequence, structure, and RBP binding features. Furthermore, network analysis and spatial statistics will characterize RBP-mRNA interactions and subcellular distribution patterns. Structure-function integration will assess how RNA accessibility influences RBP binding and regulatory outcomes. The model’s predictive accuracy will be validated through cross-platform testing, established positive controls, and evolutionary conservation analysis. This transdisciplinary approach is expected to reveal the combinatorial code of RNA localization, providing insights into the spatial organization of the transcriptome and the emergent properties of RNA-protein regulatory networks.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to advance the understanding of mesoscale RNA localization by producing integrated datasets, computational tools, and mechanistic models. The RNA Localization Atlas will unify mRNA patterns, RBP binding profiles, and translation metrics for 15,000 human genes. Three software packages—LocoPredict, GranuleNet, and StructureBind—will be released to facilitate predictive modeling of localization and granule composition. Quantitative models will characterize the combinatorial RBP code, structural grammar, and network architecture governing RNA assembly. These findings are expected to elucidate emergent properties such as specificity amplification, robustness, and phase behavior. The research will provide insights into RNA biology, membraneless organelle formation, and neuronal synaptic plasticity. Furthermore, the project will identify how RBP mutations contribute to neurodegenerative diseases, potentially guiding mRNA therapeutic design. All data and tools will be disseminated through open-access publications, permanent repositories, and annual workshops to ensure long-term sustainability and support future investigations into the principles of cellular organization and comparative biology.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget allocates $960,000 over three years to support a personnel-intensive synthesis project focused on computational biology and RNA research. Approximately 75% of the funding sustains a multidisciplinary team, including postdoctoral researchers and graduate students, tasked with developing machine learning architectures, integrating spatial transcriptomics, and performing network analysis. Computing resources, comprising 9% of the budget, provide necessary GPU access for model training and 50TB of cloud storage for large-scale data management. Travel and workshop expenditures, totaling 11%, facilitate essential cross-disciplinary collaboration, conference dissemination, and the training of 20–30 participants annually through NCEMS workshops. Furthermore, 3% of the budget supports open science infrastructure, ensuring the long-term accessibility of the RNA Localization Atlas and associated software tools. These investments are expected to yield validated computational models and integrated datasets, ultimately enhancing the utility of public data. This strategic allocation ensures the project remains sustainable, reproducible, and impactful within the broader scientific community.

title: Emergent Mechanics of Bacterial Microcompartments: Integrating Structural and Metabolic Data for Encapsulated Pathway Efficiency Modeling
abstract: Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) function as metabolic organelles that utilize protein shells to encapsulate enzymes, potentially enhancing pathway efficiency and selectivity beyond cytoplasmic capabilities. This study integrates structural biology, metabolomics, and systems biology to decode how mesoscale shell architecture influences metabolic flux, toxic intermediate sequestration, and substrate selectivity. Data from the EMDB, MetaboLights, BRENDA, and NCBI will be synthesized to evaluate the hypothesis that emergent efficiency results from shell pore selectivity, enzyme co-localization, and internal environment optimization. The computational framework combines finite element diffusion modeling, kinetic pathway analysis, and machine learning to correlate shell composition with functional outcomes. Comparative analysis across carboxysomes and metabolosomes aims to identify shared principles of encapsulated metabolism. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of BMC efficiency and design principles for synthetic compartments. All analysis pipelines and curated datasets will be made publicly available to support further research in metabolic engineering and synthetic biology.
background_and_significance: Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) are proteinaceous organelles that organize metabolic pathways within prokaryotic cells. These structures, ranging from 40 to 200 nanometers, encapsulate enzymes to create distinct biochemical environments. While structural data from the Protein Data Bank and Electron Microscopy Data Bank have characterized shell architectures, the mechanisms governing emergent system-level functions remain poorly understood. This project will integrate structural, kinetic, and genomic data from resources such as BRENDA, MetaboLights, and NCBI GenBank to investigate how mesoscale organization influences metabolic flux and pathway regulation. By synthesizing these fragmented datasets, the study aims to elucidate how shell permeability and enzyme encapsulation collectively determine cellular phenotypes. This research will provide a quantitative framework for understanding BMC function, offering insights into fundamental biological organization and potential applications in metabolic engineering. Ultimately, this transdisciplinary approach will bridge the gap between molecular structure and system-level behavior, addressing critical questions regarding the emergent properties of these complex bacterial organelles.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates the emergent properties of bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) by addressing three interconnected research questions regarding mesoscale organization. The study examines how shell architecture dictates selective permeability, hypothesizing that the ratio of shell protein paralogs and non-random pore clustering facilitate substrate retention. These hypotheses will be tested by integrating structural data from the Protein Data Bank with genomic information from NCBI and metabolic data from BRENDA. Furthermore, the research explores how enzyme co-localization generates kinetic advantages through substrate channeling, intermediate concentration, and toxic sequestration. These mechanisms will be evaluated using finite element diffusion models and validated against metabolomics and fitness data. Finally, the study seeks to identify universal principles governing BMC function across diverse metabolic pathways by analyzing scaling relationships between shell volume and enzyme loading. This synthesis is expected to provide a quantitative framework for understanding compartmentalized metabolism, ultimately informing the design of synthetic organelles with predictable functional outcomes.
methods_and_approach:
This project integrates multi-omics data to characterize bacterial microcompartment (BMC) systems through structural biology, enzymology, and genomics. Data will be aggregated from established repositories, including the Protein Data Bank, BRENDA, and MetaboLights, to construct a unified database. UniProt identifiers will facilitate cross-platform mapping, while BioPython and MDAnalysis will standardize structural parameters such as pore geometry and electrostatic potential. 

Computational analysis will employ finite element modeling to simulate metabolite diffusion through shell pores by solving Nernst-Planck equations. These permeability coefficients will inform ordinary differential equation models of encapsulated pathways, enabling the assessment of emergent metabolic properties. Furthermore, machine learning models will be trained to predict pore selectivity based on structural and sequence features. The study will validate these predictions against existing experimental datasets and well-characterized BMC systems. This interdisciplinary approach aims to elucidate the relationship between shell architecture and metabolic function, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding BMC-mediated compartmentalization across diverse bacterial species.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to advance the understanding of bacterial microcompartment (BMC) function by producing four categories of deliverables: an integrated database, computational models, machine learning tools, and quantitative design principles. The database will aggregate structural, kinetic, and genomic data for community use via programmatic access. Validated computational models will simulate shell permeability and pathway flux, while machine learning tools will predict pore selectivity and BMC classification. These outputs will formalize principles governing mesoscale emergent properties, such as selectivity, kinetic enhancement, and robustness. By establishing BMCs as a model for mesoscale organization, this research will inform metabolic engineering, evolutionary biology, and synthetic biology. The project will facilitate future hypothesis generation and method development through open-access repositories and community-driven governance. Dissemination will occur through peer-reviewed publications, workshops, and conference presentations. Ultimately, these efforts are expected to provide a foundational framework for studying compartmentalized metabolism, ensuring long-term utility through persistent identifiers and integration with existing biological databases.
budget_and_resources: The proposed three-year budget of $1,085,000 supports a transdisciplinary synthesis project requiring significant personnel, computational, and collaborative resources. Two postdoctoral researchers will conduct structural bioinformatics, finite element modeling, kinetic analysis, and machine learning, while two graduate students will contribute to analysis modules to facilitate workforce development. A part-time research software engineer will ensure code sustainability, documentation, and infrastructure maintenance. Computational requirements include $90,000 for cloud-based GPU instances, high-performance computing allocations, and long-term data storage. Travel funding of $60,000 supports annual working group meetings, conference dissemination, and inter-laboratory collaboration visits. Furthermore, $40,000 is allocated for two workshops to train researchers in modeling approaches and discuss project findings. Open science infrastructure, including repository hosting and open-access publication fees, is budgeted at $15,000 to ensure community accessibility. This investment is expected to produce sustainable databases, computational tools, and trained personnel, thereby advancing molecular and cellular biology research beyond the initial funding period.

title: Integration of Super-Resolution and Signaling Data for Modeling Emergent Receptor Clustering in T Cell Activation Thresholds
abstract: T cell activation is regulated by receptor clustering at immune synapses, where mesoscale spatial organization influences signaling thresholds beyond simple receptor occupancy. This project integrates super-resolution imaging from the Image Data Resource, phosphoproteomics from PRIDE, structural data from the PDB, and single-cell transcriptomics from the Human Cell Atlas to decode these emergent activation mechanisms. The study investigates how microclusters ranging from 100 to 500 nm establish activation thresholds through phosphatase segregation, kinase recruitment, and feedback loops. Computational methods, including spatial stochastic simulations and machine learning, will be employed to correlate cluster properties with T cell fate decisions across diverse subsets. This transdisciplinary approach aims to generate quantitative models of activation thresholds and identify critical cluster features that dictate immune responses. The resulting models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be made publicly available to facilitate further research into the principles of immune modulation, immunotherapy, and autoimmune disease pathology.
background_and_significance: T cell activation is a critical immunological decision-making process governed by the mesoscale organization of T cell receptor (TCR) microclusters at the immune synapse. While the kinetic segregation model suggests that TCR triggering relies on the exclusion of CD45 from these clusters, the quantitative relationship between cluster geometry and signaling thresholds remains poorly defined. Current research often examines imaging, phosphoproteomics, and transcriptional responses in isolation, failing to integrate these components into a cohesive model of cellular fate. This project will synthesize publicly available data from the Image Data Resource, PRIDE, and the Human Cell Atlas to bridge these knowledge gaps. By parameterizing computational models with high-resolution structural and spatial data, the study will investigate how collective microcluster properties dictate downstream signaling networks. Ultimately, this synthesis is expected to elucidate the fundamental principles of mesoscale emergence, providing a quantitative framework for optimizing immunotherapies and understanding the mechanisms underlying T cell activation, anergy, and exhaustion.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates the mesoscale organization of T cell activation through three interconnected research questions, utilizing existing public datasets to test specific mechanistic hypotheses. The study first examines how cluster geometry, including radius, density, and inter-cluster spacing, determines signaling thresholds by analyzing super-resolution imaging and phosphoproteomic data. Second, the research explores whether positive and negative feedback loops, involving LAT phosphorylation, actin stabilization, and ATP depletion, generate bistable activation switches. These dynamics will be evaluated by integrating temporal phosphoproteomic and metabolic datasets. Third, the project assesses how variations in protein expression and membrane composition across T cell subsets influence activation sensitivity, correlating transcriptomic profiles with functional signaling outputs. All hypotheses will be validated through cross-dataset consistency, using computational models parameterized by structural data to test predictions against independent imaging and omics repositories. This synthesis is expected to define the quantitative relationships between cluster organization and cellular decision-making, providing generalizable principles for emergent signaling in biological systems.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates heterogeneous data from six public repositories to characterize T cell receptor (TCR) signaling across multiple biological scales. The study synthesizes super-resolution imaging, phosphoproteomics, structural data, and single-cell transcriptomics to construct a comprehensive model of immune synapse dynamics. Data harmonization involves standardized image processing via OME-NGFF and uniform phosphoproteomic re-analysis, followed by cross-modality alignment using a hierarchical Bayesian framework. Computational methods include automated image segmentation, spatial stochastic simulations using Smoldyn, and machine learning models to predict activation states from cluster geometry. Network inference will further identify feedback loops and signaling cascades. Validation strategies rely on cross-dataset testing, known biological controls, and cross-species comparisons using ImmGen data. This transdisciplinary effort, supported by a team of immunologists, computational biologists, and data scientists, is expected to elucidate the relationship between mesoscale organization and signaling output. The project will proceed over three years, culminating in the release of integrated models and documentation of emergent signaling bistability.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project aims to advance the understanding of emergent T cell activation through five primary deliverables. Integrated datasets will harmonize TCR microcluster properties with phosphoproteomic and transcriptomic profiles, while open-source computational tools, including image analysis packages and stochastic simulation frameworks, will facilitate standardized data processing. Mechanistic models formulated as differential equations will investigate how cluster geometry and feedback loops regulate signaling thresholds and bistability. Furthermore, predictive machine learning frameworks will be developed to correlate cluster configurations with T cell fate. These efforts are expected to elucidate how mesoscale spatial organization generates emergent signaling properties, such as digital activation thresholds. Beyond T cell biology, the established paradigms and analytical methods may be applied to diverse receptor systems where clustering influences cellular outcomes. This synthesis provides a foundation for future research in rational immunotherapy design, autoimmune pathology, and synthetic biology. All findings, datasets, and software will be disseminated through open-access channels to ensure long-term scientific utility.
budget_and_resources: The proposed annual budget of $620,000 supports a synthesis-focused research program, with no funding allocated for primary data generation. Personnel costs, totaling $480,000, provide for two postdoctoral researchers, two graduate students, and a research software engineer to conduct computational modeling, image analysis, and data integration. Four principal investigators will provide scientific direction and mentorship through institutional cost-sharing. Computing resources, requiring $60,000 annually, facilitate large-scale image processing, machine learning, and high-performance simulations via cloud and specialized infrastructure. Travel funds of $40,000 support quarterly working group meetings, conference dissemination, and collaborative laboratory visits to foster transdisciplinary engagement. An additional $25,000 is dedicated to annual synthesis workshops, monthly webinars, and the development of accessible training materials. Finally, $15,000 is allocated for open science infrastructure, covering repository archiving, documentation hosting, continuous integration, and open-access publication fees. This financial structure ensures the project maintains robust, reproducible, and publicly accessible computational tools while advancing the core mission of the NCEMS.

title: Integration of Damage Proteomics and Chromatin Data for Modeling Emergent DNA Repair Pathway Choice
abstract: DNA repair pathway selection functions as an emergent decision-making process, where chromatin context, cell cycle stage, and damage characteristics collectively dictate repair mechanisms. This project aims to decode these mesoscale phenomena by integrating DNA damage proteomics from PRIDE, ChIP-seq data from ENCODE, ATAC-seq chromatin accessibility profiles, and cell cycle proteomics. The study investigates how protein assemblies at damage sites facilitate pathway selection beyond individual protein-DNA interactions. It is hypothesized that emergent choices arise from competitive recruitment kinetics, chromatin-mediated accessibility, and feedback loops that amplify initial commitment. The methodology employs kinetic modeling, machine learning, and network analysis to predict pathway outcomes, further validated by COSMIC mutation signatures. Comparative analysis across diverse cell types will elucidate how repair decisions adapt to varying genomic contexts. Expected outcomes include predictive models of pathway selection and identified principles for modulating repair, which may inform future cancer therapies and genome editing strategies.
background_and_significance: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) pose significant genomic risks, necessitating precise repair via pathways such as homologous recombination and non-homologous end joining. This selection process reflects emergent mesoscale behavior, where collective properties of repair foci—spanning 100–1000 nanometers—transcend individual molecular interactions. Although extensive data exist within repositories like PRIDE, ENCODE, and COSMIC, these resources remain fragmented, preventing a comprehensive understanding of how mesoscale assemblies dictate pathway choice. This project will synthesize multi-omic datasets, including proteomics, ChIP-seq, and chromatin accessibility maps, to model the kinetic and structural parameters governing repair decisions. By integrating these disparate data, the study aims to elucidate how chromatin features and protein recruitment dynamics influence repair outcomes across diverse cell types. Such insights may improve cancer therapeutic strategies and enhance the precision of genome editing technologies. Ultimately, this interdisciplinary synthesis provides a robust framework for understanding how complex biological assemblies generate emergent decision-making, addressing critical gaps in current DNA repair research.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: This project investigates the emergent nature of DNA repair pathway choice at the mesoscale by addressing three interconnected research questions. First, the study examines how competitive recruitment kinetics of 53BP1 and BRCA1 generate pathway commitment. It is hypothesized that this choice emerges from kinetic competition involving initial recruitment rates, cooperative binding, and feedback loops. Predictions will be tested by integrating PRIDE proteomics and ENCODE ChIP-seq data to correlate recruitment ratios with pathway outcomes. Second, the research explores how chromatin accessibility landscapes bias selection. A model integrating histone modifications, nucleosome positioning, and 3D genome organization is expected to predict pathway usage more accurately than local sequence features alone. Third, the study evaluates how cell type-specific contexts modulate these rules. By synthesizing multi-omics data, the project aims to determine if universal mechanisms exist across cell types. These analyses will elucidate whether repair foci function as analog sensors or digital switches, establishing a framework for understanding emergent decision-making.
methods_and_approach: This project integrates multi-omics data from public repositories, including proteomics, chromatin biology, genomics, and cell biology, to investigate DNA repair pathway dynamics. Proteomics datasets from PRIDE and ProteomeXchange will characterize protein recruitment and post-translational modifications, while ENCODE and 4D Nucleome data will provide chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, and 3D genome organization. Genomic outcomes will be assessed using mutation signatures from COSMIC, alongside cell-type-specific expression data from the Human Protein Atlas. Data harmonization will involve mapping to GRCh38 coordinates, standardizing protein identifiers, and applying batch effect corrections to ensure cross-study comparability. Computational efforts will employ ordinary differential equation models to describe repair factor recruitment kinetics, alongside machine learning frameworks to predict pathway choice based on chromatin features. These models will be validated through cross-dataset testing and comparison with known biological controls. This transdisciplinary approach, supported by expertise in DNA repair, proteomics, and systems biology, is expected to elucidate the regulatory mechanisms governing DNA damage response pathways.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This project establishes a comprehensive framework to investigate emergent DNA repair pathway choice through five primary deliverables. First, RepairChoiceDB will integrate multi-omic data, including proteomics and chromatin features, to standardize pathway annotations across diverse cell types. Second, kinetic ordinary differential equation models will quantify competitive repair factor recruitment, capturing bistable dynamics and cell cycle-dependent variations. Third, the PathwayPredict machine learning tool will provide genomic pathway probability predictions, offering insights into feature importance and confidence intervals. Fourth, a chromatin feature atlas will map pathway preferences across the human genome, identifying regions of strong bias. Finally, containerized analysis pipelines will ensure reproducibility across all computational workflows. This research characterizes DNA repair as a mesoscale emergent phenomenon, where collective protein behavior dictates pathway selection. These findings are expected to inform cancer therapeutics, genome editing strategies, and studies of aging. By integrating diverse biological data, this project provides a scalable methodology for analyzing complex cellular processes and facilitating future mechanistic discovery.
budget_and_resources: The proposed budget supports a transdisciplinary synthesis project requiring significant personnel, computational, and collaborative resources. A full-time computational biologist will lead algorithm development and machine learning, while a chromatin biologist will ensure biological validity. Two graduate research assistants will contribute to project components, and a research software engineer will maintain production-quality tools and reproducibility standards. Computational requirements include cloud-based GPU instances for large-scale data processing and long-term storage for model artifacts. Travel funds are allocated for annual working group meetings, conference presentations, and collaborative visits to facilitate integration. Outreach efforts include a methods training workshop, a scientific symposium, and the development of professional training materials. Open science infrastructure, including DOI registration, documentation hosting, and continuous integration, will ensure long-term reproducibility. Finally, publication fees and software licenses support the dissemination of findings. This budget reflects the intellectual and technical demands of integrating heterogeneous datasets to elucidate emergent DNA repair pathway choices.
